0.title: Nehemiah: The God Who Remembers
0.overview:
The message. Nehemiah is the story of God rebuilding a broken people, and of how far even a rebuilt people still falls short. The wall of Jerusalem goes up in fifty-two days against mockery and plots, so plainly that the enemies “perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God” (6:16). Then the law is read, and the people bind themselves by covenant to obey it. Yet by the time Nehemiah returns from a stay at the Persian court, nearly every promise has been broken. Stone walls could keep enemies out; they could not change a heart. The book teaches God’s people to pray, to build and to keep his word, and leaves them waiting for the King and the new covenant that only God could give.

Background: the world of the book. Nearly a century and a half after Nebuchadnezzar burned Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, the Persian Empire ruled from India to Egypt. Exiles had gone home under Cyrus about 538 BC, the temple had been rebuilt, and Ezra had come to teach the law in 458 BC. But Judah was still a small, poor district of the province “Beyond the River”, its capital in ruins. Under this same king, Artaxerxes I, an attempt to rebuild its walls had been stopped by force (Ezra 4:21–23). Round it lay jealous neighbours: Sanballat, governor of Samaria to the north; Tobiah, an official in Ammon to the east; Geshem the Arab to the south; and the men of Ashdod to the west (4:7).

Background: the writer. The book opens “The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah” (1:1), and much of it (chapters 1–7, parts of 12, and 13) is his own memoir in the first person. Nehemiah was a Jew, probably born in exile, who rose to be cupbearer to the king at Susa, the winter palace where Esther had been queen a generation earlier. A cupbearer served the king’s wine: a post of great trust and close access. Other parts, especially chapters 8–10 and the registers, are told in the third person or drawn from temple records. In the Hebrew Bible Ezra and Nehemiah are one book, and Jewish tradition held that Ezra wrote it and Nehemiah finished it. Many scholars think a later editor joined the memoirs and records, since the priestly list of 12:22 reaches into the reign of Darius II. This commentary reads it as faithful history built on Nehemiah’s memoir and genuine records, compiled not long after the events.

When it happened. Nehemiah heard the news in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, about 445 BC (1:1). He arrived as governor that year, finished the wall in fifty-two days (6:15), and governed twelve years (5:14). About 433 BC he went back to the Persian court, and “after some time” returned to find the reforms undone (13:6–7). Letters found at Elephantine in Egypt, written about 407 BC, name the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria. Malachi seems to have preached at about this time, against the same sins. The last chapter of Nehemiah is the latest history the Old Testament tells.

How to read it. Nehemiah is history, to be believed and learned from. Its lists are not filler: for families rebuilding their lives, a name on the register was a title deed. Listen for the short prayers that break into the story, and for the word that runs through them, remember. Nehemiah begins by asking God to “Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses” (1:8) and ends, “Remember me, O my God, for good” (13:31).

How the book makes its case. The book tells of a wall rebuilt [1–7], a people renewed by the word [8–10], and a city dedicated, then found failing [11–13]. Nehemiah prays for four months before he speaks to the king, who grants his request, “for the good hand of my God was upon me” (2:8) [1–2]. Priests and goldsmiths, rulers and daughters each take a stretch of the wall [3], and meet mockery and threats with prayer and guard duty [4]. The worse danger is within: the rich are enslaving their poorer brothers for debt, and Nehemiah, who as governor “did not do so, because of the fear of God” (5:15), makes them give it back [5]. Plots against him fail and the wall is finished [6–7]. Then Ezra reads the law, the Levites give the sense, and the weeping people are told, “the joy of the LORD is your strength” (8:10); they keep the Feast of Booths [8]. A great prayer tells Israel’s whole history as the story of a God “ready to forgive, gracious and merciful” who “did not forsake them” (9:17), and the people sign a covenant to keep his law, his Sabbath and his house [9–10]. The city is peopled, and the wall dedicated with two choirs walking on top of it until “the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away” (12:43) [11–12]. Then Nehemiah returns to find Tobiah the Ammonite lodged in a temple storeroom, the Sabbath a market day and the marriages of Ezra’s day back again, and has to ask, “Why is the house of God forsaken?” (13:11) [13].

A handbook for leaders? Nehemiah is often read as a manual of leadership. He is indeed a striking leader, and we are meant to learn from his prayer, courage and refusal to profit from his office. Others read his memoir as self-justifying. Neither does the book justice. Its hero is “the God of heaven” (2:20), whose good hand is on the work. And Nehemiah’s prayers to be remembered are not claims to have earned God’s favour: in the same breath he asks, “spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love” (13:22). This commentary’s view is that Nehemiah is a real example of godly service, given to show what God can do through one praying servant, and also how much a people needs that no servant can supply.

Where it leads: to Christ. Nehemiah is hardly quoted in the New Testament, and its links to Christ are by pattern and by the need it exposes. By need: the covenant is soon broken, and even the high priest’s grandson marries Sanballat’s daughter (13:28). The book leaves us longing for the covenant God promised through Jeremiah: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). By pattern: Nehemiah confesses his people’s sins as his own, “which we have sinned against you” (1:6), and Christ bore sins that were not his. His enemies falsely said he had prophets proclaim, “There is a king in Judah” (6:7); centuries later the true King rode into that city and died under the charge “King of the Jews”. Nehemiah built a wall that would fall again. Christ said, “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). And the book’s last prayer was answered outside that city’s walls, when a dying thief said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom,” and heard, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43).

For us. Nehemiah calls Christians to care about God’s people, to pray before planning and while planning, and to do the work in front of them. It warns that the greatest dangers often come from inside: greed, compromise and slow neglect of God’s house and God’s day. It shows the joy that comes when God’s word is read clearly and understood. And it frees us from trusting our own reforms. Like Nehemiah, we often have to begin again, but we pray to a God who remembers his people for good, in Christ, and who is building a city “whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10).

1.title: The Man Who Wept for a City
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel,<sup>2</sup>that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.<sup>3</sup>And they said to me, "The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire."<sup>4</sup>As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.<sup>5</sup>And I said, "O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,<sup>6</sup>let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned.<sup>7</sup>We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.<sup>8</sup>Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples,<sup>9</sup>but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.'<sup>10</sup>They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.<sup>11</sup>O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man." Now I was cupbearer to the king.
1.overview:
Where we are. The book opens about 445 BC, thirteen years after Ezra came to Jerusalem to teach the law, and nearly a century after the first return. The temple stands; the city round it does not. Far away in Susa, a Jew named Nehemiah asks about it.

The message. When God’s people lie in ruin and disgrace, the work of rebuilding begins on its knees, and it rests on what God has said. Nehemiah grieves, confesses his people’s sin as his own, and holds God to his word: the God who kept his threat to scatter an unfaithful people will keep his promise to gather those who return, because they are his, redeemed by his own hand.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small, poor community under Persian rule, rebuilding a city their neighbours mocked (see the introduction). They needed to know that their shame was not the end of the story, because God’s covenant still stood, and that everything God would do through Nehemiah began with prayer.

How the chapter makes its case. News comes from Jerusalem: the survivors are in “great trouble and shame”, the wall broken down and the gates burned (vv. 1–3). Nehemiah weeps, fasts and prays, and keeps praying for four months (v. 4; compare 2:1). His prayer praises the great and awesome God who keeps covenant (v. 5), asks him to listen and confesses “we have sinned” (vv. 6–7), quotes back his word through Moses (vv. 8–9), pleads that the people are his redeemed (v. 10), and asks for mercy before “this man” (v. 11). Only in the last line do we learn that the man praying stands beside the king as his cupbearer.

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God. Nehemiah stands between a sinful people and a holy God, says “we” of sins committed before he was born, and has access to the king. Christ is the Intercessor that pattern points to: he took on sins that were not his own (2 Corinthians 5:21), pleads for a people bought with his blood, and “always lives to make intercession” for them (Hebrews 7:25). And the God who keeps his word of judgment and his word of mercy kept both at the cross, for “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. Ask how God’s people are, and let the answer cost you something. Bring that grief to God before you make plans, say “we” rather than “they”, and pray his own promises back to him. We come with a stronger plea than Nehemiah’s: God has bought his people with the blood of his Son, and he does not throw away what cost him that much.
1.theology:
Nehemiah prays God's own words back to him. The threat of scattering had been kept to the letter; therefore the promise of gathering will be kept too. That is the ground of all confident prayer: not the strength of our feeling, but the fact that God has spoken and does not go back on his word.

He confesses as we and pleads that the people are God’s because God bought them back. Both point beyond him to the true Intercessor, who took on sins that were not his and pleads for a people bought with his own blood (vv. 6-11 below).
1.examples:
Nehemiah's first act in his own book is to ask how God's people are, and his second is to pray. He was born in exile, yet he still said I and my father's house have sinned.

The king he prayed about was the one who had stopped the wall, and Nehemiah asked God to soften that very man. We learn he is the king's cupbearer only after he has finished praying.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Wall of Jerusalem Is Broken Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s work begins with someone who asks how God’s people are, and grieves at the answer. In the winter palace at Susa, Nehemiah questions his brother Hanani and the men from Judah about the survivors and the city (vv. 1–2). The news is shame for the people and ruin for the city, its wall broken and its gates burned, leaving Jerusalem open and despised (v. 3). Nehemiah does not shrug it off as a distant problem or hurry into a plan. He sits down, weeps and mourns, and then gives himself to fasting and prayer before the God of heaven, and goes on praying for months (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer comes before building in this book, and the order is not incidental; it is the foundation. Nehemiah will plan brilliantly, but he will never plan first.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus also wept over Jerusalem, but looking the other way in time. Nehemiah wept because its walls were down. Jesus wept because he knew they would come down again: they will not leave one stone upon another (Luke 19:41-44).

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now it happened in the month of Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the citadel, that Hanani, one of my brothers, came with certain men from Judah. And I asked them concerning the Jews who escaped, who had survived the exile, and concerning Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah, safe and well placed in the Persian palace, begins his story by asking how God’s people and God’s city are faring.

The words of Nehemiah. What follows is, for most of its length, a memoir in the first person: I asked, I sat down, I was cupbearer. We are hearing the man himself (see the introduction).

In the month of Chislev. Chislev is November into December, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes I, about 445 BC. Susa the citadel was the winter palace of the Persian kings, the same address as the book of Esther (Esther 1:2), where Esther, a Jewish girl, had become queen a generation earlier under this king’s father. God had put his people in that palace before.

Hanani, one of my brothers. Nehemiah was very likely born in exile, had never seen Jerusalem, and held a post at the centre of the most powerful court on earth. Then his brother Hanani (“my brother Hanani” again at 7:2) arrives with men from Judah, and the first thing Nehemiah does in his own book is ask a question.

And I asked them. He asked about the people first and the place second, and the striking thing is that he asked at all. The comfortable can go a long time without asking how God’s people are, because the answer might cost something.

Chislev, then Nisan, in the same year? Nisan (2:1), in March or April, falls in the same “twentieth year” though it comes after Chislev. Nehemiah probably counted the king’s years from the autumn, or from his accession, rather than from the spring.
verseByVerse.note: Susa lay in what is now south-western Iran, months of travel from Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to me, "The remnant there in the province who had survived the exile is in great trouble and shame. The wall of Jerusalem is broken down, and its gates are destroyed by fire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The news from Jerusalem is double: God’s people are in disgrace, and their city lies open, its wall broken and its gates burned.

The wall of Jerusalem is broken down. An ancient city without a wall was hardly a city. Anyone could walk in at night, traders would not risk their goods there, and nobody of means would live there. The temple stood on its hill, rebuilt seventy years before, in the middle of a settlement that could not shut a door.

Great trouble and shame. The word shame runs through this book: the “derision” Nehemiah means to end (2:17), the taunt he turns back to God (4:4), the “taunts of the nations” (5:9). The wall is stone and mortar, but it is built against a word: the sneer of neighbours who looked at the ruin and said that the God of Israel could not look after his own.

Which ruin is meant? It is not certain. The walls had been down since 586 BC, and some think Hanani means that old desolation. But under this same Artaxerxes the Jews had begun rebuilding the walls, their neighbours wrote to the king, and his officials “by force and power made them cease” (Ezra 4:23). A fresh wreck fits a man who sits down and weeps for days far better than a fact everyone had known for a century and a half.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as I heard these words I sat down and wept and mourned for days, and I continued fasting and praying before the God of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah lets the news break his heart, then turns his grief into months of fasting and prayer before the God who rules over every empire.

I sat down and wept. Then came days of weeping and mourning, and then fasting and prayer. How long is shown by the next date in the book: this is Chislev, and Nehemiah speaks to the king in Nisan (2:1), four months later. The man who will get a wall built in fifty-two days spends more than twice that long on his knees before he lays a stone.

The God of heaven. This is the title Cyrus used in his decree (Ezra 1:2), the name that sets God above every empire. Nehemiah serves the Persian king of kings, and he prays to the God who reigns over that king.

What the ruin cost him. Nehemiah was safe, well fed and well placed, and the ruin was months of travel away. Yet it cost him four months of grief, because it was God’s city and God’s people, and their shame was God’s shame. What does the state of the church cost you: a congregation dwindling, a family that has walked away from the faith? Do not bury that grief, and do not rush past it into a plan. Take it before the God of heaven, who has bound himself by covenant to his people, and keep taking it until he opens a door. When we do not know how to pray, “the Spirit helps us in our weakness” (Romans 8:26).

Jesus, yes; the church, no? Many people today would honour Nehemiah’s tears and still find their object strange. God, perhaps, or Jesus; but why weep over an institution? Many have given up on the church as too compromised, too slow and too full of disappointing people. But Nehemiah grieved over a real place with burned gates and a people in “great trouble and shame” (v. 3), many of them half-hearted, some soon to betray him. He loved them because God had bound himself to them, not because they were impressive. Christ did not love an ideal church and then put up with the actual one; he “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25) while she was still unlovely, so that she might become beautiful. To say yes to him and no to his people is to want the Bridegroom without the bride. Someone who walked away hurt is not wrong to have been hurt. But the cure for a disappointing church has never been a faith kept to oneself. It is a Saviour who has not given up on her, and has not given up on us either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bold prayer rests on who God is and what he has said. Nehemiah begins with God’s greatness and his faithfulness to his covenant (v. 5). He asks to be heard, and confesses the nation’s sin as his own: “Even I and my father’s house have sinned” (vv. 6–7). He holds God to his word through Moses: the scattering threatened for unfaithfulness has come, so the gathering promised to those who return will come too (vv. 8–9). He pleads that the people are God’s own, redeemed by his power (v. 10), and asks for success that very day before “this man”, the king (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Nearly every line of this prayer is borrowed. Its first sentence is Daniel's, its request to be heard is Solomon's, its promise is Moses' in Deuteronomy, and its plea for the people is the argument Moses used after the golden calf. He prays in the language God has already used, which is why he can pray with confidence.
verseByVerse.examples: The book begins with Nehemiah asking God to remember the word (v. 8) and ends with him asking God to remember me, O my God, for good (13:31). Everything between is a man working in reliance on God’s promise and trusting God to keep the record of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said, "O LORD God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him and keep his commandments,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he says a word about Jerusalem, Nehemiah says who God is: great, awesome, and faithful to the covenant he has made.

The great and awesome God. The words are Daniel’s, almost exactly (Daniel 9:4). Daniel prayed them in Babylon about ninety-four years before, when he read in Jeremiah that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years (Daniel 9:2), and God answered him with the decree of Cyrus. Now the temple was standing and the walls were not, and Nehemiah takes up Daniel’s prayer where Daniel left it.

Who keeps covenant and steadfast love. Daniel had the words in turn from Moses (Deuteronomy 7:9). Covenant is the promise God has bound himself to; steadfast love (hesed) is the loyalty behind the promise, the love that keeps coming back. But the sentence carries a condition: he keeps covenant “with those who love him and keep his commandments”. The next two verses confess that Israel had not. The prayer’s first sentence has already named the problem it has to solve.

The one who kept the condition. The gospel’s answer is a man who did love God with all his heart and kept his commandments for others. In Christ, God keeps covenant with people who could never have kept the condition themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned. We have acted very corruptly against you and have not kept the commandments, the statutes, and the rules that you commanded your servant Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah asks God to listen, and confesses the nation’s sin as his own: not “they have sinned” but “we have sinned”.

Let your ear be attentive. The request to be heard is Solomon’s language at the dedication of the temple: “let your eyes be open and your ears attentive to the prayer of this place” (2 Chronicles 6:40). Solomon asked God to hear prayers made toward that house when his people sinned. Nehemiah is praying just such a prayer.

Even I and my father’s house have sinned. Listen to the pronouns: “the people of Israel”, then “we”, then “I and my father’s house”. He does not stand at a distance and describe the nation’s failures to God; he puts himself and his family inside the guilt. Born long after the exile began, he could have said “they”. He never does.

They or we? When you pray about what is wrong in the church, is the subject of the sentence “they” or “we”? Nehemiah’s “we” was honest, for he was a sinner himself. There is one Intercessor who could truthfully have said “they”, and still took the sin as though it were his: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, 'If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah holds God to his own word: the God who kept his threat to scatter an unfaithful people will keep his promise to gather them when they return.

Remember the word. This is not one verse of Moses but the gist of several: the warning of Leviticus 26:33 and Deuteronomy 4:27, the gathering of Deuteronomy 30:4, nearly word for word, and the chosen place of Deuteronomy 12:11. Nehemiah is quoting the whole covenant back to the God who made it.

If you are unfaithful. The first half of that word had come true to the letter: they had been unfaithful, they had been scattered, and the proof is that Nehemiah is praying from Persia. So the second half is just as sure. The exile was the evidence that God keeps his word, and a God who kept the threat will keep the promise.

Confess, then remember. Unfaithful is the word Leviticus uses for Israel’s treachery, and Leviticus had said what should happen next: “if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers … then I will remember my covenant” (Leviticus 26:40–42). That is exactly the order of this prayer. Nehemiah has confessed, and now he asks God to remember, the first of many times the word appears in this book.

What it means for God to remember. We use the word for something that had slipped our minds, so asking God to remember can sound as if he might forget. He cannot: “Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15). When Scripture says God remembers, it means he acts on what he has promised. “God remembered Noah”, and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1); “God remembered his covenant with Abraham”, and the Exodus began (Exodus 2:24). To ask God to remember is to hold him to his own word.

Remembered in Christ. Our real fear usually runs the other way: not that God will forget his promises, but that he will remember our sins. The gospel answers both. When the Saviour was about to be born, Zechariah sang that God had come “to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant” (Luke 1:72). In Jesus, God kept every promise he had made, and laid our sins on him, so that they are no longer counted against us. So pray as Nehemiah prayed: find what God has said in Scripture, say it back to him, and ask him to do as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: They are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah’s plea is not that the people deserve help, but that they belong to God, who bought them back by his own power.

Your servants and your people. These are Moses’ words on the worst day in Israel’s history. After the golden calf, Moses lay on his face for forty days and pleaded: “do not destroy your people and your heritage, whom you have redeemed through your greatness” (Deuteronomy 9:26).

A greater price. Redeemed means bought back, and you do not throw away what cost you that much. That argument is stronger now than when Moses and Nehemiah made it, because the price is greater: “you were ransomed … not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Whoever has been bought at that price has an Intercessor who can say to the Father, of the weakest of his people: they are yours, and look what they cost.

verseByVerse.quote: O Lord, let your ear be attentive to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name, and give success to your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man." Now I was cupbearer to the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah asks for success that very day with the king who had stopped the work, and only then tells us that he stands at that king’s side as his cupbearer.

Your servants who delight to fear your name. He is not alone. Others were praying too, people who “delight to fear your name”, and he asks God to hear them all together.

Today, and this man. “Today”, because he has picked a day. “This man”, because the most powerful ruler on earth is, before God, a man. And this man had caused the problem: Artaxerxes had ordered the building stopped “until a decree is made by me” (Ezra 4:21). The king had left one way open, a new decree of his own, and Nehemiah was praying to take it, asking the emperor to reverse his own order in a court where a servant who displeased the king could lose his head.

Now I was cupbearer to the king. Only now do we learn who has been praying. The cupbearer stood within arm’s length of the throne, trusted with the king’s life. That is the whole chapter in its last line: a man with a broken heart for God’s city and access to the king.

A greater Intercessor. Nehemiah would go in trembling, afraid of the king’s face (2:2). Our Intercessor sits at the right hand of the throne: “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses”, so we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:15–16), and “he always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). The cupbearer had to wait for his moment; the Son never has to wait at all.
verseByVerse.note: A cupbearer tasted the king’s wine to guard against poison, and often became a trusted adviser.

keyVerse.quote: Remember the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, ‘If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the peoples, but if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts are in the uttermost parts of heaven, from there I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there.’
keyVerse.note: Here is the ground of the whole prayer, and of all confident prayer. Nehemiah does not lean on the strength of his feelings but on what God has said: the threat of scattering had been kept to the letter, so the promise of gathering will be kept too. To pray like this is to ask God to do exactly what he has promised, and in Christ every one of those promises finds its Yes.

1.reflection:
Nehemiah’s first act in his book is to ask how God’s people are (v. 2), and the answer costs him months of grief (v. 4). What keeps us from asking, or from letting the answer reach us? What about the church today grieves you, and what do you do with that grief?

Nehemiah prays “we have sinned” and “I and my father’s house have sinned” (v. 6), though he was born long after the exile began. Where do you find it easier to say “they”? How does Christ, who took sins that were not his own, change the way we pray about the church’s failures?

The heart of the prayer is God’s own word said back to him (vv. 8–9). Which promises of God could you pray back to him this week, and what difference does it make to pray on the ground of what he has said rather than on how strongly we feel?

Nehemiah prayed for four months and then asked for success “today” (v. 11). How do patient waiting and a definite request belong together in prayer? Is there something you have been praying about where it may be time to act?

2.title: Vision in the Dark
2.text: <sup>1</sup>In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence.<sup>2</sup>And the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart." Then I was very much afraid.<sup>3</sup>I said to the king, "Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?"<sup>4</sup>Then the king said to me, "What are you requesting?" Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen.<sup>10</sup>But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.<sup>11</sup>So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days.<sup>12</sup>Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me but the one on which I rode.<sup>13</sup>I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire.<sup>14</sup>Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal that was under me to pass.<sup>15</sup>Then I went up in the night by the valley and inspected the wall, and I turned back and entered by the Valley Gate, and so returned.<sup>16</sup>And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, and I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work.<sup>17</sup>Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision."<sup>18</sup>And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, "Let us rise up and build." So they strengthened their hands for the good work.<sup>19</sup>But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?"<sup>20</sup>Then I replied to them, "The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem."
2.overview:
Where we are. Four months have passed since Hanani’s news (1:1; 2:1). Nehemiah has prayed through the winter for mercy “in the sight of this man” (1:11), and now the moment comes, at the king’s table, with the cup in his hand.

The message. God answers prayer through the decisions of kings and the courage of ordinary servants, and when his good hand is on a work, mockery cannot stop it. Nehemiah is afraid and speaks anyway; he prays and he plans; he sees the ruin for himself and then calls God’s people to build on the ground of what God has done. To the scoffers he gives one answer: “The God of heaven will make us prosper” (v. 20).

Why it was said. The last attempt to build the wall had been stopped by royal order and armed force (Ezra 4:21–23), and the neighbours who had stopped it were still there (see the introduction). The first readers needed to see that the same king could be turned by God, and that opposition was to be expected, but not feared.

How the chapter makes its case. At the king’s table Nehemiah’s sadness finally shows, and in fear he tells the truth about the city of his fathers’ graves (vv. 1–3). Asked what he wants, he prays in a breath and asks to be sent, with letters and timber, and the king grants it, “for the good hand of my God was upon me” (vv. 4–8). He arrives with an escort, to the displeasure of Sanballat and Tobiah (vv. 9–10), inspects the ruins alone by night (vv. 11–16), and calls the leaders to build, telling them of God’s hand; they answer, “Let us rise up and build” (vv. 17–18). To the jeer of rebellion he replies in the name of the God of heaven (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. By pattern. Nehemiah left the palace and the king’s presence to live among ruins and derision for the sake of God’s people, sent with the king’s authority to rebuild. Christ left far more: he “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), came without letters or horsemen, and faced the same charge of rebellion against the emperor (John 19:12). He is building what will never lie in ruins again: “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

For us. Pray before you speak, and keep praying while you speak. Count the cost honestly, do the homework, and then call others to the work by telling them what God has done. Expect scorn when you build for God, and answer it not with your own credentials but with his name.
2.theology:
God's providence works through a servant's sad face, a king's question, a prayer in a pause and a practical list of letters and timber. Prayer and planning are not rivals: the man who prayed four months also knew what beams he needed. And the good hand of God rests equally on Ezra, who refused an escort, and on Nehemiah, who accepted one; faith does not follow one fixed method.

The builder who left a palace for a ruin is a real but limited likeness of Christ, as the note on vv. 19-20 explains.
2.examples:
A frightened man prayed in the pause between a question and an answer, and the king said yes. He then rode the ruins by night until the rubble was too thick for his animal to pass, and measured the problem before he asked anyone to lift a stone.

He had been in the city three days and already said the trouble we are in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Good Hand of My God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God turns the heart of a king in answer to a servant’s prayer. After four months of hidden grief, Nehemiah’s sadness shows as he serves the king his wine, and the king sees it at once (vv. 1–2). Afraid, Nehemiah still tells the truth, speaking of the city of his fathers’ graves rather than naming the city this king had stopped (v. 3). Asked what he wants, he prays in an instant and makes a bold, well-prepared request: to be sent to rebuild, with letters of safe passage and timber from the king’s forest (vv. 4–8). The king grants it all, and Nehemiah gives the reason: “the good hand of my God was upon me” (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: After months of prayer, the answer came when a servant’s sadness showed on his face, something he had not planned and could not have staged. God turned the king's heart (Prov 21:1) by way of Nehemiah's sad face.

verseByVerse.quote: In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when wine was before him, I took up the wine and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad in his presence. And the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, seeing you are not sick? This is nothing but sadness of the heart." Then I was very much afraid. I said to the king, "Let the king live forever! Why should not my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers' graves, lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah’s hidden grief finally shows before the king, and though terrified, he tells the truth with great care.

Now I had not been sad in his presence. Nisan is March into April (see the note on 1:1–2). For four months he had carried the grief and kept it off his face. A Persian king did not care to see sorrow near him; in the book of Esther “no one was allowed to enter the king’s gate clothed in sackcloth” (Esther 4:2). Then one day, with the cup in his hand, the mask slipped.

Then I was very much afraid. The king had seen straight through him, and an unhappy servant close to the royal cup could look like a dangerous one. Courage in Scripture is not the absence of fear but doing the next right thing while afraid, leaning on the God who has heard four months of prayer rather than on nerve. Anyone dreading a conversation they must have is in good company here.

The place of my fathers’ graves. What he does not say matters. He does not say “Jerusalem”. This king had once been told it was “that rebellious and wicked city” (Ezra 4:12) and had ordered its building stopped. So Nehemiah speaks of his fathers’ graves, a claim anyone in any nation would understand, and lets the king reach the name for himself. It was truthful, and it was wise.
verseByVerse.note: A Persian king could put to death anyone who came before him unbidden (Esth 4:11); his servants' faces were expected to show only contentment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to me, "What are you requesting?" So I prayed to the God of heaven. And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may rebuild it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah prays in a breath, then makes a request as bold as his long prayers had been.

So I prayed to the God of heaven. A king has asked a question and is waiting. There are perhaps three seconds before silence becomes insolence, and into them Nehemiah puts a prayer: no words aloud, no bowed head the king would notice, a cry sent upward between the question and the answer.

That I may rebuild it. The request is enormous: send the king’s own cupbearer to rebuild the city the king had forbidden to be rebuilt.

Where quick prayer comes from. That kind of prayer does not come from nowhere. The long prayer made the short one possible; the habit made the reflex. In the pause before you answer a hard question at work or at home, is the God of heaven the first one you turn to? What makes it possible is not a technique for that moment but the prayer before it, and the Spirit by whom God’s children cry to their Father is given for moments like this (Romans 8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to me (the queen sitting beside him), "How long will you be gone, and when will you return?" So it pleased the king to send me when I had given him a time. And I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors of the province Beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah, and a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fortress of the temple, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall occupy." And the king granted me what I asked, for the good hand of my God was upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king grants everything Nehemiah asks, and Nehemiah knows why: the good hand of his God was on him.

The queen sitting beside him. The queen is an eyewitness’s detail. And the king’s question is already a yes: not whether, but when. In the end Nehemiah governed Judah for twelve years (5:14) before returning to the king (13:6).

Let letters be given me. Then the petition turns practical: letters to the governors “Beyond the River” for safe passage, and a letter to the keeper of the king’s forest for beams for the gates, the wall and his own house. He had spent those months planning as well as praying.

The keeper of the king’s forest. The word for the king’s forest, pardes, is the Persian word for a royal park that has given us our word paradise. The timber for Jerusalem’s gates came out of the king’s paradise.

The good hand of my God. This is the sentence used of Ezra: “the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him” (Ezra 7:6), and “the good hand of his God was on him” (7:9). Thirteen years later the same hand rests on Nehemiah. The king did the granting; God’s hand is the reason he did. “The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1).

Daniel’s seventy weeks. Many Christian interpreters have counted Daniel’s seventy weeks from a word “to restore and build Jerusalem” (Daniel 9:25) to the coming of the Messiah, starting either from this commission in about 445 BC or from Ezra’s in about 458. The calculations differ, and faithful Christians hold them with an open hand (this commentary’s note on Daniel 9:25 prefers the count from Ezra’s commission). What is not in doubt is that the city rebuilt under these decrees was the one into which the Anointed One came.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — Let Us Rise Up and Build
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s people rise to build, the work rests on what God has done, and opposition is answered in his name. Nehemiah arrives with the king’s letters and an escort, and Sanballat and Tobiah are angry that anyone should seek Israel’s good (vv. 9–10). He rests three days, then rides the ruins by night, telling no one, to see the problem for himself (vv. 11–16). Only then does he call the leaders: “we” are in trouble, so let us build; and he tells them of God’s hand and the king’s words (vv. 17–18). When the enemies jeer and cry rebellion, he answers that the God of heaven will prosper his servants, and that the scoffers have no share in Jerusalem (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter’s key word is good: God's good hand (v. 8), the good of Israel that the enemy resents (v. 10), the hand upon him for good and the good work (v. 18). The book will end on it: Remember me, O my God, for good (13:31).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen. But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard this, it displeased them greatly that someone had come to seek the welfare of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah arrives with royal authority, and the neighbours who profit from Jerusalem’s weakness are angry that anyone should seek its good.

Officers of the army and horsemen. Thirteen years earlier Ezra had made the same journey and was “ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen” (Ezra 8:22), because he had told the king that God protects those who seek him. Nehemiah rides in with cavalry. Both men had the good hand of God upon them.

Sanballat and Tobiah. Sanballat was governor of Samaria, to the north; Tobiah was an official in Ammon, across the Jordan, with friends inside Jerusalem (6:17–19). A weak Jerusalem suited them both. Their complaint is the most honest thing they say in the whole book: someone had come “to seek the welfare of the people of Israel”.

What it does not mean. Neither way is a rule for everyone. Sometimes faith refuses the means on offer, so that all will see God did it; sometimes it accepts them with thanks, because God provided them.

Uncertain wording. “The Horonite” probably means that Sanballat came from Beth-horon, north-west of Jerusalem, though some link the name with Horonaim in Moab. “The Ammonite servant” is also unclear: “servant” may be an official title, a servant of the Persian king governing the region of Ammon, or Nehemiah’s scornful word for a man he regarded as an underling.
verseByVerse.note: Sanballat's name is Babylonian, meaning "Sin [the moon god] gives life", though he gave his sons names honouring the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: So I went to Jerusalem and was there three days. Then I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. And I told no one what my God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There was no animal with me but the one on which I rode. I went out by night by the Valley Gate to the Dragon Spring and to the Dung Gate, and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem that were broken down and its gates that had been destroyed by fire. Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and to the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal that was under me to pass. Then I went up in the night by the valley and inspected the wall, and I turned back and entered by the Valley Gate, and so returned. And the officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing, and I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, and the rest who were to do the work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah quietly inspects the ruins by night, seeing the problem for himself before he tells anyone the plan.

There three days. Three days first, as Ezra had done on arriving (Ezra 8:32): after a journey of months, no one starts a revolution on the first morning.

I told no one. The plan was God’s, “put into my heart”, and he kept it to himself. Tobiah had friends in the city, and a plan announced before it is ready is a plan handed to the opposition.

The route of the ride. The ride runs out by the Valley Gate on the west, down to the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate at the southern tip, round to the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool. There, on the steep eastern slope, the fallen wall and terraces were too choked for his animal to pass, so he went up the valley looking at the wall from below, and came back in by the gate he had left by.

I inspected the walls. He would not call people to a work he had not seen with his own eyes. Jesus asked the same honesty of anyone who would follow him: “which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost” (Luke 14:28)? And though nobody yet knew what Nehemiah was doing, he already calls them “the rest who were to do the work”.

Uncertain wording. The “Dragon Spring” is named only here. The Hebrew word can mean a serpent, a sea monster or a jackal, and no one knows which spring is meant, beyond its place on the route between the Valley Gate and the Dung Gate.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in, how Jerusalem lies in ruins with its gates burned. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer suffer derision." And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, "Let us rise up and build." So they strengthened their hands for the good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah calls the people to build by telling them what God has done, and they answer with one voice, “Let us rise up and build.”

You see the trouble we are in. He had lived in the city three days. He could have said “you”. He said “we”, as he had in his prayer (1:6). And at last he names the city: “Jerusalem”, twice. “Derision” is the “shame” Hanani reported (1:3): the neighbours’ sneer, which a wall would silence.

I told them of the hand of my God. He did not begin with a work rota. He told them what God had done, and then what the king had said. The people of Jerusalem had watched the last attempt at a wall pulled down by force; what could make them try again was the news that God had moved.

For the good work. They strengthened their hands “for the good work”. The enemy hated the good; God’s hand was for it; the people put their hands to it. When Nehemiah’s last recorded words ask God to remember him “for good” (13:31), he is asking to be counted among those who served this good work. Christians too are “created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10), and are moved to them the same way: by hearing what God’s hand has done.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant and Geshem the Arab heard of it, they jeered at us and despised us and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?" Then I replied to them, "The God of heaven will make us prosper, and we his servants will arise and build, but you have no portion or right or claim in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah answers mockery and the charge of rebellion not with the king’s letters but with the name of the God of heaven.

And Geshem the Arab. Now there are three: Sanballat from Samaria to the north, Tobiah from Ammon to the east, Geshem the Arab from the desert to the south. Their first weapon is a laugh, then the old charge of rebellion, which had stopped the wall before (Ezra 4:12–16). This time it was absurd, with the king’s letters in Nehemiah’s baggage, but it is the charge the world reaches for whenever God’s people build, and it is the charge that sent the Son of God to the cross: “Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar” (John 19:12).

No portion or right or claim. Nehemiah had the king’s letters and did not wave them; he answered in God’s name. The last word, “claim”, may be rendered “memorial”, as the ESV’s footnote says: Sanballat and his friends will have no memorial in Jerusalem, and the man who says so will end his book asking God to remember him.

He came with neither. Nehemiah left a palace to live among ruins and derision because he loved God’s people. The likeness to Christ is real, and so is its limit: Nehemiah went with letters and horsemen. The Son of God “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and came with neither, into a far greater ruin, to build a city whose enemies will have no memorial in it at all.

keyVerse.quote: And I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, “Let us rise up and build.” So they strengthened their hands for the good work.
keyVerse.note: The chapter turns on two kinds of hand. God’s good hand had moved a king who once stopped the work, and when the people heard of it, they strengthened their own hands to build. That is how God’s people are still moved to his work: not first by plans or pressure, but by hearing what God has done.

2.reflection:
Nehemiah had kept his grief hidden for four months, and when it showed he was “very much afraid” (v. 2), yet he told the truth. Where do you need courage to say something true and costly? What does it mean that courage is not the absence of fear?

Between the king’s question and his answer, Nehemiah “prayed to the God of heaven” (v. 4). How do long seasons of prayer make quick prayers possible? What could help you turn to God first in the pressured moments of an ordinary day?

Nehemiah prayed, planned, asked for letters and timber, accepted an escort, and inspected the ruins before he spoke (vv. 7–16). How do trusting God and careful planning fit together? Is one of them easier for you than the other?

The people were moved to build when they heard “of the hand of my God” (v. 18), and the scoffers were answered with God’s name, not Nehemiah’s credentials (v. 20). What has God done that could move your church to the work he has given it, and how should we answer scorn?
