3.overview:
Where we are. Nehemiah has inspected the ruins by night and called the leaders to build, and they have answered, “Let us rise up and build” (2:18). Before telling of the opposition that followed (chapter 4), the book stops to record who built what.

The message. God’s city is rebuilt by all his people together, each in his place, and God remembers every one of them. High priest and perfumer, rulers and goldsmiths, villagers, and a father with his daughters each take a stretch of wall; only one group of proud men refuses. Nothing done for God is too small to be written down.

Why it was said. For families rebuilding their lives in a poor and despised province, a name on this list was a lasting honour and a title to their place among God’s people (see the introduction). It also told later generations that the wall was not one man’s achievement but the work of a whole people under God.

How the chapter makes its case. The record runs anticlockwise round the city from the Sheep Gate by the temple. Priests begin, consecrating the gate (vv. 1–2); families and townsmen follow along the north wall, where only the nobles of Tekoa hold back (vv. 3–5). Down the west side come Gibeonites, goldsmiths, a perfumer, rulers, and Shallum with his daughters (vv. 6–12), and round the southern gates to the Pool of Shelah (vv. 13–15). Up the eastern side Levites, priests and householders build, many opposite their own homes (vv. 16–27), until the goldsmiths and merchants close the circuit at the Sheep Gate (vv. 28–32).

Where it leads. By promise and pattern. In the chapter of the new covenant, Jeremiah had promised that “the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the tower of Hananel” to “the corner of the Horse Gate”, never again to be overthrown (Jeremiah 31:38–40). These builders worked along that very line, yet their wall fell again. The city that will never fall is the one Christ builds, in which his people are “being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22), and whose foundations bear the names of “the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (Revelation 21:14). The Sheep Gate, where the work began and ended, let in the sacrifices; the Lamb is the one they pointed to.

For us. Every Christian has a stretch of wall. Find the work God has put next to you, often opposite your own house, and do it beside others whose gifts differ from yours. Do not be too proud to stoop, and do not think hidden work is forgotten: “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work” (Hebrews 6:10).
3.theology:
Nobody builds this wall alone; every section joins someone else’s. The people of God are built together, and God keeps the names of those who work.

The wall follows the line named in Jeremiah’s promise that the city would be rebuilt for the LORD (Jer 31:31-40), but Nehemiah’s wall was only a first part of what was promised. The city that will never be overthrown is the one John saw, with names inscribed on its gates and foundations (Rev 21:12-14).
3.examples:
The list is full of reversals. A priest from a family once barred because it could not prove its descent built two sections; descendants of the Gibeonites who tricked Joshua built Jerusalem's wall; and while the nobles of Tekoa would not bend their necks, a district ruler took the Dung Gate.

Goldsmiths and perfumers lifted stone, Shallum's daughters carried it, and many men built opposite their own houses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — They Built the Sheep Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The work begins with the worship of God and spreads to every kind of person. The high priest and his brothers build and consecrate the Sheep Gate, where the sacrifices came in (vv. 1–2). Along the north wall families and townsmen set gates and repair stretches, while the nobles of Tekoa alone refuse to stoop (vv. 3–5). Down the western side Gibeonites, goldsmiths, a perfumer and district rulers lift stone, and Shallum builds with his daughters (vv. 6–12). Round the south, villagers rebuild the Valley Gate and a long stretch of wall, and rulers take the Dung Gate and the Fountain Gate by the Pool of Shelah (vv. 13–15). No task is beneath anyone, and no name is lost.
verseByVerse.theology: Thirty-one times the chapter says next to him or after him: every stretch of wall joins someone else's.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brothers the priests, and they built the Sheep Gate. They consecrated it and set its doors. They consecrated it as far as the Tower of the Hundred, as far as the Tower of Hananel. And next to him the men of Jericho built. And next to them Zaccur the son of Imri built.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The work begins with the high priest at the gate where the sacrifices came in.

How to read this list. This is Nehemiah’s work sheet, going anticlockwise round the city from the temple corner and back. Nobody keeps a record like this unless every name on it mattered.

Eliashib the high priest. The first man on the wall is the most senior man in Israel’s religion, the high priest, with his hands on the stones. He begins at the Sheep Gate, through which the flocks came in for the sacrifices, the only gate in the list that is consecrated. Nearly five centuries later there was a pool “by the Sheep Gate” where Jesus told a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years to get up and walk (John 5:2–8).

The Tower of Hananel. Remember the Tower of Hananel: it appears in a promise of Jeremiah’s that this chapter begins to keep (see the note on vv. 28–32). And “next to him the men of Jericho built”: the city whose walls fell flat when Israel first entered the land sends men to put up Jerusalem’s.

A good start, a faithful finish. Hold one fact about Eliashib for later. In chapter 13 his grandson is married to the daughter of Sanballat (13:28), and an Eliashib, probably this one, has given Tobiah a room in the temple (13:4–7). The man who built the first gate let the enemy in through his own family. A good start is not the same as a faithful finish.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate stood at the north-east corner, near the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate. They laid its beams and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And next to them Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz repaired. And next to them Meshullam the son of Berechiah, son of Meshezabel repaired. And next to them Zadok the son of Baana repaired. And next to them the Tekoites repaired, but their nobles would not stoop to serve their Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Families build side by side, and the only people too proud to work are the nobles of one town.

Meremoth the son of Uriah. Notice the name Hakkoz. When the exiles first came home, the family of Hakkoz could not find its name in the genealogies and was “excluded from the priesthood as unclean” (Ezra 2:61–62). Eighty years later Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, is the priest into whose hands Ezra weighed the temple’s silver and gold (Ezra 8:33), and here he builds two sections (v. 21). The family that nearly lost its place gave more than almost anyone.

But their nobles would not stoop. Tekoa was a hill town some ten miles south, the town of Amos (Amos 1:1). Its ordinary men came in and worked. Its great men would not bend their necks to the work, like an ox that will not take the yoke. The Tekoites answered by doing a second section (v. 27).

A yoke for every proud neck. There is a yoke offered to every proud neck, and it is not heavy: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). Jesus, who says it, stooped lower than any noble of Tekoa was ever asked to.

Uncertain wording. Literally the nobles did not bring their neck into the service of their lord, and the last word can be read as singular or plural. The ESV takes it as the Lord God; others read “their lords”, the overseers of the work. Either way, they refused the yoke.

verseByVerse.quote: Joiada the son of Paseah and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah repaired the Gate of Yeshanah. They laid its beams and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And next to them repaired Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon and of Mizpah, the seat of the governor of the province Beyond the River. Next to them Uzziel the son of Harhaiah, goldsmiths, repaired. Next to him Hananiah, one of the perfumers, repaired, and they restored Jerusalem as far as the Broad Wall. Next to them Rephaiah the son of Hur, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired. Next to them Jedaiah the son of Harumaph repaired opposite his house. And next to him Hattush the son of Hashabneiah repaired. Malchijah the son of Harim and Hasshub the son of Pahath-moab repaired another section and the Tower of the Ovens. Next to him Shallum the son of Hallohesh, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired, he and his daughters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Outsiders, craftsmen, rulers and daughters lift stone together, and God keeps the record of each.

The men of Gibeon and of Mizpah. Round the north-west corner and down the western side the names keep coming. Melatiah the Gibeonite and the men of Gibeon were descendants of the Canaanites who tricked Joshua and were made “cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD” (Joshua 9:27). The outsiders who were made servants of the altar are building its city’s wall.

Goldsmiths and a perfumer. Goldsmiths and a perfumer, men with soft hands, lift rough stone. Two rulers of half the district of Jerusalem take sections (vv. 9, 12), and Jedaiah builds opposite his house (v. 10), the first of several who built the stretch they would sleep behind.

Shallum’s daughters. Shallum’s daughters are the only women mentioned on the wall. Their names are not given, but they carried stone beside their father, and Scripture kept the fact.

Why the list is kept. That is what the list is for: “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Hebrews 6:10). Most work done for God is done by people whose names are forgotten within fifty years. Not one of them is forgotten by him.

Uncertain wording. “The Gate of Yeshanah” may be a name, or may mean “the Old Gate”, as many translations render it. And the verb in “they restored Jerusalem” usually means “leave” or “abandon”: some think the builders left part of the old city outside the wall here, but most translations take it as a rarer word meaning “restore”.

verseByVerse.quote: Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah repaired the Valley Gate. They rebuilt it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars, and repaired a thousand cubits of the wall, as far as the Dung Gate. Malchijah the son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem, repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And Shallum the son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt it and covered it and set its doors, its bolts, and its bars. And he built the wall of the Pool of Shelah of the king's garden, as far as the stairs that go down from the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Villagers and rulers take the long and the dirty stretches on the southern side.

The Valley Gate. Hanun and the men of Zanoah rebuild the Valley Gate and a thousand cubits of wall, about five hundred yards, the only stretch in the chapter given a length, and a long one. Perhaps the wall there needed less repair, or Zanoah simply sent many men.

The Dung Gate. The Dung Gate was the gate through which the city’s refuse went out to the valley, and a district ruler took it, where the nobles of Tekoa would not bend their necks at all.

The Pool of Shelah. Shelah is the pool Isaiah called Shiloah, “the waters of Shiloah that flow gently” (Isaiah 8:6), the pool the Gospels call Siloam, where Jesus sent a blind man to wash, and he “came back seeing” (John 9:7). John adds that the name means “Sent”, and the one who sent the blind man there had himself been sent by the Father.
verseByVerse.note: Shelah means "sent", the meaning John draws out for Siloam (John 9:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–32 — Each Opposite His Own House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Up the eastern side the circuit is completed by people building where they live and worship. A ruler named Nehemiah works near the tombs of David, and Levites and district rulers follow (vv. 16–19). Meremoth, whose family was once shut out of the priesthood, does a second stretch past the high priest’s house, and priests and householders build opposite their own homes (vv. 20–24). Near the court of the guard, where Jeremiah was held, the temple servants and the Tekoites build (vv. 25–27). Priests above the Horse Gate, a gatekeeper, and finally goldsmiths and merchants close the circle at the Sheep Gate (vv. 28–32), along the line of Jeremiah’s promise.
verseByVerse.theology: Seven times a man or a group repairs another section, a second stretch after finishing a first. Nobody was forced to; they saw a gap and filled it. Several build the wall in front of their own door.

verseByVerse.quote: After him Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, repaired to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool, and as far as the house of the mighty men. After him the Levites repaired: Rehum the son of Bani. Next to him Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, repaired for his district. After him their brothers repaired: Bavvai the son of Henadad, ruler of half the district of Keilah. Next to him Ezer the son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section opposite the ascent to the armory at the buttress. After him Baruch the son of Zabbai repaired another section from the buttress to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. After him Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz repaired another section from the door of the house of Eliashib to the end of the house of Eliashib. After him the priests, the men of the surrounding area, repaired. After them Benjamin and Hasshub repaired opposite their house. After them Azariah the son of Maaseiah, son of Ananiah repaired beside his own house. After him Binnui the son of Henadad repaired another section, from the house of Azariah to the buttress and to the corner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Up the eastern side many build opposite their own houses.

Nehemiah the son of Azbuk. This Nehemiah, son of Azbuk and ruler of half the district of Beth-zur, is not the governor telling the story. He worked near “the tombs of David”, the royal burial place inside the old city. Then come the Levites.

Baruch and Meremoth. Baruch builds to the door of the high priest’s house, and Meremoth, from the family once shut out of the priesthood, does his second stretch along it (vv. 20–21).

Building opposite their houses. Nehemiah seems to have assigned men where they lived when he could. A man builds carefully when his own children sleep on the other side of the stones. The work God gives most of us is like that: the stretch of wall nearest home.

verseByVerse.quote: Palal the son of Uzai repaired opposite the buttress and the tower projecting from the upper house of the king at the court of the guard. After him Pedaiah the son of Parosh and the temple servants living on Ophel repaired to a point opposite the Water Gate on the east and the projecting tower. After him the Tekoites repaired another section opposite the great projecting tower as far as the wall of Ophel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men build where Jeremiah, in prison, bought a field as a sign that the land would be lived in again.

The court of the guard. The court of the guard was where Jeremiah had been held prisoner while the Babylonians besieged the city (Jeremiah 32:2), and where he bought a field, because God had told him that “houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land” (Jeremiah 32:15). On the same spot, a century and a half later, men of that land are building.

The temple servants living on Ophel. The temple servants who lived on Ophel, the ridge south of the temple, work opposite the Water Gate. It is in the square before that gate that the whole people will gather to hear Ezra read the law (8:1). And the Tekoites repair a second section.

verseByVerse.quote: Above the Horse Gate the priests repaired, each one opposite his own house. After them Zadok the son of Immer repaired opposite his own house. After him Shemaiah the son of Shecaniah, the keeper of the East Gate, repaired. After him Hananiah the son of Shelemiah and Hanun the sixth son of Zalaph repaired another section. After him Meshullam the son of Berechiah repaired opposite his chamber. After him Malchijah, one of the goldsmiths, repaired as far as the house of the temple servants and of the merchants, opposite the Muster Gate, and to the upper chamber of the corner. And between the upper chamber of the corner and the Sheep Gate the goldsmiths and the merchants repaired.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The circuit closes at the Sheep Gate, along the line Jeremiah named when he promised a city rebuilt for the LORD.

A promise beside this chapter. In the chapter in which Jeremiah announced the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33), he added that “the city shall be rebuilt for the LORD from the tower of Hananel” to “the corner of the Horse Gate”, and “shall not be plucked up or overthrown anymore forever” (Jeremiah 31:38–40). The Tower of Hananel is in verse 1 of this chapter; the Horse Gate is in verse 28. The people with their trowels were building along the very line Jeremiah’s promise had named.

Still to come. Yet not the whole of it. Jerusalem’s walls came down again under Rome. The city that will never be plucked up is still to come, and when John saw it, its gates and foundations bore the names of the twelve tribes and of “the twelve apostles of the Lamb” (Revelation 21:12, 14). The God who had every builder’s name written down builds his last city with names on its stones, and does not overlook the work done for him (Hebrews 6:10). And the Lamb whose apostles are named there is Jesus, the sacrifice to which every sheep brought in through the Sheep Gate had pointed.

Uncertain wording. The “Muster Gate” is named only here. Its Hebrew name has to do with counting or inspecting, perhaps of troops, but its purpose is not known.

keyVerse.quote: Above the Horse Gate the priests repaired, each one opposite his own house.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers up the chapter: “each one” doing his part, at the stretch nearest home, and all of it along the line where Jeremiah had promised the city would be rebuilt “to the corner of the Horse Gate” (Jeremiah 31:40). Ordinary faithfulness in one’s own place is how God builds his city, and he remembers every builder.

3.reflection:
Priests, goldsmiths, a perfumer, rulers, villagers and Shallum’s daughters all worked on the wall (vv. 1–12). What does this list teach about how God’s work gets done? Whose work in your church goes unnoticed, and how could you honour it?

The nobles of Tekoa “would not stoop to serve” (v. 5), while their townsmen did two sections. Where are you tempted to think some work is beneath you? How does Jesus’ invitation to take his yoke, from one who is “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), answer that pride?

Many built “opposite his own house” (vv. 10, 23, 28–30). What is the stretch of wall nearest your own home: your family, street, workplace or congregation? What would it mean to build there faithfully?

God had every builder’s name written down, and Hebrews 6:10 says he does not overlook our work. How does that encourage you in work no one else sees? How does the promise of a city that will never be overthrown (Revelation 21:14) change the way you view your labour for Christ?

4.title: Trowel and Sword
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews.<sup>2</sup>And he said in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, "What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that?"<sup>3</sup>Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, "Yes, what they are building— if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall!"<sup>4</sup>Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads and give them up to be plundered in a land where they are captives.<sup>5</sup>Do not cover their guilt, and let not their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders.<sup>6</sup>So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.<sup>7</sup>But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry.<sup>8</sup>And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it.<sup>9</sup>And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night.<sup>10</sup>In Judah it was said, "The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall."<sup>11</sup>And our enemies said, "They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them and stop the work."<sup>12</sup>At that time the Jews who lived near them came from all directions and said to us ten times, "You must return to us."<sup>13</sup>So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows.<sup>14</sup>And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes."<sup>15</sup>When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work.<sup>16</sup>From that day on, half of my servants worked on construction, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail. And the leaders stood behind the whole house of Judah,<sup>17</sup>who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other.<sup>18</sup>And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. The man who sounded the trumpet was beside me.<sup>19</sup>And I said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another.<sup>20</sup>In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us."<sup>21</sup>So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out.<sup>22</sup>I also said to the people at that time, "Let every man and his servant pass the night within Jerusalem, that they may be a guard for us by night and may labor by day."<sup>23</sup>So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
4.overview:
Where we are. The builders are on the wall, each family at its own stretch (chapter 3). The enemies who jeered at the plan (2:19) now watch it happening, and the work meets its first real test.

The message. When God’s work goes forward, opposition grows, from mockery outside to weariness and fear within. God’s people answer it by taking everything to God and staying at the work, watchful and ready, with the Lord in view. The danger is real and the guard is needed, but the battle is the Lord’s: “Our God will fight for us” (v. 20).

Why it was said. The returned community lived surrounded by hostile neighbours, and the last time they had tried to build a wall it had been stopped by force (see the introduction). They were tired and afraid, and some of their own relatives were urging them to give up. The chapter shows them how to endure.

How the chapter makes its case. Sanballat and Tobiah mock the “feeble Jews” and their burned stones (vv. 1–3). Nehemiah hands the taunt to God (vv. 4–5), and the wall is joined all round to half its height, “for the people had a mind to work” (v. 6). Then enemies on every side plot an attack, and the people pray and set a guard (vv. 7–9). Inside Judah the workers say they cannot go on, and their families beg them to come home (vv. 10–12). Nehemiah stations them by families and tells them, “Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome” (vv. 13–14). God frustrates the plot, and from then on they build with one hand and hold a weapon with the other, ready to rally at the trumpet (vv. 15–23).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. The builders were mocked and threatened, and admitted, “By ourselves we will not be able” (v. 10). Christ took the full weight of the mockery, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42), and faced alone the enemies his people could never defeat, sin and death. Because he prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), his people’s first prayer for their enemies is now for mercy; and because he won, they stand with Paul’s confidence: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

For us. Expect opposition when you build for God, and do not let mockery set the terms: take it to God and lay the next stone. When you are worn out in the middle of the work, remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and stand beside your brothers and sisters. Pray, and keep watch, never one without the other.
4.theology:
Prayer and sensible precautions are never set against each other in this chapter: we prayed to our God and set a guard. Nor are God's fighting and theirs (vv. 14, 20). God rules everything, and he works through ordinary means: he usually gives his help through his people’s own effort.

Sanballat's scornful question, whether burned stones can be made alive, is answered in Christ, who makes dead people into living stones (see vv. 1-3). And the hard prayer of vv. 4-5 leaves justice with God; Nehemiah never takes revenge himself.
4.examples: The hardest discouragement came from inside, at the halfway point, when their own families told them ten times to come home. Nehemiah answered fear with the first line of his own prayer, and from then on every builder worked with one hand on the work and one on the weapon. The governor slept in his clothes like everyone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Will They Revive the Stones?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mockery is met with prayer and work. Sanballat jeers before the army of Samaria, asking whether these feeble Jews can bring burned stones back to life, and Tobiah adds that a fox would knock their wall down (vv. 1–3). Nehemiah does not answer them. He turns to God, asking him to hear how his people are despised and to turn the taunt back on those who have set themselves against his work (vv. 4–5). Then he and the people go on building, and the wall is joined all the way round to half its height, because the people’s hearts were in the work (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The first weapon is laughter. Nehemiah does not answer it; he takes it to God and goes back to the wall, and the best reply to they cannot was a wall at half its height.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was angry and greatly enraged, and he jeered at the Jews. And he said in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria, "What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they restore it for themselves? Will they sacrifice? Will they finish up in a day? Will they revive the stones out of the heaps of rubbish, and burned ones at that?" Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, "Yes, what they are building— if a fox goes up on it he will break down their stone wall!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The enemies’ first weapon is ridicule: public scorn meant to make God’s people feel feeble and their work foolish.

He jeered at the Jews. He jeers in public, “in the presence of his brothers and of the army of Samaria”, which means it is meant to be carried back to the builders. Laughter is cheaper than soldiers, and sometimes it works as well.

What are these feeble Jews doing? Five questions, each a small dose of doubt. Are you strong enough? Do you think you can pray it up? Do you know how long this will take? And the cleverest one last. Limestone that has been through a fire goes soft and crumbles; stones dug out of burned rubble were close to useless. He was not wrong about the stones.

Will they revive the stones? But look at his verb. Revive means make alive, the word Ezra used when he thanked God for “a little reviving” (Ezra 9:8). Can dead stones come to life? Sanballat meant it as a joke, but it is exactly what God does: “As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men … you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:4–5). God builds with burned and broken material; it is the only material he has ever had.

If a fox goes up on it. A fox weighs next to nothing, and the fox was the animal of Jerusalem’s ruin: “Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it” (Lamentations 5:18), in Hebrew the same creature. Tobiah is saying that Zion is still what Lamentations said it was, a place for wild dogs and foxes.

The weapon of the sneer. In much of the West today the pressure on faith is not the sword but the smile. Few will hurt you for believing; many will find it quaint. Mockery does not argue; it isolates. It makes conviction feel like bad manners, until the believer wonders whether everyone sensible has moved on. And it works because most of us live on approval far more than we admit; ridicule exposes that idol by threatening it. Nehemiah’s answer was not a cleverer reply. He turned to God (vv. 4–5) and went back to work (v. 6), because his standing rested somewhere the laughter could not reach. Ours can too. The gospel tells of one who was mocked far worse, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42), and who bore it so that the verdict that finally counts on us is the Father’s welcome, not the crowd’s laugh. People who have heard that verdict can afford to look foolish for a while.
verseByVerse.note: In the Hebrew numbering 4:1–6 is 3:33–38, and 4:7–23 is 4:1–17.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O our God, for we are despised. Turn back their taunt on their own heads and give them up to be plundered in a land where they are captives. Do not cover their guilt, and let not their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked you to anger in the presence of the builders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah answers the mockers not with words to them but with prayer to God, handing over to him both the insult and the judgment.

Hear, O our God. Nehemiah does not answer Sanballat; he speaks to God. Taunt is the word for the “shame” of 1:3, and he asks God to send it back where it came from. The second sentence is borrowed from Jeremiah, whose enemies were plotting to kill him: “Forgive not their iniquity, nor blot out their sin from your sight” (Jeremiah 18:23).

A prayer against enemies. A Christian may ask how this sits with “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). First, Nehemiah takes no revenge; he hands the matter to God, which is exactly what the New Testament commands: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). Second, his reason is not a private insult but that they “provoked you to anger”: they were setting themselves against God’s own work. Third, the cry for justice is not abolished in the New Testament; the martyrs under the altar still pray, “how long before you will judge and avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10)?

The Christian’s first prayer. But the Christian’s first prayer for an enemy is now Stephen’s: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60). If someone has wronged you badly, you may tell God the whole of it and ask him to deal justly. You may not take it into your own hands, and you pray for their repentance before anything else. That is beyond us by nature. It becomes possible because we were God’s enemies when Christ died for us (Romans 5:10), and his Spirit teaches us to forgive as we have been forgiven. Justice for the one who never repents is safe with God.

verseByVerse.quote: So we built the wall. And all the wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind to work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah’s whole reply to the mockery is to keep building, and the wall is joined all round to half its height because the people’s hearts are in the work.

So we built the wall. That is the whole of Nehemiah’s reply to the five questions and the fox: he prayed, and then he laid the next stone. The separate gangs of chapter 3 had met, and there was now one continuous wall right round the city, at half height.

For the people had a mind to work. A mind to work is, literally, a heart to work: the people’s hearts were in it. Mockery can take the heart out of a people faster than any army; here it did not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As the gaps close, the danger grows outside and inside, and the answer is to remember the Lord. Enemies from every side plot to attack, and the people pray and set a guard day and night (vv. 7–9). Within Judah the burden-bearers are exhausted and the rubble seems endless, the enemy boasts of a surprise attack, and families living near the enemy beg their men to come home (vv. 10–12). Nehemiah stations the people by families at the weakest places, armed, and tells them not to fear but to remember the great and awesome Lord and to fight for their homes (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The cure Nehemiah gives for fear is to remember who God is: what he had said to God in his first prayer, he now says to the people.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem was going forward and that the breaches were beginning to be closed, they were very angry. And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it. And we prayed to our God and set a guard as a protection against them day and night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the gaps close, the enemies close in from every side, and God’s people answer with both prayer and a guard.

They all plotted together. Look at the map: Samaria to the north, the Ammonites to the east, the Arabs to the south, and now the Ashdodites from the old Philistine coast to the west. In chapter 2 there were three enemies; now Jerusalem is surrounded. The laughter stopped when the gaps began to close, and the plotting began.

We prayed to our God and set a guard. They prayed and set a guard: not one instead of the other. Faith that refuses to lock the door is presumption, and a locked door without prayer is not safety.

verseByVerse.quote: In Judah it was said, "The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. There is too much rubble. By ourselves we will not be able to rebuild the wall." And our enemies said, "They will not know or see till we come among them and kill them and stop the work." At that time the Jews who lived near them came from all directions and said to us ten times, "You must return to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most dangerous discouragement comes from inside: exhausted workers, an endless heap of rubble, and loving families begging them to come home.

The strength of those who bear the burdens is failing. This time the voice is Judah’s own, and it is a lament. The men carrying earth and stone up the slope were spent, and the heaps of rubble never seemed to get smaller.

The middle of the work. It came straight after “half its height”. The start of a great work has its own energy, and the end has the finish line in sight; the middle is where the strength goes. Many readers are at a halfway point just now, a marriage in its hard years, a long illness, a work for God with no end in sight, and know this sentence from the inside: “By ourselves we will not be able”. That is true. It was never meant to be done by themselves. To the builders of the temple a lifetime before, God had said through Zechariah, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 4:6), and that Spirit now lives in his people.

You must return to us. Then the enemy boasts of a surprise attack (v. 11), and Jews from the villages near the enemy urge their families “ten times”, over and over, to come home. The hardest pressure to go back often comes from people who love you.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 12 is compressed, and its last words can be read more than one way. The ESV takes them as Jews living near the enemy calling their men home; the KJV reads them as a warning that the enemy would come at the builders from every side. Either way, the pressure was coming from all directions.

verseByVerse.quote: So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in open places, I stationed the people by their clans, with their swords, their spears, and their bows. And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah meets fear by putting families together at the weakest places and turning their eyes from the enemy to the great and awesome Lord.

I stationed the people by their clans. He put the people where the wall was lowest and where the enemy could see them, and he put them there by families. A man stands his ground when his own brothers are beside him.

Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome. “Great and awesome” are the first words of Nehemiah’s prayer in Susa (1:5). Months of praying had put them into his mouth, and now he gives them to the people. The cure for fear is not a better estimate of the enemy but a memory of God: fear grows when the enemy fills the whole view, and shrinks when the Lord is remembered for what he is.

And fight. Remembering God did not make the fighting unnecessary; it made it possible.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Our God Will Fight for Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God frustrates the enemy’s plan, and his people return to work, ready to fight. Once the plot is known, everyone goes back to his own stretch of wall (v. 15). From then on half of Nehemiah’s men build and half stand armed, every builder wears a sword, and the burden-bearers work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other (vv. 16–18). A trumpeter stays at Nehemiah’s side, so that wherever the attack comes all can rally, for “Our God will fight for us” (vv. 19–20). They work from dawn till the stars come out, sleep inside the city, and never take off their clothes (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Fight for your brothers (v. 14) and our God will fight for us (v. 20) come in the same speech. God's fighting did not make theirs unnecessary, and theirs did not make his unnecessary.

verseByVerse.quote: When our enemies heard that it was known to us and that God had frustrated their plan, we all returned to the wall, each to his work. From that day on, half of my servants worked on construction, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail. And the leaders stood behind the whole house of Judah, who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens were loaded in such a way that each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other. And each of the builders had his sword strapped at his side while he built. The man who sounded the trumpet was beside me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God frustrates the plot, the people go straight back to work, now building with one hand and holding a weapon with the other.

Each to his work. The attack depended on surprise, and the surprise was lost. Nehemiah credits God, and the result is not a celebration but a return to work, “each to his work”, back to the particular stretch of wall that was his.

With one hand. Building with one hand and holding a weapon with the other is a true picture of God’s people in this world, with one correction. The church is not given a literal sword: “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Its sword is “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). But the posture is the same. We build, and we guard what we build, and we never get a season in which only one of those is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: And I said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, "The work is great and widely spread, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another. In the place where you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally to us there. Our God will fight for us." So we labored at the work, and half of them held the spears from the break of dawn until the stars came out. I also said to the people at that time, "Let every man and his servant pass the night within Jerusalem, that they may be a guard for us by night and may labor by day." So neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the men of the guard who followed me, none of us took off our clothes; each kept his weapon at his right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spread thin along the wall, the people are held together by a trumpet and a promise, and their leader shares every hardship with them.

Our God will fight for us. The words echo Moses at the Red Sea: “The LORD will fight for you” (Exodus 14:14). The trumpet was the practical half of that faith: the builders were far apart, so wherever the attack came, all would run to its sound. God fights, and his people fight, and when they win it is still God’s victory.

Within Jerusalem. Everyone slept inside the city so there would be guards by night and workers by day (v. 22), and the governor slept in his clothes with his weapon beside him, like every other man on the wall.

He faced the enemies alone. Nehemiah was a leader who asked nothing he did not do himself. Christ, our leader, went further. He did not only share his people’s watch; he faced alone the enemies they could not survive, sin and death, and defeated them. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

Uncertain wording. The last words of verse 23 are obscure in Hebrew. The ESV reads that each kept his weapon at his right hand; the KJV, that they put off their clothes only for washing. Either way the point is plain: no one let down his guard.

keyVerse.quote: And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes.”
keyVerse.note: Here is the chapter’s answer to mockery, weariness and threat. Fear grows when the enemy fills the whole view; it shrinks when the Lord is remembered as “great and awesome”, the words Nehemiah had prayed in Susa (1:5). Remembering God does not make the struggle unnecessary; it makes it possible.

4.reflection:
Sanballat’s weapon was ridicule (vv. 1–3). Where do you feel the pressure of the sneer rather than the sword? How does knowing that Christ was mocked for us, and that the Father welcomes us, free us to look foolish for a while?

Nehemiah answered his enemies only in prayer, asking God to deal with them (vv. 4–5). How does this prayer sit beside Jesus’ “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34) and Stephen’s prayer (Acts 7:60)? What do you do with the anger you feel toward someone who has wronged you?

The strongest discouragement came from inside: “By ourselves we will not be able” (v. 10), and loved ones urging the builders home (v. 12). Where are you halfway up the wall right now? What would it mean to “remember the Lord” there (v. 14)?

The people “prayed to our God and set a guard” (v. 9), and built with one hand while holding a weapon with the other (v. 17). How do prayer and practical watchfulness belong together in a Christian’s life, family and church? What are we called to build, and what must we guard?

5.title: The Enemy Within
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there arose a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers.<sup>2</sup>For there were those who said, "With our sons and our daughters, we are many. So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive."<sup>3</sup>There were also those who said, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine."<sup>4</sup>And there were those who said, "We have borrowed money for the king's tax on our fields and our vineyards.<sup>5</sup>Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children. I said to them, "You are exacting interest, each from his brother." And I held a great assembly against them<sup>8</sup>and said to them, "We, as far as we are able, have bought back our Jewish brothers who have been sold to the nations, but you even sell your brothers that they may be sold to us!"
