Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies?<sup>10</sup>Moreover, I and my brothers and my servants are lending them money and grain. Let us abandon this exacting of interest.<sup>11</sup>Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them."<sup>12</sup>Then they said, "We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say." And I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised.<sup>13</sup>I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, "So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied." And all the assembly said "Amen" and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.<sup>14</sup>Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor.<sup>15</sup>The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God.<sup>16</sup>I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.<sup>17</sup>Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us.<sup>18</sup>Now what was prepared at my expense for each day was one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people.<sup>19</sup>Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
5.overview:
Where we are. The wall stands at half its height, built under threat with a sword at every builder’s side (chapter 4). Now the most dangerous crisis of all breaks out, not outside the city but inside it.

The message. God’s people cannot be rebuilt on the backs of their own poor. A people God redeemed from slavery must not sell one another back into it, and the fear of God shows first in how the strong treat the weak, in money, land and power. Nehemiah calls the rich to give back what they have taken, and he can, because for twelve years he has refused what was his by right.

Why it was said. The returned community was small and poor, squeezed by famine and by a Persian tax paid in silver (see the introduction). Its nobles were doing what the powerful usually do in hard times, and the law they lived under forbade it among the redeemed.

How the chapter makes its case. Families cry out: they need grain, they have mortgaged their land, they have borrowed for the king’s tax, and their children are going into slavery (vv. 1–5). Nehemiah is angry, thinks before he speaks, and charges the nobles in a great assembly: we buy our brothers back, and you sell them (vv. 6–8). He calls them to the fear of God and to the honour of his name before the nations, and demands that land and interest be returned that very day (vv. 9–11). They agree and swear before the priests, and the assembly says “Amen” and praises the LORD (vv. 12–13). Then Nehemiah sets his own twelve years beside the charge, “because of the fear of God”, and leaves the record with God (vv. 14–19).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Nehemiah is a redeemer who spends his own silver buying back brothers sold to the nations (v. 8), and a governor who will not lord it over the people (v. 15). Christ is the Redeemer that pattern points to: he bought his people back not with silver but with himself, and “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). And the need is plain: even inside a rebuilt wall God’s people devour one another, until a grace stronger than law changes their hearts.

For us. Ask how the church treats its poorer members, and how you use any advantage over people who need you. Give back what was wrongly taken, and lead as a servant. The gospel frees us for both: we were bought back at a cost we could never repay, and the redeemed do not sell their brothers.
5.theology:
How God's people handle money among themselves is part of keeping covenant with God, not a side issue. The law forbade interest from a poor brother because God had brought them all out of slavery (Lev 25:36-42); to re-enslave a brother was to undo the Exodus. And a leader's authority to call others to that standard rests on his own practice: Nehemiah demanded the fear of God and had lived by it for twelve years.

Rulers lord it over their people; Nehemiah would not, and Christ went further still (vv. 14-18 below). Nehemiah's prayer to be remembered is that of a servant who knows his record is safe with God and his standing rests on God's steadfast love.
5.examples:
Nehemiah was very angry, and took counsel with himself before he spoke. His charge was simple: we buy our brothers back, and you sell them. He said let us stop, because his own household had been lending too.

In twelve years as governor, with famine and taxes pressing, he bought no land and fed 150 men a day without drawing his allowance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Let Us Abandon This Exacting of Interest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The most dangerous enemy in this chapter is not Sanballat but greed inside the wall. Hungry families cry out against their own nobles: they have pledged fields, vineyards and houses for grain in a famine, borrowed to pay the king’s tax, and seen their children enslaved (vv. 1–5). Nehemiah, angry but deliberate, charges the nobles before a great assembly with profiting from their brothers, the very people God had freed from slavery in Egypt (vv. 6–8). He appeals to the fear of God and to the taunts of the nations, puts his own household under the same rule, and demands that everything be returned that day (vv. 9–11). The nobles agree and swear, and the assembly praises the LORD (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The most dangerous enemy of this chapter is not Sanballat but a brother with a list of debts. God had freed them all from slavery in Egypt, and to make a brother a slave again was to undo that rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there arose a great outcry of the people and of their wives against their Jewish brothers. For there were those who said, "With our sons and our daughters, we are many. So let us get grain, that we may eat and keep alive." There were also those who said, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain because of the famine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the building, the poor of Judah cry out against their own wealthy brothers, because famine has driven them to pledge everything they own simply to eat.

A great outcry. The wall is at half height, the enemy is circling, and the loudest cry in Jerusalem is not against Sanballat but against fellow Jews. It echoes Egypt, where God “heard their cry because of their taskmasters” (Exodus 3:7), and the law had joined that cry to money-lending: “if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate” (Exodus 22:27). The people redeemed from taskmasters had taskmasters again, and they were their own brothers.

And of their wives. The women who had to feed the children cried loudest. A famine had come (v. 3), the king’s tax had not stopped for it (v. 4), and the families at the bottom were going under.

With our sons and our daughters. The complaints rise in order: first grain, then the land pledged to buy it, and then, in verse 5, the children.

verseByVerse.quote: And there were those who said, "We have borrowed money for the king's tax on our fields and our vineyards. Now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children are as their children. Yet we are forcing our sons and our daughters to be slaves, and some of our daughters have already been enslaved, but it is not in our power to help it, for other men have our fields and our vineyards."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Debt for the king’s tax has driven families to the bottom: their children are being sold into slavery, and with their land gone they have no way to buy them back.

The king’s tax. Persia taxed the land in silver whether the harvest came or not. A farmer with no crop and a tax demand borrowed from whoever had silver, and the ones who had silver were the nobles.

Our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers. This is the bottom of the spiral: first the crop, then the field, then the child. We are the same blood, they say; my child is worth what his child is worth. And there is no way back, because the fields that could have redeemed her belong to someone else now.

Why could an Israelite sell his child? The law allowed a family sunk in debt to pay it off in labour, but it set firm limits on that bitter remedy: a brother was to be treated as a hired worker, not a slave, set free in the seventh year or at the Jubilee, and sent away with gifts (Exodus 21:2–11; Leviticus 25:39–43; Deuteronomy 15:12–15). It was a safety net against starvation, not a licence to own people, and a world away from the man-stealing Scripture condemns (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10). The nobles were tearing even that net, using a famine to take the land that was a family’s only way back to freedom.

Why this matters. You can build a magnificent defence round a people and still let them be devoured from inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words. I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles and the officials. I said to them, "You are exacting interest, each from his brother." And I held a great assembly against them and said to them, "We, as far as we are able, have bought back our Jewish brothers who have been sold to the nations, but you even sell your brothers that they may be sold to us!" They were silent and could not find a word to say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah is rightly angry, thinks before he acts, and confronts the nobles in public: others buy brothers back from slavery, and they sell them into it.

I was very angry. The text does not apologise; a father selling his daughter to pay interest to a rich Jew ought to make a godly man angry. But “I took counsel with myself”, literally, his heart deliberated within him. The anger went through his heart before it went through his mouth.

We … have bought back our Jewish brothers. Nehemiah and others had spent their own silver redeeming Jews sold abroad, while the nobles sold Jews into slavery at home. The law forbade it for a reason that goes back to the Exodus: “they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves” (Leviticus 25:42). To enslave a brother was to undo what God had done. The nobles “were silent and could not find a word to say.”

A test for our anger. Nehemiah’s anger was on someone else’s behalf, not his own; it waited until it had thought; and it went straight to the people responsible, openly. Anger on my own account, unthought, and expressed to everyone except the person concerned, has none of the three. None of us manages this by temper or resolve: self-control is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), and where our anger has wounded, the way back is confession to God and to the one we hurt.

Where Christians differ: is charging interest sin? For much of church history all lending at interest was forbidden, and some Christians still refuse it. Others, since the Reformation, distinguish the loan to a poor neighbour in distress, which the law protected (Exodus 22:25), from other lending; even Israel might charge interest to a foreigner (Deuteronomy 23:20). This commentary’s view: ordinary lending, savings and mortgages at fair interest are lawful; what Scripture condemns is profiting from another’s desperation, as these nobles did, taking fields and children as pledges. Care for the poor is not optional.

Uncertain wording. “Exacting interest” (vv. 7, 10) is built on a Hebrew word for lending, and scholars debate whether it means charging interest, as the ESV takes it, or lending against pledges such as fields and children. The two went together in practice (v. 11), and either way the nobles were profiting from a brother’s need.

verseByVerse.quote: So I said, "The thing that you are doing is not good. Ought you not to walk in the fear of our God to prevent the taunts of the nations our enemies? Moreover, I and my brothers and my servants are lending them money and grain. Let us abandon this exacting of interest. Return to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive orchards, and their houses, and the percentage of money, grain, wine, and oil that you have been exacting from them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah calls the nobles back to the fear of God, whose name their greed was shaming before the nations, and demands that they give everything back at once.

Walk in the fear of our God. The phrase is in the very law they were breaking: “Take no interest from him or profit, but fear your God, that your brother may live beside you” (Leviticus 25:36). Moses had set the fear of God against the moneylender’s profit, and Nehemiah simply quotes the reason back.

The taunts of the nations. It is the word the book began with, the “shame” of 1:3. The wall was built to silence the neighbours’ sneer, and the nobles inside it were giving them fresh cause. What would Sanballat say of a God whose people sold each other’s children?

Let us abandon this exacting of interest. He says “let us”, not exempting his own household, which had been lending too; as in his first prayer (1:6), he puts his own name inside the rebuke. And he asks for no gradual easing, but the land and the interest back “this very day”.

Uncertain wording. “The percentage” is literally “the hundredth”, probably one per cent a month; some suggest that, with a slight change of letters, it should read “the loan”. Either way, what had been taken was to be returned.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "We will restore these and require nothing from them. We will do as you say." And I called the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised. I also shook out the fold of my garment and said, "So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this promise. So may he be shaken out and emptied." And all the assembly said "Amen" and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nobles promise to give everything back, Nehemiah binds them by oath, and the assembly praises God.

We will do as you say. To their credit, they did not argue. But promises made in a crowded room evaporate on the way home, so Nehemiah had them swear before the priests.

I also shook out the fold of my garment. The fold of a robe was a man’s pocket. Nehemiah turned his inside out and shook it empty in front of them: that is what God will do to the house of the man who breaks this oath. Paul made a similar gesture at Corinth, when the synagogue turned on him (Acts 18:6).

All the assembly said “Amen.” A debt cancellation ended in worship. When wrong money is given back, God is praised; it is one of the plainest tests of whether a revival is real.

The one who kept it. None of us keeps this law of open-handed love perfectly. Christ did, and “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). So the nobles show the way back for anyone this chapter convicts: not despair, but confession and restitution before a God who forgives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–19 — Because of the Fear of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nehemiah could call others to the fear of God because he had lived by it himself. For twelve years as governor he refused the food allowance that earlier governors had squeezed from the people, bought no land in a famine when land was cheap, kept his servants at work on the wall, and fed 150 men and visiting foreigners every day at his own expense, because the people were already carrying too heavy a load (vv. 14–18). He did not publish this to the people or ask them for thanks. He asked God to remember it (v. 19), the first of four such prayers in the book, and left his record in God’s hands.
verseByVerse.theology: The first of Nehemiah's four prayers to be remembered (5:19; 13:14, 22, 31). It is not a claim to have earned God's favour; the man who prays it will also ask to be spared according to the greatness of your steadfast love (13:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, twelve years, neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowance of the governor. The former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people and took from them for their daily ration forty shekels of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear of God. I also persevered in the work on this wall, and we acquired no land, and all my servants were gathered there for the work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For twelve years Nehemiah refused the governor’s allowance and bought no land, because the fear of God ruled his use of power.

Because of the fear of God. His predecessors had lived off the people, and even their servants lorded it over them. Nehemiah lived by the fear he had just demanded of the nobles (v. 9), for twelve years (about 445 to 433 BC). And lording it over people is exactly what Jesus said rulers do: “the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them”, while “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:25, 28).

We acquired no land. In a famine, with families mortgaging their fields, land could be had for almost nothing. The governor bought none, and kept his own servants on the wall, not on estates.

Why we no longer trust the people in charge. Trust in leaders, political, corporate and religious, has fallen steeply in our generation, and not without reason. Too many have treated office as a ladder: the generous allowance, the property bought cheap in someone else’s crisis, one set of rules for the governed and another for the governors. So we suspect every claim to serve of being a bid to rule (see the note on John 18:38). Nehemiah, not flawless, is a quiet answer: for twelve years he turned down what everyone agreed was his due. A leader who fears no one above him will sooner or later use the people below him. Cynicism cannot cure that; it can only expect it. The cure is authority that is itself under authority, and the Bible’s fullest picture of it is a King who knelt with a towel and then went to a cross for the people he ruled. Those who follow him are meant to show that kind of power in every office, kitchen and committee they are given.

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 is compressed in Hebrew: the former governors took “bread and wine” and forty shekels of silver (about a pound in weight), and it is not clear whether the silver was a daily charge, as the ESV takes it, or a sum on top of the food, as older translations read it. Either way the burden was heavy.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, there were at my table 150 men, Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the nations that were around us. Now what was prepared at my expense for each day was one ox and six choice sheep and birds, and every ten days all kinds of wine in abundance. Yet for all this I did not demand the food allowance of the governor, because the service was too heavy on this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah paid for a large official table himself rather than add to the load of a worn-out people.

There were at my table 150 men. A governor’s table was an official duty: officials to feed, envoys from neighbouring peoples to entertain, an ox and six choice sheep a day. Nehemiah paid for it.

Because the service was too heavy. “The service” is the labour on the wall. Men carrying stone all day, with a sword at their side and a famine at home, were not going to be taxed to feed the governor as well.

A greater Governor. There is a greater Governor who did far more than decline an allowance: “For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). Nehemiah bought back brothers sold to the nations with his silver (v. 8). Christ bought back his people with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember for my good, O my God, all that I have done for this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah leaves his unseen service with God, and asks him to remember it for good.

Is this prayer boastful? It is not a bid for salvation. The man who prays it (and three more like it, 13:14, 22, 31) also asks God to “spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love” (13:22); he knows he will be kept by mercy. What he asks is that the service he gave, unseen and unpaid, not be lost.

All that I have done for this people. He did not publish his twelve years of self-denial to the people or ask them for thanks. He told God. The governor who went without had a Master who would not forget: “God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name” (Hebrews 6:10). Nothing given up for his people’s sake, in an office or a kitchen or a hospital corridor, goes unrecorded.

keyVerse.quote: But I did not do so, because of the fear of God.
keyVerse.note: “The fear of God” ties the chapter together: Nehemiah demanded it of the nobles (v. 9) and had lived by it as governor for twelve years. It shows what keeps power safe in human hands: not a lack of opportunity, but a ruler who knows he answers to a greater Ruler, the one whose Son came not to be served but to serve.

5.reflection:
The worst threat in this chapter came from inside the wall, from brothers profiting from brothers (vv. 1–5). Where might a church today let its poorer or weaker members be quietly devoured, and what would it look like to notice?

Nehemiah was very angry, yet he “took counsel with myself” before he spoke, and then went straight to the people responsible (vv. 6–7). How does that compare with the way your anger usually works? What would change if you applied his three tests?

Nehemiah said “let us” stop, including his own household, and he could ask the nobles to give up their gain because he had given up his own for twelve years (vv. 10, 14–18). Why does a leader’s own practice matter so much? Where are you asking of others what you have not done yourself?

Nehemiah bought back brothers with his silver; Christ “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). How should knowing that you were bought back at such cost shape the way you use money, time and power over others this week?

6.title: Finished
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that there was no breach left in it (although up to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates),<sup>2</sup>Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm.<sup>3</sup>And I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?"<sup>4</sup>And they sent to me four times in this way, and I answered them in the same manner.<sup>5</sup>In the same way Sanballat for the fifth time sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand.<sup>6</sup>In it was written, "It is reported among the nations, and Geshem also says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports you wish to become their king.<sup>7</sup>And you have also set up prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, 'There is a king in Judah.' And now the king will hear of these reports. So now come and let us take counsel together."<sup>8</sup>Then I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind."<sup>9</sup>For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now, O God, strengthen my hands.<sup>10</sup>Now when I went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night."<sup>11</sup>But I said, "Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in."<sup>12</sup>And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.<sup>13</sup>For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me.<sup>14</sup>Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these things that they did, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid.<sup>15</sup>So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days.<sup>16</sup>And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.<sup>17</sup>Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them.<sup>18</sup>For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah: and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as his wife.<sup>19</sup>Also they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to make me afraid.
6.overview:
Where we are. The wall is finished except for the doors in the gates (v. 1). Open threats have failed (chapter 4) and the greed inside the city has been dealt with (chapter 5), so now the enemies turn from the wall to the man building it.

The message. When God’s work cannot be stopped, the enemy aims at the worker: his time, his name, his courage and his conscience. Nehemiah stays at his post, answers a lie in one sentence, prays for strength, and will not buy his safety with a sin; and God finishes the work so plainly that even its enemies see his hand in it. Yet the chapter ends with a warning: the one gap no wall can close is the one opened from inside.

Why it was said. The returned community lived among neighbours who could write to the Persian king, hire prophets and marry into leading families (see the introduction). They needed to know how to stand when the pressure turned personal and subtle, and that God’s work stands by God’s help.

How the chapter makes its case. Four invitations to a meeting at Ono get the same answer: “I am doing a great work and I cannot come down” (vv. 1–4). An open letter accuses Nehemiah of plotting to be king; he denies it in one sentence and prays, “O God, strengthen my hands” (vv. 5–9). A hired prophet urges him to hide in the temple; he sees that God would never send him to sin, and hands his enemies to God (vv. 10–14). The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the nations lose heart, seeing “the help of our God” (vv. 15–16). But Tobiah’s letters keep coming, carried by Judah’s own nobles, bound to him by oath and marriage (vv. 17–19).

Where it leads. By promise, and by pattern. The slander “There is a king in Judah” (v. 7) was false of Nehemiah but true of God’s promise: a King had been sworn to Judah, and when he came, that charge was written above his cross, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (John 19:19). Like Nehemiah, he would not come down from his great work when mocked (Matthew 27:40). And Christ builds a city with no traitor inside, where “nothing unclean will ever enter” (Revelation 21:27).

For us. Expect pressure on God’s work to become personal, and do not answer it by leaving your post, defending yourself endlessly, or doing wrong to stay safe. Pray for strength, test every voice by God’s word, and watch the loyalties that open doors from inside. The work is his, and he finishes it.
6.theology:
God's work is finished by God's help, and even his enemies are made to see it (v. 16). A message that urges sin for safety’s sake is not from God, however holy it sounds (v. 12).

The slander that Nehemiah meant to be king was false, but God really had promised Judah a king (see vv. 5-9). Christ is the builder whose city has no enemy inside its walls.
6.examples:
Nehemiah gave the same answer four times, answered a long lie with a single sentence, and would not buy his safety with a sin. The enemies set out to make him afraid and ended up afraid themselves.

Yet a man who built two sections of the wall had married his daughter into Tobiah's family.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — I Am Doing a Great Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the wall could not be stopped, the enemy aimed at the builder: first his time, then his reputation. With the wall complete except for the doors (v. 1), Sanballat and Geshem invite Nehemiah four times to a meeting in the plain of Ono, far from Jerusalem, meaning to harm him, and four times he refuses, because the work is too great to leave (vv. 2–4). A fifth message comes as an open letter, spreading the charge that he plans to rebel and has prophets proclaiming him king (vv. 5–7). Nehemiah answers in one sentence, names the lie as invented, sees that its aim is to make the builders’ hands drop, and prays, “O God, strengthen my hands” (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: When the wall could not be stopped, the enemy aimed at the man: first his time, then his reputation. Nehemiah gave up neither.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Sanballat and Tobiah and Geshem the Arab and the rest of our enemies heard that I had built the wall and that there was no breach left in it (although up to that time I had not set up the doors in the gates), Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm. And I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?" And they sent to me four times in this way, and I answered them in the same manner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the wall complete, the enemies try four times to lure Nehemiah to a meeting far from Jerusalem, and four times he refuses to leave the work God has given him.

No breach left in it. The wall now runs right round the city; only the gates wait for their doors. Everything else has failed, so the enemy changes target, from the wall to the builder.

In the plain of Ono. Ono lay in the lowlands toward the coast, a long day’s ride from Jerusalem, on neutral ground. (Hakkephirim may be a place name, or simply mean “the villages”.) It sounded like diplomacy; it was a trap.

I cannot come down. Ono was literally down, off the hills, but the words say more. The work was great because it was God’s, and a man given it cannot spend his days in meetings with people who want it to fail.

Another told to come down. At the cross the crowd shouted, “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40). Not a prophecy, but the same faithfulness at infinitely greater cost: he stayed until “It is finished” (John 19:30).

Four times in this way. Persistence is the enemy’s method, and it works on most of us: the fourth request feels unreasonable to refuse. Which of the invitations crowding your own calendar would take you off the wall God has given you? Not everything that asks for your time is wicked; some of it only makes sure the great work does not get done.
verseByVerse.note: Ono lay in the coastal plain, some twenty miles from Jerusalem and far from help.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way Sanballat for the fifth time sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand. In it was written, "It is reported among the nations, and Geshem also says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports you wish to become their king. And you have also set up prophets to proclaim concerning you in Jerusalem, 'There is a king in Judah.' And now the king will hear of these reports. So now come and let us take counsel together." Then I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind." For they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now, O God, strengthen my hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sanballat publishes a slander that Nehemiah plans to be king; Nehemiah denies it in one sentence and asks God to strengthen his hands.

With an open letter in his hand. Unsealed, it was read by the servant who carried it and by anyone along the road: the slander was published before Nehemiah saw it.

You and the Jews intend to rebel. The charge was dangerous because it had worked before: under this same king, a letter calling Jerusalem “that rebellious and wicked city” had stopped the building by force (Ezra 4:12, 23; see the introduction). “Come and let us take counsel together” was the trap of Ono again, with a threat attached.

There is a king in Judah. False about Nehemiah, who never claimed a crown; but God really had promised Judah a king. Two generations earlier Zechariah had proclaimed in Jerusalem, “Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). When he came, the charge Sanballat invented was nailed over his head: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (John 19:19).

No such things as you say have been done. One sentence of denial, not a long defence; a man who answers every slander at length has already stopped building. Then he prayed. At the start “they strengthened their hands for the good work” (2:18); now the enemy wants those hands to drop, and he asks God to strengthen them. That is still where strength for God’s work comes from (Hebrews 12:12).

Uncertain wording. “O God” is not in the Hebrew at the end of verse 9, which reads simply “and now strengthen my hands”. Most translations take it as one of Nehemiah’s short prayers; some read it as a statement, “so I strengthened my hands”. Both fit a man who prays and then works harder.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — With the Help of Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fear was the enemies’ last weapon, and it turned back on them. A prophet named Shemaiah, hired by Tobiah and Sanballat, urges Nehemiah to hide inside the temple from assassins; Nehemiah refuses, because a leader should not run and a layman may not enter the holy place, and he sees that a message urging sin cannot be from God (vv. 10–14). The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the nations who meant to frighten the builders are afraid themselves, seeing that God had done it (vv. 15–16). Yet Judah’s nobles, tied to Tobiah by oath and marriage, keep writing to him, praise him to Nehemiah, and carry Nehemiah’s words back (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The section turns on fear: the enemies tried to make the builders afraid, and ended up afraid themselves (v. 16).

verseByVerse.quote: Now when I went into the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home, he said, "Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple. Let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you. They are coming to kill you by night." But I said, "Should such a man as I run away? And what man such as I could go into the temple and live? I will not go in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prophet urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple, and he refuses: a leader must not run, and a layman may not enter the holy place.

Shemaiah the son of Delaiah. The third attack comes in a prophet’s voice, urgent and apparently concerned: they are coming for you tonight; hide with me in the holy place and we will bar the doors. It sounds like a friend saving his life.

Should such a man as I run away? He refused for two reasons. A governor who hid would tell every builder that the danger was real and the leader was saving himself. And Nehemiah was not a priest, and the law said “any outsider who comes near shall be put to death” (Numbers 18:7). A king of Judah had once walked in to burn incense and walked out a leper for the rest of his life (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Nehemiah would not buy his safety with a sin.

The Priest who went in. Nehemiah could not enter the holy place to save his own life. Christ, the true Priest, entered the true holy place to save ours, “by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12).

Uncertain wording. Why Shemaiah was “confined to his home” is not known. The word means shut in or restrained (as when Jeremiah is “banned from going to the house of the LORD”, Jeremiah 36:5), and it may point to illness, uncleanness, or a sign acted out to match his warning.
verseByVerse.note: Shemaiah's oracle may have been framed as poetry, a short rhythmic warning designed to sound like a true prophet's.

verseByVerse.quote: And I understood and saw that God had not sent him, but he had pronounced the prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. For this purpose he was hired, that I should be afraid and act in this way and sin, and so they could give me a bad name in order to taunt me. Remember Tobiah and Sanballat, O my God, according to these things that they did, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah saw through the prophecy because it urged him to sin; it had been bought to disgrace him, and he leaves those behind it to God.

God had not sent him. How did he know? Not by some special sense, but because the prophecy told him to break God’s law. A word that tells you to sin in order to be safe did not come from God, whoever speaks it and however holy he sounds.

In order to taunt me. “Taunt” again, the word the book began with (1:3). They could not bring shame on the wall, so they tried to bring it on the man.

The prophetess Noadiah. A prophetess and other prophets had the same message: be afraid. Nehemiah takes no revenge; he hands them to God, as at 4:4–5.

Testing the spirits now. The test still holds: “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1). Counsel that urges you to do what Scripture forbids (to lie a little to protect yourself, to break a vow because the cost has risen, to hide from a duty because someone says God is telling you to) can be answered as Nehemiah answered it: “I will not go in.”

verseByVerse.quote: So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wall is finished in fifty-two days, and the enemies who tried to frighten the builders lose heart, seeing that God has done it.

In fifty-two days. Elul is August into September, five months after Nehemiah spoke to the king in Nisan (2:1), with the long road from Susa in between.

Could a wall go up so fast? Much of it was repair: the old foundations and much of the fallen stone were still there, and chapter 3 shows the whole population at work at once, each family on its own short stretch. Many archaeologists also think Nehemiah’s circuit was smaller than the city of the kings, enclosing mainly the City of David and the temple hill. A later Jewish historian gives a much longer period, but the book’s figure is plain, and believable for a people working that hard under threat.

All the nations around us were afraid. The fear the enemies manufactured (vv. 9, 13, 14, 19) came home to them; the men who laughed at “these feeble Jews” (4:2) looked at the finished wall and saw God in it. It is the song of the returned exiles: “then they said among the nations, ‘The LORD has done great things for them’” (Psalm 126:2). God sometimes makes his enemies his witnesses, and Nehemiah lets them say it: the work was done “with the help of our God.”

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew consonants for “were afraid” can also be read “saw”, as some older translations take them (the King James Version among them). The ESV’s reading fits the chapter’s theme of fear turned back on those who spread it.
verseByVerse.note: Counting back fifty-two days from 25 Elul puts the start of the work early in the month Ab, in high summer.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah's letters came to them. For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah the son of Arah: and his son Jehohanan had taken the daughter of Meshullam the son of Berechiah as his wife. Also they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to make me afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah’s nobles, bound to Tobiah by oath and marriage, kept up a friendship with him, so the enemy had a way in that no wall could close.

The nobles of Judah sent many letters. The book is honest enough not to stop at the triumph: while the wall was going up, the nobles were writing to the enemy.

The son-in-law of Shecaniah. The sons of Arah were a family of the first return (Ezra 2:5). And Meshullam son of Berechiah had built two sections of this wall with his own hands (3:4, 30). He had built against Tobiah by day and married his daughter into Tobiah’s family.

Reported my words to him. Tobiah’s friends praised him to Nehemiah’s face and carried Nehemiah’s words back to him. The wall had closed every gap in the stone, and the enemy walked in through the family.

A warning for every work of God. Walls keep out the enemy who attacks; they do nothing against the one you marry into, correspond with and speak well of. This problem will run on to the last chapter, where Tobiah is found living in a room in the temple (13:4–9). The only city whose gates can safely stand open is the one into which “nothing unclean will ever enter” (Revelation 21:27), because its King has dealt with the enemy inside as well as the one outside.

keyVerse.quote: And when all our enemies heard of it, all the nations around us were afraid and fell greatly in their own esteem, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished with the help of our God.
keyVerse.note: Every scheme in the chapter was meant to make the builders afraid, and here the fear lands on the schemers. Nehemiah does not claim the credit; the finished wall makes even God’s enemies confess whose work it was. It is the chapter’s answer to every pressure on God’s people: what God has begun, he finishes.

6.reflection:
Nehemiah answered four identical invitations with the same words: “I am doing a great work and I cannot come down” (v. 3). What “great work” has God given you in this season, and which reasonable-sounding demands most often pull you away from it?

Faced with a public lie, Nehemiah gave one sentence of denial and then prayed, “O God, strengthen my hands” (vv. 8–9). How do you usually respond when your name is attacked? What would it look like to answer briefly, keep working and leave your reputation with God?

Nehemiah knew Shemaiah’s message was false because it urged him to break God’s law (vv. 10–13). Where might well-meaning or spiritual-sounding counsel push you towards something Scripture forbids? How can we test the voices we listen to?

The wall was finished, but the nobles kept up their ties with Tobiah (vv. 17–19). What loyalties, friendships or habits can open a door from inside in a Christian’s life or a church’s life, and how does Christ’s finished work give us both a warning and a hope here?

7.title: The People of God Counted

7.overview:
Where we are. The wall is finished and the doors are hung (6:15; 7:1). Now the city must be guarded and, harder still, filled, so the chapter turns from building with stone to building with people. Most of it is the register of the first return, made ninety years before (compare Ezra 2).

The message. A wall does not make a city; a people does. Before Nehemiah decides who will live in Jerusalem, God moves him to look back at whom God had brought home, and the long list of families, towns and temple workers is a record of God’s faithfulness to his promise to gather his scattered people (1:9). And the hard cases at the end, people who could not prove their place, leave a question only God could answer.

Why it was said. In the returned community a name on the register was a title deed to land and, for a priest, the right to serve (see the introduction). Copying the old list showed that Nehemiah’s Jerusalem was not a new start but the same people God had brought back.

How the chapter makes its case. With the doors hung, Nehemiah gives charge of the city to two God-fearing men and orders its gates and watches (vv. 1–3). The city is wide but nearly empty, and God puts it into his heart to enrol the people; he finds the register of the first return (vv. 4–5). It lists the leaders (vv. 6–7), the lay families and towns (vv. 8–38), and the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants (vv. 39–60). Then come those who could not prove their descent (vv. 61–65), the totals (vv. 66–69) and the gifts (vv. 70–72). It ends where Ezra 3 begins, with the seventh month and a people about to gather (v. 73).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it leaves open. Bethlehem is on the list, the town from which Micah promised a ruler would come (Micah 5:2), resettled by these families. And the register ends with priests who could not prove their place, waiting for God to answer. Christ is the Priest who arose, though he had no priestly genealogy at all (Hebrews 7:14–16), and through him everyone who cannot prove a place before God is given one: “to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

For us. God knows his people by name, and ordinary faithfulness is not forgotten. Look for your place before God not in a record you can produce but in Christ, and then take your place among his people: a church is not its building but the people God has gathered into it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The City Was Wide and Large
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wall round an empty city is not yet a city. With the doors hung and the temple’s gatekeepers, singers and Levites appointed, Nehemiah gives charge of Jerusalem to his brother Hanani and to Hananiah, chosen because he was faithful and feared God more than most (vv. 1–2). He orders the gates kept shut until the day is well begun and sets the citizens to guard their own streets (v. 3). But the city is large and nearly empty, with few houses rebuilt (v. 4). God puts it into his heart to enrol the people, and the first thing he finds is the register of those who came home at the first (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The fifty-two days had produced a wall round a place where hardly anyone lived, and the rest of the book is about filling it with a people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the wall had been built and I had set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites had been appointed, I gave my brother Hanani and Hananiah the governor of the castle charge over Jerusalem, for he was a more faithful and God-fearing man than many. And I said to them, "Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun is hot. And while they are still standing guard, let them shut and bar the doors. Appoint guards from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, some at their guard posts and some in front of their own homes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the wall complete, Nehemiah sets the city’s worship and security in order, and puts it in the hands of men chosen above all for faithfulness and the fear of God.

The gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites. With the doors hung, the first appointments are not soldiers but men from the temple: gatekeepers, singers and Levites. The wall was built to guard a place of worship.

A more faithful and God-fearing man. Hanani is the brother who brought the news to Susa (1:2). Hananiah, commander of the fortress by the temple, was chosen for his character: not the most able or best connected man, but “a more faithful and God-fearing man than many.” That is still the first question to ask of anyone given charge of anything in God’s house.

Until the sun is hot. The gates stay shut well into the morning, when a dawn attack is no longer possible, and the guards are the city’s own people, “some in front of their own homes.” It is the principle of chapter 3 again: a man watches best the street where his children sleep.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew can also mean “while the sun is hot”, and some read it as an order not to leave the gates open in the heat of midday, when guards rested and streets were empty. Either way, no hour was to be careless.

verseByVerse.quote: The city was wide and large, but the people within it were few, and no houses had been rebuilt. Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles and the officials and the people to be enrolled by genealogy. And I found the book of the genealogy of those who came up at the first, and I found written in it:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new wall enclosed a nearly empty city, so God moved Nehemiah to enrol the people, and he began with the record of those God had first brought home.

The people within it were few. A new wall round the hills, new doors in the gates, and inside, open ground, rubble, a scattering of families and the temple: walls for a city that did not yet exist. A church can be like that: a fine building, a well-drawn constitution, and very few people inside who know why they are there.

My God put it into my heart. It is the phrase he used of the wall itself (2:12): the census was as much from God as the wall. And the first thing he did was look at the past. Before he decided who should live in Jerusalem, he reminded himself whom God had brought home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–60 — Those Who Came Up at the First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The register shows whom God had brought home, family by family. It opens with the exiles who returned from Babylon under twelve leaders, headed by Zerubbabel and Jeshua (vv. 6–7). Then come the lay families listed by clan (vv. 8–25) and the men of towns with long histories, among them Bethlehem, Anathoth, Bethel and Jericho (vv. 26–38). Then the temple households: priests in large numbers (vv. 39–42), only a handful of Levites, singers and gatekeepers (vv. 43–45), and the temple servants and the sons of Solomon’s servants, families who may have begun as outsiders (vv. 46–60). It is almost the same list as Ezra 2, and the repetition is the point: Nehemiah’s people are the people God gathered.
verseByVerse.theology: It is the same list as Ezra 2, copied a second time, and the repetition is the point: Nehemiah's people are the people God brought home. Where the numbers differ between the copies, the differences are reported below rather than hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: These were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried into exile. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list begins with the exiles who came home from Babylon under twelve leaders, a small company standing for the whole of Israel.

They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua. Zerubbabel, of David’s line, and Jeshua the high priest led the first return about 538 BC and rebuilt the altar (Ezra 3:2).

Twelve leaders. Ezra’s copy names eleven. Twelve is the number of the tribes: this small company stood for the whole of Israel. The Nehemiah and Mordecai in the list are other men of those names, who came home ninety years before the governor telling this story.
verseByVerse.note: In Ezra's copy the eleven leaders lack the name Nahamani, which Nehemiah's includes.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Parosh, 2,172. The sons of Shephatiah, 372. The sons of Arah, 652. The sons of Pahath-moab, namely the sons of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818. The sons of Elam, 1,254. The sons of Zattu, 845. The sons of Zaccai, 760. The sons of Binnui, 648. The sons of Bebai, 628. The sons of Azgad, 2,322. The sons of Adonikam, 667. The sons of Bigvai, 2,067. The sons of Adin, 655. The sons of Ater, namely of Hezekiah, 98. The sons of Hashum, 328. The sons of Bezai, 324. The sons of Hariph, 112. The sons of Gibeon, 95.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Family by family, the register names ordinary households who left the comfort of Babylon for a ruined land, trusting God’s promise.

Then the families. Eighteen lines of names and numbers, most appearing nowhere else in the Bible. They are here because they left Babylon, where most Jews stayed, for a ruined country and an uncertain welcome, on the strength of a promise.

Why the numbers differ. A careful reader who compares this chapter with Ezra 2 will find that many of the numbers differ. The family of Adonikam is 666 in Ezra and 667 here; Azgad is 1,222 there and 2,322 here. Numbers are the easiest thing in any manuscript to miscopy, and these are two copies of one list made by hand. Some also think the two copies were brought up to date at different times.

Where Christians differ: are differences like these errors in Scripture? Many scholars count them simply as mistakes in the Bible. Others, with the historic confessions, hold that Scripture as first given is without error. This commentary’s view: these are slips that crept in as scribes copied long columns of figures, and perhaps updates to the list; the copies we have let us see them plainly. Nothing in the faith hangs on the size of the family of Azgad.

verseByVerse.quote: The men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188. The men of Anathoth, 128. The men of Beth-azmaveth, 42. The men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743. The men of Ramah and Geba, 621. The men of Michmas, 122. The men of Bethel and Ai, 123. The men of the other Nebo, 52. The sons of the other Elam, 1,254. The sons of Harim, 320. The sons of Jericho, 345. The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 721. The sons of Senaah, 3,930.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The towns on the list carry Israel’s history, and their resettlement prepared the ground for promises still to be kept, Bethlehem above all.

The men of Bethlehem. From here the list runs by towns, and the towns have histories. Bethlehem (v. 26) is the town of David, of which Micah had said, “from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel” (Micah 5:2). Some of those 188 may have been forebears of families still living there when Joseph went up “to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem” (Luke 2:4). The Ruler was born in a town that had been emptied and then resettled by people on this list.

The men of Anathoth. Anathoth (v. 27) was Jeremiah’s town. With the Babylonian army outside Jerusalem, he had bought a field there, on God’s word, as a sign that fields would again be bought in this land (Jeremiah 32:15). Here are 128 men of Anathoth, home again, on land a prophet had paid for in a siege.

Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth. Put these (v. 29) beside Gibeon (v. 25) and you have the four cities of the Gibeonites, the Canaanites who deceived Joshua and were spared (Joshua 9:17). Their descendants went into exile with Judah and came home with Judah, and in chapter 3 the men of Gibeon built a stretch of the wall. Kiriath-jearim is also where the ark stayed for decades, until David brought it up (1 Samuel 7:1–2; 2 Samuel 6:2–3). The ark had once rested in a town of the outsiders.

Michmas, Bethel and Ai, Jericho, Ono. Then Michmas, where Jonathan climbed the cliff (1 Samuel 14); Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder, and Ai, where Israel was first defeated in the land, in one line (v. 32); Jericho, whose men built beside the high priest (3:2); and Ono (v. 37), the plain where Sanballat tried to lure Nehemiah (6:2). Jewish families lived there, which is perhaps why the invitation sounded reasonable.

verseByVerse.quote: The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, namely the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Priests came home in large numbers, more than four thousand men.

The priests. Four priestly families come to 4,289 men, while the Levites, who assisted the priests, number seventy-four (v. 43). The priests had an honoured place to come home to; the Levites, whose work was carrying and serving, had mostly stayed away. When Ezra brought his own company, eighty years later, he had to send back specially for Levites because he found none (Ezra 8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites: the sons of Jeshua, namely of Kadmiel of the sons of Hodevah, 74. The singers: the sons of Asaph, 148. The gatekeepers: the sons of Shallum, the sons of Ater, the sons of Talmon, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hatita, the sons of Shobai, 138. The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, the sons of Hasupha, the sons of Tabbaoth, the sons of Keros, the sons of Sia, the sons of Padon, the sons of Lebana, the sons of Hagaba, the sons of Shalmai, the sons of Hanan, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Gahar, the sons of Reaiah, the sons of Rezin, the sons of Nekoda, the sons of Gazzam, the sons of Uzza, the sons of Paseah, the sons of Besai, the sons of Meunim, the sons of Nephushesim, the sons of Bakbuk, the sons of Hakupha, the sons of Harhur, the sons of Bazlith, the sons of Mehida, the sons of Harsha, the sons of Barkos, the sons of Sisera, the sons of Temah, the sons of Neziah, the sons of Hatipha. The sons of Solomon's servants: the sons of Sotai, the sons of Sophereth, the sons of Perida, the sons of Jaala, the sons of Darkon, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Shephatiah, the sons of Hattil, the sons of Pochereth-hazzebaim, the sons of Amon. All the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants were 392.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Singers, gatekeepers and temple servants, some of them descended from foreigners, have their place in the register of God’s people.

The singers: the sons of Asaph. The singers are the descendants of Asaph, David’s chief musician; ninety years after the return they are still singing his psalms, and Nehemiah has just appointed them again (v. 1).

The temple servants. Then the temple servants and “the sons of Solomon’s servants”, 392 between them (v. 60), probably descended from foreigners given to the work of the temple long before (Ezra 8:20). Families who began as outsiders and servants are listed in the register of God’s people, alongside the priests.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 61–73 — Until a Priest Should Arise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The register ends honestly, with the people whose place was uncertain. Three lay families could not prove they belonged to Israel, and three priestly families could not find their names in the records, so they were kept from the most holy food until a priest should arise with Urim and Thummim to give God’s answer (vv. 61–65). Then the totals: more than forty-two thousand people, with their servants, singers and animals (vv. 66–69). Governor, leaders and ordinary people gave gold, silver and priests’ garments for the work (vv. 70–72). And the chapter closes on a date, the seventh month, with Israel settled in their towns and ready for the gathering that follows (v. 73).
verseByVerse.theology: The register ends on an open question about who is a priest, and on a date.

verseByVerse.quote: The following were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not prove their fathers' houses nor their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: the sons of Delaiah, the sons of Tobiah, the sons of Nekoda, 642. Also, of the priests: the sons of Hobaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, the sons of Barzillai (who had taken a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and was called by their name). These sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but it was not found there, so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to partake of the most holy food until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some who came home could not prove they belonged, and three priestly families were barred until God should settle their case.

They could not prove their fathers’ houses. Now the hard part of the list: 642 people of three families who came home “but they could not prove their fathers’ houses nor their descent, whether they belonged to Israel” (vv. 61–62). They are not sent away, only recorded as unproven.

Excluded from the priesthood as unclean. Three families of priests searched for their names in the records and could not find them, and were barred from the most holy food “until a priest with Urim and Thummim should arise.” The Urim and Thummim were the means by which the high priest had once received God’s answer to a question. There was no one who could use them, so the question was left open, waiting for God.

The sons of Barzillai. The third family has a sad little story in the brackets of verse 63. A priest had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite, who provided for David in his flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 19:31–32), and took the famous name of his wife’s family; his descendants lost the name that made them priests. It is possible to gain a distinguished name and lose a birthright.

The sons of Hakkoz. Hakkoz was another of the three. In chapter 3 Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, built two sections of the wall (3:4, 21), and Ezra calls him “Meremoth the priest” (Ezra 8:33). Somewhere in those eighty years the family that could not find its name was found. God had not forgotten them.

A Priest with no genealogy. One Priest did arise who could not have passed this test either: “it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests” (Hebrews 7:14). He had no priestly genealogy to produce. He “has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life” (Hebrews 7:16). Everyone who cannot prove his place before God can have it through him.

The exhausting work of proving we belong. Those families searching the records are closer to us than they look. We have no genealogies, but we spend our lives producing proof all the same: the CV, the right school, the follower count, the record of being a decent person. An identity that has to be earned has to be defended every day against everyone who might be doing better, which is why so much of modern life feels like an audition that never ends. The gospel does not tell us to search harder for the right document. It tells of a Priest who had none, and who gives his own standing to those who have none either: “to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). A belonging that is given cannot be lost to the next person’s success.

Uncertain wording. No one knows exactly what the Urim and Thummim were. Kept in the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:30), they were used to seek the LORD’s judgment (Numbers 27:21), perhaps as lots giving yes or no. They are not mentioned in use after Saul’s day (1 Samuel 28:6), and this verse suggests they had been lost by the return.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337. And they had 245 singers, male and female. Their horses were 736, their mules 245, their camels 435, and their donkeys 6,720.
verseByVerse.commentary:
More than forty-two thousand came home, with their servants and animals, though the family figures do not add up to the total.

The arithmetic. The family and town figures (vv. 8–62) total 31,089, but the stated total is 42,360. Ezra’s copy has the same total, and its figures come to 29,818. Perhaps the total counts people the lists do not, such as members of other tribes or unnamed families; perhaps the difference lies in the copying. Honestly, we do not know. The singers, too, are 245 here and 200 in Ezra. None of this is hidden, and none of it touches the point: tens of thousands came home, with their servants and their donkeys, because God had said they would.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the heads of fathers' houses gave to the work. The governor gave to the treasury 1,000 darics of gold, 50 basins, 30 priests' garments and 500 minas of silver. And some of the heads of fathers' houses gave into the treasury of the work 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver. And what the rest of the people gave was 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priests' garments. So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants, and all Israel, lived in their towns. And when the seventh month had come, the people of Israel were in their towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaders and ordinary people alike gave for the work, and the list closes on the seventh month, with the people ready to gather.

The governor gave to the treasury. The governor here is probably the governor of the first return, since this is still the old register, though some think Nehemiah’s own gift is meant. Ezra’s copy gives round totals (Ezra 2:69), and these itemized gifts come close to them in silver and garments. And notice “the rest of the people”: the ordinary families gave as much gold as the heads of houses.

When the seventh month had come. The chapter’s last sentence is also how Ezra 3 opens (Ezra 3:1). Ninety years earlier the list ended, the seventh month came, and the people gathered as one man to build an altar. Now the list ends, the seventh month comes, and the next verse says “all the people gathered as one man” (8:1). This time they ask for a book. The sacrifice first, then the Word: God had given them both, and the city was about to be filled with the second.

Uncertain wording. The coin translated “darics” may be the Persian gold daric or the Greek drachma; the Hebrew word could stand for either. The mina was a weight of silver, not a coin.
verseByVerse.note: A daric was a gold coin of about 1/4 ounce, a mina about 1¼ pounds (ESV notes).

7.theology:
A wall does not make a city; a people does. Nehemiah defines the people of the rebuilt city by the people God had brought home, and the list of ordinary families is itself a record of God's faithfulness to his promise to gather (1:9).

The register leaves open who is a priest, until a priest should arise who could give God’s answer. Christ is that Priest, though he had no priestly genealogy at all (vv. 61-65).
7.examples:
A new wall stood round an empty city, and its first appointment went to a man chosen because he feared God more than most.

The towns on the list have histories: Bethlehem, where the Ruler would be born, and Anathoth, home to land a prophet had bought during the siege. And the figures that do not add up are left for the reader to see.

keyVerse.quote: Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles and the officials and the people to be enrolled by genealogy.
keyVerse.note: The wall was finished, but the city was empty, and the next step came from God as surely as the first. Nehemiah’s census looks back to the people God had already brought home, so that the rebuilt city would be filled with the people of his promise. A city, and a church, is made of people God has gathered, not of walls.

7.reflection:
Nehemiah chose Hananiah because he was “a more faithful and God-fearing man than many” (v. 2). What qualities do we tend to look for when we choose leaders in a church or a home group, and how does this verse challenge them?

The new wall surrounded a city where “the people within it were few” (v. 4). In what ways can a church have the walls without the people? What does it mean for you to take your place among God’s gathered people, not just admire the building?

The register is full of ordinary families who left Babylon on the strength of a promise, and towns with a history, including Bethlehem (vv. 8–38). Why do you think God keeps lists like this in Scripture? What does it tell you about how he regards ordinary faithfulness?

Some could not prove they belonged, and had to wait for a priest to settle their case (vv. 61–65). Where are you tempted to prove your worth, to God or to others? How does Christ, the Priest with no genealogy, answer that need (Hebrews 7:14–16; John 1:12)?

8.title: The Open Book
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And all the people gathered as one man into the square before the Water Gate. And they told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses that the LORD had commanded Israel.<sup>2</sup>So Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard, on the first day of the seventh month.<sup>3</sup>And he read from it facing the square before the Water Gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand. And the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law.<sup>4</sup>And Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that they had made for the purpose.
