8.overview:
Where we are. The wall is finished, the people are in their towns, and the seventh month has come (7:73). Now the book turns from walls to the word. Chapters 8–10 tell how the rebuilt people were renewed by God’s law, and Ezra the scribe, unmentioned until now, steps forward.

The message. A people is truly rebuilt only around God’s word, read clearly and understood. When the law is opened it first shows God’s people their sin, and they weep; but the same word declares the day holy and sends them to feast, because the joy of the LORD, not their walls and not their sorrow, is their strength. Understanding leads to grief over sin, then to joy in God, then to glad obedience.

Why it was said. The returned community had walls but not yet renewed hearts, and many had grown up in exile with little clear teaching of the law (see the introduction). This chapter showed them, and every later generation, where a people’s life and strength come from.

How the chapter makes its case. The people gather as one man and ask Ezra to bring the Book of the Law; he reads from early morning until midday, and every ear is attentive (vv. 1–3). They stand as the book is opened, say “Amen, Amen” and bow down, while the Levites give the sense so that all understand (vv. 4–8). They weep at what they hear, but their leaders tell them the day is holy: go, feast, share with those who have nothing, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (vv. 9–12). Next day the leaders study further and find the command to live in booths, and the whole community keeps the feast as not since Joshua, with the law read every day (vv. 13–18).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The Levites gave the sense of the law; the risen Christ, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets”, interpreted to his disciples “in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” and opened their minds to understand (Luke 24:27, 45). The booths recalled God living among his people in a tent, and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), offering living water at this same feast (John 7:37–38). And the joy that is his people’s strength is made sure in him, who “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2).

For us. Come to God’s word hungry, and let it both wound and heal: grieve over the sin it shows you, then take the joy it offers in Christ, and share that joy with those who have nothing. Let understanding turn into prayer, feasting and obedience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A rebuilt people gathers round God’s word, wanting it and having it made plain. On the first day of the seventh month the whole people, men and women and all who could understand, gather in the square before the Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring the Book of the Law (vv. 1–2). He reads from early morning until midday, and every ear is attentive (v. 3). Standing on a wooden platform with leaders beside him, he opens the book, and the people stand, answer “Amen, Amen” and bow to the ground in worship (vv. 4–6). The Levites move among them, reading clearly and giving the sense, so that the people understand (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The walls were finished to protect this: a people gathered round God's Word, wanting it, standing for it, and having it made plain.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people gathered as one man into the square before the Water Gate. And they told Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses that the LORD had commanded Israel. So Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly, both men and women and all who could understand what they heard, on the first day of the seventh month.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole people gather as one and ask for God’s word, and Ezra brings the law before men, women and all who can understand.

As one man. Ninety years before, when the first exiles came home, the seventh month came and “the people gathered as one man” to build an altar (Ezra 3:1). Now the wall is up, the seventh month has come again (7:73), and they gather in the square by the Water Gate, below the temple. And the striking thing is who asks: not Nehemiah calling a meeting, or Ezra announcing a lecture, but the people, who wanted to hear it.

They told Ezra the scribe. Ezra had come to Jerusalem thirteen years before Nehemiah, a priest and “scribe skilled in the Law of Moses” who had “set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach” it (Ezra 7:6, 10). This is his first appearance in the book.

Both men and women. Men and women, and every child old enough to follow: Moses had commanded this very scene, that they might “hear and learn to fear the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 31:12). And the first day of the seventh month was a holy day already, “a memorial proclaimed with blast of trumpets” (Leviticus 23:24), the Feast of Trumpets. The trumpets called them together; the book told them why.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish tradition kept this day as Rosh Hashanah, the new year.

verseByVerse.quote: And he read from it facing the square before the Water Gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women and those who could understand. And the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For five or six hours the people stood and listened to God’s word, and they listened with all their attention.

From early morning until midday. From first light to noon, standing in an open square as the sun climbed, listening to Scripture. And they listened.

The ears of all the people were attentive. Put that beside Nehemiah’s first prayer. In Susa he had asked God, “let your ear be attentive” (1:6). God had heard, and the wall was the proof. Now the direction is reversed, and the people’s ears are attentive to God.

How long could we listen? Not to a sermon about Scripture, but to Scripture itself? These people had gone most of their lives without a clear reading of the law, and they were hungry. We have it in our own language beside the bed, and hunger is what we most often lack. We cannot produce it in ourselves; we ask for it from the Lord who still opens minds to the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform that they had made for the purpose. And beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah on his right hand, and Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam on his left hand. And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it all the people stood. And Ezra blessed the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, "Amen, Amen," lifting up their hands. And they bowed their heads and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the book was opened, the people stood, said “Amen, Amen” and bowed to the ground, receiving God’s word as God speaking to them.

A wooden platform. The word is literally a tower: a raised wooden stand built for the day, so that a crowd filling a city square could see and hear. Thirteen leaders stood with him, beside the reader, not in front of him.

All the people stood. As the scroll was unrolled, the whole square rose to its feet. Nobody had to tell them to; they stood because God was about to speak. Centuries later, in Nazareth, Jesus “stood up to read”, unrolled the scroll of Isaiah, and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16, 21).

Amen, Amen. Amen means it is true, let it be so. They said it twice, with their hands raised, and then went down on their faces. Before a word of the law had been read, they had agreed with it and bowed to it. That is the posture in which Scripture is rightly heard.

The great God. Ezra named him “the great God”, the title Nehemiah had used in his prayer in Susa (1:5) and shouted to the builders (4:14). The God great enough to turn a king’s heart and finish a wall was now speaking to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, the Levites, helped the people to understand the Law, while the people remained in their places. They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites read the law clearly and explained it, so that everyone listening understood what God was saying.

The Levites helped the people. Thirteen Levites move among the crowd as Ezra reads. The people stay where they are; the teachers come to them.

What preaching is for. This one sentence describes what preaching is for, in three things. They read the text itself, the Law of God, not something about it. They read it “clearly”. And they “gave the sense”: they explained it, so that the meaning got through. The test was not whether the teachers had been impressive, but “so that the people understood.”

Christ the Teacher. The greatest Teacher did exactly this. On the road to Emmaus, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself”; and afterwards “he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:27, 45). The Levites could explain the law. Only Christ could open the mind that hears it, and he still does.

Teaching that turns into prayer. Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and Hodiah will lead the people in confessing their sins in the next chapter (9:4–5). Teaching that is understood turns into prayer.

Uncertain wording. The exact sense of “clearly” is uncertain; the ESV’s footnote offers “with interpretation” or “paragraph by paragraph”. Many think it included putting the Hebrew into Aramaic, the everyday language most of these people had grown up with in exile. Whatever the method, the aim is plain: “so that the people understood the reading.”
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish tradition traced the synagogue practice of reading Scripture with an Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum) back to this day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — The Joy of the LORD Is Your Strength
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word first wounds and then heals, and its last word to his people is joy. Hearing the law, the people weep over how far they have fallen from it (v. 9). But Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites tell them that the day is holy to the LORD: go home and feast on the best, send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, and do not grieve, “for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (vv. 9–11). The people go and make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words declared to them (v. 12). The understanding that made them weep in the morning sent them to feast in the afternoon.
verseByVerse.theology: The tears were right, but they were not the last word; God called his people to a feast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people said to all the people, "This day is holy to the LORD your God; do not mourn or weep." For all the people wept as they heard the words of the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people wept because the law showed them their sin, but their leaders told them that this holy day was not a day for mourning.

All the people wept. They wept because they understood. They heard what God had commanded, and they knew their fathers had not done it, and neither had they: commands about the Sabbath, about marriage, about the poor. They were standing in the ruins that the law’s curses on disobedience had brought. The law had done what it is for: “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20).

Nehemiah and Ezra side by side. The governor and the priest and scribe stand together here, one of the few places they do (8:9; 12:26, 36). Their first word to a weeping crowd is not that they should weep more, but “This day is holy to the LORD your God.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, "Go your way. Eat the fat and drink sweet wine and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready, for this day is holy to our Lord. And do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s holy day is a feast to be shared, and his people’s real strength is not their walls or their sorrow but the joy of the LORD.

Eat the fat and drink sweet wine. Go home and feast, and send portions to anyone who has nothing, so no one in the city is left out. It is the custom Esther records for Purim, “gifts of food to one another and gifts to the poor” (Esther 9:22). God’s holy days are feasts, and feasts are shared. A church’s celebrations, a festival meal, a baptism, a lunch after worship, should be planned with an eye to the person who would otherwise eat alone.

The joy of the LORD is your strength. The word for strength is the word for a stronghold, a fortress: “The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Psalm 27:1). They had spent fifty-two days building a wall with swords at their sides. Now Nehemiah tells them their real fortress is not the wall but the joy of the LORD.

Whose joy? The words can mean joy in the LORD, the gladness of people who know him; and they can mean the LORD’s own joy, his delight over his people. Scripture gives us both: “he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17). The people weeping in that square were the people God was singing over, and the fortress that would hold them was not how sorry they were but how glad he was to have them back.

Weeping, then joy. That is still the order. Anyone who has seen his own sin clearly knows the weeping. The joy that holds a Christian up is not a feeling he generates; it is the Father’s joy over a son come home (Luke 15:24), bought by the One who kept the law we have broken and “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2).

What it does not mean. Not that sorrow for sin is out of place; the tears were right (2 Corinthians 7:10). But they were not the last word, and a Christian who stays in them has not yet heard all that God has said.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Levites calmed all the people, saying, "Be quiet, for this day is holy; do not be grieved." And all the people went their way to eat and drink and to send portions and to make great rejoicing, because they had understood the words that were declared to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The understanding that made the people weep in the morning made them rejoice in the afternoon, because they now grasped the kindness of the God who had spoken.

Be quiet, for this day is holy. The Levites go through the crowd as they had during the reading, now with a different message: hush, this is a holy day, stop grieving. The men who explained the law explained that it was a feast.

Because they had understood. Nothing new had been read. What had changed was that they understood not only what God required but what kind of God had given it, and that he called them to a feast in spite of all they had failed to do. Joy that does not come from understanding does not last; this did.

Understood Scripture and joy. The disciples knew the same thing after the resurrection: on the Emmaus road two of them felt their hearts burn as Jesus opened the Scriptures (Luke 24:32), and in the end they all “returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke 24:52). Understood Scripture, opened by the Lord, ends in joy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Understanding God’s word leads to glad obedience. On the second day the heads of families, the priests and the Levites gather with Ezra to study the law more closely, and find the command to live in booths during the feast of the seventh month, in memory of how God brought Israel out of Egypt (vv. 13–15). The whole community gathers branches and builds booths on roofs and in courtyards, in the temple courts and the city squares, keeping the feast as it had not been kept since the days of Joshua, with very great rejoicing (vv. 16–17). Every day of the feast the law is read, and the week ends in a solemn assembly (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Booths remembered the wilderness, when God's people lived in tents and God lived among them in his own tent, the tabernacle.

verseByVerse.quote: On the second day the heads of fathers' houses of all the people, with the priests and the Levites, came together to Ezra the scribe in order to study the words of the Law. And they found it written in the Law that the LORD had commanded by Moses that the people of Israel should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month, and that they should proclaim it and publish it in all their towns and in Jerusalem, "Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders came back to study the law more closely, found the command to live in booths, and at once set about obeying it.

On the second day. The leaders are back, wanting to understand better so that they can lead their households. A real hearing of God’s word, unlike a merely emotional one, wants more of it the next day.

Dwell in booths. The Feast of Booths began on the fifteenth of this month, only two weeks away (Leviticus 23:34), and the command came with its reason, the rescue it remembered: “that your generations may know that I made the people of Israel dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Leviticus 23:43). So word went out to every town to bring branches.

Uncertain wording. “Wild olive” is literally “tree of oil”, and which tree is meant is not certain: perhaps the oleaster, perhaps a resinous pine, as older translations have it.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people went out and brought them and made booths for themselves, each on his roof, and in their courts and in the courts of the house of God, and in the square at the Water Gate and in the square at the Gate of Ephraim. And all the assembly of those who had returned from the captivity made booths and lived in the booths, for from the days of Jeshua the son of Nun to that day the people of Israel had not done so. And there was very great rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole community built booths all over the city and lived in them, keeping the feast with a completeness and joy not seen since Joshua’s day.

Each on his roof. Imagine the city that week: flat roofs covered with shelters of green branches, courtyards full of them, the temple courts, the squares by the gates. The empty city of 7:4 had filled with people living outdoors under leaves.

From the days of Jeshua the son of Nun. This needs care, because the feast itself had been kept since Joshua. Solomon kept it (2 Chronicles 8:13), and the first returnees kept it ninety years before: “they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written” (Ezra 3:4). What had not happened since Joshua was this: the whole assembly, every household, actually living in booths for the week, as the law commanded.

The name Jeshua. Jeshua is the same name as Joshua, and in Greek it is Jesus. The first Joshua brought the people into the land, but not into God’s final rest: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on” (Hebrews 4:8). These returned exiles in their booths were still pilgrims, as their fathers had been in the wilderness. Their rest was still to come, through a greater Joshua, Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the rule.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every day of the feast the law was read, as Moses had commanded, and the week ended in a solemn assembly.

Day by day. Moses’ command was kept to the letter: “you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing” (Deuteronomy 31:11). A week of living in the open, eating together and hearing God’s word, and then the great closing assembly.

The feast was waiting for him. Nearly five centuries later, on the last day of this same feast, the Word himself stood in the temple courts and cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water’” (John 7:37–38). The people in their booths remembered that God had once lived among them in a tent. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and the word for “dwelt” means to pitch a tent. The Feast of Booths was waiting for him.

8.theology:
The Word first shows the people their sin, and they weep; then it declares the day holy and sends them to feast. That is law and then gospel, grief over sin and then joy in God’s welcome, in the right order.

Their stronghold was not the wall but the joy of a God who rejoices over his people, and Christ, who opens the Scriptures so that hearts burn, is the one in whom that joy is made sure.
8.examples:
The people asked for the book, listened from first light to noon, and stood when the scroll opened. They wept because they understood, and they rejoiced because they understood.

Three weeks after the wall was finished, the city’s roofs were covered with booths of branches.

keyVerse.quote: And do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
keyVerse.note: The people had wept as the law exposed their sin, and this is God’s answer through their leaders. Their fortress was not the wall they had just built, nor the depth of their sorrow, but the joy of the LORD, both their gladness in him and his delight over them. In Christ, who endured the cross for the joy set before him, that joy is made sure for every repentant sinner.

8.reflection:
The people asked for the Book of the Law and listened from early morning until midday (vv. 1–3). What helps or hinders your own hunger for God’s word? What would it look like for your church or home group to ask for Scripture the way they did?

The Levites read “clearly” and “gave the sense, so that the people understood” (v. 8). Why does understanding matter so much in hearing God’s word? How can we help one another, and especially newcomers and children, to understand it?

The people wept as they heard the law, and were told, “do not be grieved, for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (vv. 9–10). Do you tend to stay in sorrow over sin, or to skip it? How does the gospel hold both together?

The feast was shared with “anyone who has nothing ready” (v. 10), and it led straight into glad obedience (vv. 13–17). Who might be left out of your celebrations? What is one thing God’s word has shown you that you could obey this week with joy?

9.title: The God Who Never Gave Up
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the people of Israel were assembled with fasting and in sackcloth, and with earth on their heads.<sup>2</sup>And the Israelites separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.<sup>3</sup>And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day; for another quarter of it they made confession and worshiped the LORD their God.<sup>4</sup>On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God.<sup>5</sup>Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.<sup>6</sup>"You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you.<sup>7</sup>You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham.<sup>8</sup>You found his heart faithful before you, and made with him the covenant to give to his offspring the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.<sup>9</sup>"And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea,<sup>10</sup>and performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and all the people of his land, for you knew that they acted arrogantly against our fathers. And you made a name for yourself, as it is to this day.<sup>11</sup>And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.<sup>12</sup>By a pillar of cloud you led them in the day, and by a pillar of fire in the night to light for them the way in which they should go.<sup>13</sup>You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments,<sup>14</sup>and you made known to them your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by Moses your servant.<sup>15</sup>You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and you told them to go in to possess the land that you had sworn to give them.<sup>16</sup>"But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments.<sup>17</sup>They refused to obey and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them, but they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them.<sup>18</sup>Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,' and had committed great blasphemies,<sup>19</sup>you in your great mercies did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud to lead them in the way did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night to light for them the way by which they should go.<sup>20</sup>You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst.<sup>21</sup>Forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell.<sup>22</sup>"And you gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner. So they took possession of the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan.<sup>23</sup>You multiplied their children as the stars of heaven, and you brought them into the land that you had told their fathers to enter and possess.<sup>24</sup>So the descendants went in and possessed the land, and you subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hand, with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they would.<sup>25</sup>And they captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already hewn, vineyards, olive orchards and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in your great goodness.<sup>26</sup>"Nevertheless, they were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies.<sup>27</sup>Therefore you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who made them suffer. And in the time of their suffering they cried out to you and you heard them from heaven, and according to your great mercies you gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies.<sup>28</sup>But after they had rest they did evil again before you, and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, so that they had dominion over them. Yet when they turned and cried to you, you heard from heaven, and many times you delivered them according to your mercies.<sup>29</sup>And you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey your commandments, but sinned against your rules, which if a person does them, he shall live by them, and they turned a stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck and would not obey.<sup>30</sup>Many years you bore with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not give ear. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands.<sup>31</sup>Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.<sup>32</sup>"Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you that has come upon us, upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until this day.<sup>33</sup>Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly.<sup>34</sup>Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law or paid attention to your commandments and your warnings that you gave them.<sup>35</sup>Even in their own kingdom, and amid your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their wicked works.<sup>36</sup>Behold, we are slaves this day; in the land that you gave to our fathers to enjoy its fruit and its good gifts, behold, we are slaves.<sup>37</sup>And its rich yield goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.<sup>38</sup>"Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing; on the sealed document are the names of our princes, our Levites, and our priests.
9.overview:
Where we are. The wall is finished, the law has been read, and the Feast of Booths has just ended in great rejoicing (8:17). Two days later the people gather again, in sackcloth: the grief set aside on the feast day (8:9–11) is given its day, and this great prayer prepares the written covenant of chapter 10.

The message. Israel’s history, told honestly, is the story of a faithful God and an unfaithful people, and the only reason there is still an Israel to pray is that God “did not forsake them” (vv. 17, 19, 31). So the answer to our sin is neither excuse nor despair, but to bless God, agree that he has been right in all he has done, and cast ourselves on the mercy that has carried his people through every failure.

Why it was said. The returned exiles were back in the land but not free: their harvests went in tribute to a foreign king (vv. 36–37; see the introduction). They needed to understand why, and whether God was finished with them.

How the chapter makes its case. The people hear the law, confess and are called to bless God (vv. 1–5). The prayer begins with God alone: Maker of all, who chose Abram, rescued Israel from Egypt, gave his law and Sabbath and fed them in the desert (vv. 6–15). Then the long rebellion, the golden calf, the good land enjoyed and God forgotten, the prophets killed, and each time the same answer: he “did not forsake them” (vv. 16–31). Reaching the present, they ask God not to think their hardship small, confess him righteous in it all, and own that they are slaves in their own land (vv. 32–37). They answer with a covenant in writing (v. 38).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The law promised life to the one who does it (v. 29), and no one in this history did; it needed a Man who would keep it and bear the curse for those who had not (Galatians 3:12–13). And God could keep his promise not to forsake a people who had forsaken him because at the cross he forsook his Son in their place (Mark 15:34). The bread from heaven and the water from the rock were already pictures of that Son (John 6:35; 1 Corinthians 10:4).

For us. Learn to tell your own story as the history of God’s patience with you. Begin confession by blessing God, and own your sin without excuse, because the one you speak to has not forsaken you. Refusing God’s service makes no one free; only the Son does (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Stand Up and Bless the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Confession is safe when it begins with God’s goodness and God’s word. Two days after the feast the people gather in fasting and sackcloth, with earth on their heads, the marks of mourning (v. 1). They stand before God as Israel and confess not only their own sins but their fathers’ (v. 2). The order of the day matters: first a quarter of the day hearing the Book of the Law, then a quarter confessing and worshipping (v. 3). Then the Levites who had taught them the law cry out to God and call the whole assembly to its feet, and their first word is not a lament but “bless” (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: The fasting came after the feasting, not before: they were told first that the joy of the LORD was their strength (8:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the twenty-fourth day of this month the people of Israel were assembled with fasting and in sackcloth, and with earth on their heads. And the Israelites separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day; for another quarter of it they made confession and worshiped the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two days after the feast, the people give a day to hearing God’s law, confessing their sins and their fathers’, and worshipping.

On the twenty-fourth day of this month. Booths had ended on the twenty-second (8:18). Three weeks earlier the people had wept at the reading of the law and been told to stop, because it was a feast day (8:9–11). Now the postponed grief is given its day, with the signs of mourning.

Confession that begins from joy. People who already know God’s delight in them can look at their sin without flinching and without despair. Confession that begins from terror usually stops short; confession that begins from joy can go all the way down.

Separated themselves from all foreigners. This was not a rejection of any foreigner who had joined himself to the LORD (the Passover of Ezra 6:21 welcomed such), but a day on which Israel stood before God as Israel and owned its own history: not the present alone, but “the iniquities of their fathers”.

For a quarter of the day. About three hours of reading, then three of confession and worship. The reading came first, because a people cannot confess sins it has not been shown. The word told them what to confess, and the worship told them to whom.

verseByVerse.quote: On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani; and they cried with a loud voice to the LORD their God. Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites who taught the law now lead the confession, and begin it by calling the people to bless God.

On the stairs of the Levites. Several of these men had moved through the crowd three weeks before, helping the people understand the law (8:7). The teachers now lead the prayer, and understanding has become confession.

Stand up and bless the LORD your God. They are in sackcloth, about to confess centuries of failure, and the first word is “bless”. The confession will be made to a God whose name is “exalted above all blessing and praise”, and that is what makes confession safe. You can tell the whole truth about yourself to a God like that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — You Are the LORD, You Alone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer begins by saying who God is, because Israel’s story makes sense only if he is its subject. He is the only God, Maker and keeper of everything, worshipped by the host of heaven (v. 6). He chose Abram, brought him out of Ur, renamed him and made a covenant with him, and he kept it, because he is righteous (vv. 7–8). He saw his people in Egypt, broke Pharaoh’s pride and made a road through the sea (vv. 9–11). He led them by cloud and fire, came down on Sinai to give them good laws and his holy Sabbath, fed them with bread from heaven and water from the rock, and sent them to take the land he had sworn to give (vv. 12–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every verb in this part of the prayer has God for its subject. The history of Israel is told as the history of what God did.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer begins not with Israel’s trouble but with who God is: the only God, Maker and keeper of all.

You have made heaven. Before a word about Persian taxes or broken covenants, they name the Maker of the highest heaven and the deepest sea, who preserves every creature and is worshipped by the angels.

You alone. This was the confession their fathers had failed to make; their worship of other gods had brought the exile on them. And it matters for everything that follows. If God is one of many, Israel’s story is a contest between powers. If he alone made and holds all things, there has never been a moment in their history that was out of his hands, including the worst ones. The New Testament says who that Maker is: “by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth … all things were created through him and for him” (Colossians 1:16).

Textual note. Some early translations begin this verse “And Ezra said”. The Hebrew lacks the words, and the ESV lets the prayer run on from the Levites of verse 5. Either way it is the whole assembly’s prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham. You found his heart faithful before you, and made with him the covenant to give to his offspring the land of the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, and the Girgashite. And you have kept your promise, for you are righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose Abram, made him a promise and kept it, because he is righteous.

The God who chose Abram. From the universe the prayer turns to one man. God chose him, brought him out and renamed him Abraham. Ur of the Chaldeans lay in southern Babylonia: the people praying had been brought home from the same country as their father Abraham.

You found his heart faithful. “Faithful” is from the same Hebrew root as “believed” in the sentence the whole Bible turns on: “he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). God found in Abraham a heart that trusted him, and counted it righteousness; and God himself proved the righteous one, keeping every word. Paul builds the gospel on that verse (Romans 4:3). The promise never rested on Abraham’s faith. It rested on God, who keeps his word.

For you are righteous. Here God’s righteousness means that he kept his word: he promised the land and he gave it. The phrase returns in verse 33, “you have been righteous in all that has come upon us”, and there it means the exile was deserved. God’s righteousness opens the prayer and closes it, once in keeping a promise and once in carrying out a sentence. He is the same God in both, and they trust him in both.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea, and performed signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants and all the people of his land, for you knew that they acted arrogantly against our fathers. And you made a name for yourself, as it is to this day. And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God saw his people’s suffering, broke Pharaoh’s pride and made a road through the sea.

You saw and heard. The prayer remembers a God who noticed. And the Exodus was not only a rescue but God making himself a name, still his name centuries later.

They acted arrogantly. The phrase is said of Pharaoh and his Egyptians, and in verses 16 and 29 the same Hebrew verb is used of Israel: “they and our fathers acted presumptuously”. The people God rescued from the arrogant became arrogant toward him, and the prayer does not spare them the comparison.

As a stone into mighty waters. The words echo the song Moses sang on the far shore: “they went down into the depths like a stone” (Exodus 15:5). A people long pursued by stronger nations remember the day God dropped the pursuers into the sea and the slaves walked through on dry ground.

verseByVerse.quote: By a pillar of cloud you led them in the day, and by a pillar of fire in the night to light for them the way in which they should go. You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven and gave them right rules and true laws, good statutes and commandments, and you made known to them your holy Sabbath and commanded them commandments and statutes and a law by Moses your servant. You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst, and you told them to go in to possess the land that you had sworn to give them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God led his people, gave them good laws and his Sabbath, and fed them in the desert.

Right rules and true laws. The people confessing that they had broken the law begin by calling it good. The law was not their problem; they were.

Your holy Sabbath. Of all the commandments, the Sabbath is the one named, and God “made it known” to them as his own rest (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 16:23). It was a gift: a day of rest given to people who had been slaves and had never had one. It will matter again when Nehemiah finds the gates open for trade on that day (13:15–22).

Bread from heaven. Jesus claimed both the bread and the water for himself: “my Father gives you the true bread from heaven … I am the bread of life” (John 6:32, 35). And Paul says of the rock, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The God who fed them in the desert was already giving them pictures of his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–31 — You Did Not Forsake Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the longest part of the prayer, and its refrain is God’s, not Israel’s: he “did not forsake them”. Their fathers acted presumptuously and chose a leader to take them back to Egypt, yet God, ready to forgive, did not forsake them (vv. 16–17). After the golden calf the cloud still led them, the Spirit still taught them, and for forty years they lacked nothing (vv. 18–21). In the land they ate, grew fat and delighted in his goodness (vv. 22–25), then threw his law behind their backs and killed his prophets. He handed them to their enemies and, when they cried, sent saviours, many times (vv. 26–29). After centuries of warnings came the exile, and still he did not make an end of them (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: Three times the prayer says God did not forsake them (vv. 17, 19, 31), and the one time he abandoned them (v. 28) was for a season, not for good.

verseByVerse.quote: "But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck and did not obey your commandments. They refused to obey and were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them, but they stiffened their neck and appointed a leader to return to their slavery in Egypt. But you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and did not forsake them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel answered this goodness with stubborn rebellion, but God, true to his name, did not forsake them.

They stiffened their neck. “Stiffened their neck”, twice: the ox that will not bend to the yoke, as the nobles of Tekoa would not (3:5). And the worst of it: “Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt” (Numbers 14:4). A people freed from slavery and fed daily from heaven would rather make bricks for Pharaoh again than trust God for the land. Keep that in mind until verse 36, where the people praying say they are slaves this day.

A God ready to forgive. Verse 17 gives the name God proclaimed to Moses on the mountain: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). He proclaimed it straight after the golden calf, the worst sin in their history. God did not reveal his mercy to people who had deserved it, but to people who had just proved they did not. “A God ready to forgive” is, in Hebrew, a God of forgivenesses, plural: forgiveness, and more of it.

Textual note. Most Hebrew manuscripts read “in their rebellion”; some ancient copies and translations read “in Egypt”, a difference of a few Hebrew letters, and the ESV follows them, as Numbers 14:4 suggests. The sin is the same either way.

verseByVerse.quote: Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt,' and had committed great blasphemies, you in your great mercies did not forsake them in the wilderness. The pillar of cloud to lead them in the way did not depart from them by day, nor the pillar of fire by night to light for them the way by which they should go. You gave your good Spirit to instruct them and did not withhold your manna from their mouth and gave them water for their thirst. Forty years you sustained them in the wilderness, and they lacked nothing. Their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after the golden calf, God went on leading, teaching, feeding and clothing his people.

Even when they had made for themselves a golden calf. They credited a metal calf with the Exodus, and the next thing the prayer records is that the cloud did not depart. The morning after the calf it was still there, described in almost the words of verse 12: nothing about God’s leading had changed, though everything about their deserving had.

Your good Spirit to instruct them. First in the list is not food but teaching. God did not only feed rebels; he went on instructing them. The same Spirit is promised to believers now, who “will teach you all things” (John 14:26).

Forty years you sustained them. Moses had said the same of their clothes and their feet (Deuteronomy 8:4), and of their sandals too (Deuteronomy 29:5). A single pair of sandals, walked in for forty years and never worn through: that is the care of God for people in the middle of their rebellion.

For anyone who has wandered. Many know what it is to have wandered in a wilderness of their own making and to look back and see that God fed them the whole way. That is not a reason to presume on him, but a reason to come home.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you gave them kingdoms and peoples and allotted to them every corner. So they took possession of the land of Sihon king of Heshbon and the land of Og king of Bashan. You multiplied their children as the stars of heaven, and you brought them into the land that you had told their fathers to enter and possess. So the descendants went in and possessed the land, and you subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hand, with their kings and the peoples of the land, that they might do with them as they would. And they captured fortified cities and a rich land, and took possession of houses full of all good things, cisterns already hewn, vineyards, olive orchards and fruit trees in abundance. So they ate and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in your great goodness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God kept his promise to the letter, and Israel feasted on his goodness.

Then the land. Kingdoms given, children multiplied “as the stars of heaven”, the Canaanites handed over (vv. 22–24). The stars go back to the night God told Abraham, “So shall your offspring be” (Genesis 15:5). Verse 8 said he kept his promise; these verses show it kept, in houses full of good things, cisterns, vineyards and orchards. That is almost word for word what Moses had promised, and warned: “houses full of all good things that you did not fill, and cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant”, and “when you eat and are full, then take care lest you forget the LORD” (Deuteronomy 6:11–12).

Delighted themselves in your great goodness. There is nothing wrong in that; it is what the gifts were for. But Moses had also sung what would happen next: “Jeshurun grew fat, and kicked” (Deuteronomy 32:15). The danger of blessing is that we come to love the house and forget who filled it. A test we can run on ourselves: when life is full, do we pray more, or less?

Why does prosperity make God feel unnecessary? As societies grow richer and safer, religious practice tends to fall, and many take that as proof that faith was only a way of coping with hard lives. Moses predicted the pattern and drew the opposite conclusion: full houses do not show that God was never there; they make it easy to forget who filled them (Deuteronomy 8:11–14). Abundance does not answer the deepest questions; it only muffles them. Alexis de Tocqueville, visiting America in the 1830s, was struck by how restless its people were in the midst of their prosperity. The gifts were meant to be signposts, and we made them the destination. The gospel does not ask us to despise the vineyards and orchards. It gives us the Giver, who became poor for our sake, so that his gifts can be enjoyed without being worshipped, and a good year can bring us to our knees in thanks instead of carrying us away from him.

Uncertain wording. “Allotted to them every corner” renders a compressed Hebrew phrase, literally “you divided them to a corner”. It may mean God apportioned the land to Israel out to its edges, or divided the conquered peoples’ territory among them. Either way, the whole land was his gift.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, they were disobedient and rebelled against you and cast your law behind their back and killed your prophets, who had warned them in order to turn them back to you, and they committed great blasphemies. Therefore you gave them into the hand of their enemies, who made them suffer. And in the time of their suffering they cried out to you and you heard them from heaven, and according to your great mercies you gave them saviors who saved them from the hand of their enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel threw God’s law over its shoulder and killed his prophets, yet when they cried out he heard and sent rescuers.

Cast your law behind their back. Not lost or forgotten, but thrown over the shoulder so that they would not have to look at it. And “killed your prophets”: Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court for delivering God’s message (2 Chronicles 24:20–21). Jesus wept over the same city for the same reason: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it!” (Luke 13:34). And then they killed him too.

You gave them saviors. Verse 27 is the book of Judges in one sentence (Judges 3:9): one rescuer after another, each for a generation. They were waiting, without knowing it, for the announcement to the shepherds: “unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord” (Luke 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: But after they had rest they did evil again before you, and you abandoned them to the hand of their enemies, so that they had dominion over them. Yet when they turned and cried to you, you heard from heaven, and many times you delivered them according to your mercies. And you warned them in order to turn them back to your law. Yet they acted presumptuously and did not obey your commandments, but sinned against your rules, which if a person does them, he shall live by them, and they turned a stubborn shoulder and stiffened their neck and would not obey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rest led to sin, sin to judgment, and every cry to rescue, many times over; and still Israel refused the law that promised life.

But after they had rest. Not in hardship but in rest: it was the good years that undid them. The word “abandoned” is honest; God did give them up to their enemies for a time. But “many times you delivered them”. If God’s mercy had a limit, they would have used it up long before.

He shall live by them. These words are Leviticus 18:5, the law’s own promise: do this and live. They did not do it, and neither has anyone else. Paul quotes the same verse and then says what God did about it: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:12–13). The one Man who kept those rules, and had earned life by them, died under the curse that belonged to those who did not.

verseByVerse.quote: Many years you bore with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not give ear. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands. Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After centuries of warnings God sent his people into exile, yet even then he did not make an end of them.

Many years you bore with them. The prophets spoke for centuries, from Elijah to Jeremiah. “A stubborn shoulder” (v. 29) is an ox shrugging off the yoke, and Zechariah had used the same words of their fathers (Zechariah 7:11). He had also said whose voice they were refusing: “the words that the LORD of hosts had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets” (Zechariah 7:12). The prophets’ words were the Spirit’s words; they were refusing God, not men. So God gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands: the exile.

Nevertheless. That word is the hinge of the whole history. The exile was deserved, and it was not the end; they were standing in Jerusalem saying so. Ezra had prayed the same: “For we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery” (Ezra 9:9).

Christ forsaken in their place. God could promise never to forsake people who had forsaken him for centuries because one day he would forsake someone else in their place. “At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice … My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). He was abandoned so that his people would hear, and keep hearing, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–38 — Behold, We Are Slaves This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The history reaches the present, and the prayer turns to its one request. The God who keeps covenant is asked not to treat as small the hardship his people have suffered since the Assyrians came (v. 32). In the same breath they confess that he has been righteous in all of it, and that every rank of the nation failed to serve him in the good land he gave (vv. 33–35). Now they are slaves in that land, its harvest going to the kings God has set over them because of their sins (vv. 36–37). There the prayer ends, in great distress, and the people answer with a firm covenant in writing, sealed with their leaders’ names (v. 38).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the confession of people who know their only hope is the character of the God they have wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, let not all the hardship seem little to you that has come upon us, upon our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria until this day. Yet you have been righteous in all that has come upon us, for you have dealt faithfully and we have acted wickedly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask God not to treat their suffering as small, and confess that he has been right in all of it.

Let not all the hardship seem little to you. Reaching the present, the prayer addresses God in the words of Moses, “the great, the mighty, and the awesome God” (Deuteronomy 10:17), and of Nehemiah’s own first prayer (1:5). The one request in the entire prayer is modest: do not let our hardship look small to you. “Since the time of the kings of Assyria”: three centuries of invasion, deportation and subjection. Look at it, Lord. Do not treat it as nothing.

Yet you have been righteous. And in the same breath they say it was all just. That is the heart of true confession: they ask God to see their suffering, and they agree with every stroke of it, with no excuses and no blaming the kings of Assyria. The one who can pray verse 33 and make no excuse for himself has been brought to the place where mercy can reach him.

verseByVerse.quote: Our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law or paid attention to your commandments and your warnings that you gave them. Even in their own kingdom, and amid your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land that you set before them, they did not serve you or turn from their wicked works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every rank of the nation shares the blame: with every good gift, they still did not serve God.

Our kings, our princes, our priests. Nobody is left outside the confession, with one exception. In verse 32 the hardship fell on “our kings, our princes, our priests, our prophets, our fathers”. In verse 34 those who did not keep the law are kings, princes, priests and fathers. The prophets have dropped out of the list. They suffered with the nation and went into exile with it (Jeremiah to Egypt, Ezekiel and Daniel to Babylon), but they were not the cause of it. The innocent went down with the guilty. One Prophet, Jesus, went further: he suffered not only with the guilty but for them.

Even in their own kingdom. They had their own king, their own land and every good thing in it, and still “they did not serve you”.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, we are slaves this day; in the land that you gave to our fathers to enjoy its fruit and its good gifts, behold, we are slaves. And its rich yield goes to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having refused to serve God in their own land, they are now slaves in it.

We are slaves this day. “Slaves” and “serve” come from the same Hebrew root. They would not serve God in their own kingdom (v. 35), and so they are slaves in their own land. God had said exactly this to Rehoboam’s generation: “they shall be servants to him, that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the countries” (2 Chronicles 12:8). Every people serves someone. Refuse the service of God and you do not become free; you learn the service of the kingdoms. The fathers had once chosen a leader to take them back to slavery (v. 17). Their children had it.

The kings whom you have set over us. The Persian king had been generous to Nehemiah, but Judah’s harvest still went east in tribute, and the empire could conscript their bodies and animals as it pleased. Even the empire is God’s doing. And there the prayer ends, in great distress.

The only way out. The way out of that slavery is not a better master in Persia. “If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing; on the sealed document are the names of our princes, our Levites, and our priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In answer to the whole history, the leaders put their commitment to God in writing. In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 10:1, the heading of the list of names that follows.

Because of all this. The whole history: the mercy and the rebellion, and the slavery they are in. They answer not with a feeling but with a document, written, sealed and signed, so that there can be no quiet forgetting later. The next chapter lists those who signed and what they promised.

A covenant with our names on it. It is right to bind ourselves to God, yet chapter 13 will show how quickly the promises of chapter 10 were broken. A covenant with our names on it cannot save us. What saves is the covenant with God’s name on it, “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20), sealed by the one party who has never failed to keep his word, and giving the Spirit who causes his people to walk in his ways (Ezekiel 36:27).

9.theology:
The whole history is told with God as its subject. God is righteous in keeping his promise (v. 8) and righteous in the judgment (v. 33), and between those two verses his people rebel again and again and he does not forsake them.

The prayer is full of things that pointed forward to Christ: the bread and the rock (John 6:35), the saviors of the judges, the prophets Jerusalem killed, and the law that promises life to the one who does it. He kept it, and bore its curse for us. God could promise never to forsake a people who had forsaken him because he would forsake his Son in their place.
9.examples:
They read Scripture for three hours before they confessed for three, and in sackcloth their first word was bless.

The morning after the golden calf the cloud was still there, and for forty years their sandals did not wear out. Their fathers had asked for a leader to take them back to slavery, and the children say we are slaves this day.

keyVerse.quote: Nevertheless, in your great mercies you did not make an end of them or forsake them, for you are a gracious and merciful God.
keyVerse.note: After centuries of rebellion and the exile itself, the prayer’s whole history turns on this “nevertheless”. Israel’s survival is not explained by anything in Israel but by the character of God, the same God who proclaimed himself “merciful and gracious” to Moses after the golden calf. That mercy, which would not make an end of a sinful people, is the mercy that finally met their sin at the cross.

9.reflection:
The people heard the law for three hours before they confessed for three, and their first word was “bless” (vv. 3–5). Why does confession go deeper when it begins with God’s word and God’s goodness rather than with our failures?

The prayer tells Israel’s history as the story of what God did, again and again, for an unfaithful people. If you told the story of your own life that way, where would you see his patience, and his refusal to forsake you?

Israel forgot God when their houses were full (vv. 25–26). When life goes well, do you pray more or less? What practical habits keep gratitude from turning into forgetfulness?

They asked God to see their hardship, yet agreed that he had been righteous in all of it (vv. 32–33). How do the cross and Christ’s cry of forsakenness let us be that honest about both our suffering and our sin?

10.title: The People Sign Their Name
