And we will forgo the crops of the seventh year and the exaction of every debt.<sup>32</sup>"We also take on ourselves the obligation to give yearly a third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God:<sup>33</sup>for the showbread, the regular grain offering, the regular burnt offering, the Sabbaths, the new moons, the appointed feasts, the holy things, and the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.<sup>34</sup>We, the priests, the Levites, and the people, have likewise cast lots for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, according to our fathers' houses, at times appointed, year by year, to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.<sup>35</sup>We obligate ourselves to bring the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of the LORD;<sup>36</sup>also to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God, the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, as it is written in the Law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks;<sup>37</sup>and to bring the first of our dough, and our contributions, the fruit of every tree, the wine and the oil, to the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God; and to bring to the Levites the tithes from our ground, for it is the Levites who collect the tithes in all our towns where we labor.<sup>38</sup>And the priest, the son of Aaron, shall be with the Levites when the Levites receive the tithes. And the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes to the house of our God, to the chambers of the storehouse.<sup>39</sup>For the people of Israel and the sons of Levi shall bring the contribution of grain, wine, and oil to the chambers, where the vessels of the sanctuary are, as well as the priests who minister, and the gatekeepers and the singers. We will not neglect the house of our God."
10.overview:
Where we are. The great prayer of chapter 9 ended, “Because of all this we make a firm covenant in writing” (9:38). This chapter is that document: the names that sealed it and the promises it made.

The message. Grace received calls for a response that is concrete, public and costly. A people God has not forsaken binds itself to walk in his law exactly where faithfulness costs: in marriage, in the calendar, in the account book, and in the giving that keeps his worship going. Yet the last promise, “We will not neglect the house of our God” (v. 39), will be broken within a few years (chapter 13), so the chapter also shows the limit of every covenant signed by sinners.

Why it was said. Judah was small, poor and surrounded by peoples whose marriages, markets and gods pressed in on every side, and the temple lived on gifts that were easily withheld (see the introduction). Their fathers had lost the land by breaking the covenant (9:34–37), and the children write down their resolve to do better.

How the chapter makes its case. First the names: Nehemiah the governor, then twenty-one priests, seventeen Levites and forty-four chiefs of the people, eighty-four in all (vv. 1–27). The rest of the people, wives and children and converts included, join them under a curse and an oath to walk in God’s law (vv. 28–29). Then the terms: no marriages with the peoples of the land (v. 30); no Sabbath trading, and the seventh year kept with its release of debts (v. 31); and the house of God supplied, with a yearly tax for its offerings, wood for the altar, and firstfruits, firstborn and tithes for its priests and Levites (vv. 32–39).

Where it leads. By covenant, and by the need it exposes. A covenant whose keeping rests on our names will fail, and the book will show it failing; God promised a new covenant in which he would write his law on his people’s hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Christ is its surety. He paid the temple tax he did not owe, for himself and his disciple (Matthew 17:27); his single sacrifice ended the yearly sin offerings this tax supplied (Hebrews 10:12); and zeal for God’s house consumed him (John 2:17).

For us. Let the grace you have received become specific: in whom you marry, how you use God’s day, how you buy, sell and lend, and how you give to the worship and ministry of your church. Make such promises gladly but humbly, resting not on your signature but on Christ, who keeps covenant for us and gives the Spirit to keep us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — On the Seals Are the Names
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace answered in writing: the covenant of 9:38 has a signature page, and the leaders put their own names first. Nehemiah the governor heads it (v. 1), followed by twenty-one priests, most of them priestly houses signing through their heads (vv. 2–8), and seventeen Levites, several of them the teachers who had explained the law and led the confession (vv. 9–13). Then come forty-four chiefs of the people, mostly the family names of the first return listed in chapter 7, with a few names from the wall (vv. 14–27). Eighty-four seals in all: those who led the people put their own names under what they asked the people to promise.
verseByVerse.theology: The same names turn up in the next chapters, some keeping the promise and some breaking it.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the seals are the names of Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, Zedekiah,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant’s signature page begins with the governor himself: Nehemiah binds himself first to what he asks of the people.

On the seals are the names. This is the signature page of “the sealed document” (9:38). A seal pressed into clay or wax was a man’s signature in that world: this is mine, and I stand behind it.

Nehemiah the governor. The first name is the governor’s. Nehemiah did not ask the people to bind themselves to anything he had not bound himself to first, as when he said, “Let us abandon this exacting of interest” (5:10). Zedekiah, next to him, was perhaps his secretary.

verseByVerse.quote: Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah, Pashhur, Amariah, Malchijah, Hattush, Shebaniah, Malluch, Harim, Meremoth, Obadiah, Daniel, Ginnethon, Baruch, Meshullam, Abijah, Mijamin, Maaziah, Bilgai, Shemaiah; these are the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-one priests sign, mostly in the names of their priestly houses.

These are the priests. Most of these are the names of priestly houses rather than individuals (many reappear in 12:1–21): a family signs through its head.

Meremoth. Meremoth (v. 5) recalls the priest of the family of Hakkoz who built two sections of the wall (3:4, 21), from a family once barred from the priesthood because it could not prove its descent (7:63–64).

Abijah. When David divided the priests into courses, the lots fell “the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah” (1 Chronicles 24:10). More than four centuries after Nehemiah, “there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah” (Luke 1:5), and while he served in the temple an angel told him he would have a son who would prepare the way for the Lord. The name on this seal belongs to the priestly division of John the Baptist’s father.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Levites: Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel; and their brothers, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan, Mica, Rehob, Hashabiah, Zaccur, Sherebiah, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Bani, Beninu.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites who had taught the law and led the confession now put their own names under it.

And the Levites. Seventeen Levites, several of them the men who explained the law at the Water Gate (8:7) and led the confession from the stairs (9:4–5). They taught it, they prayed it, and now they sign the obligations they had been explaining to everyone else. Those who teach God’s word must be the first to come under it.

verseByVerse.quote: The chiefs of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani, Bunni, Azgad, Bebai, Adonijah, Bigvai, Adin, Ater, Hezekiah, Azzur, Hodiah, Hashum, Bezai, Hariph, Anathoth, Nebai, Magpiash, Meshullam, Hezir, Meshezabel, Zadok, Jaddua, Pelatiah, Hanan, Anaiah, Hoshea, Hananiah, Hasshub, Hallohesh, Pilha, Shobek, Rehum, Hashabnah, Maaseiah, Ahiah, Hanan, Anan, Malluch, Harim, Baanah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty-four heads of families sign, mostly the families of the first return, renewing their fathers’ covenant.

The chiefs of the people. Most are familiar from the register in chapter 7: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Azgad, Bebai and the rest, even Anathoth, which is a town. The children of the first return were renewing their fathers’ covenant.

Names from the wall. Hallohesh (v. 24) is the family of Shallum, who built with his daughters (3:12). There is a Meshullam here too (v. 20), a common name, and the reader remembers another Meshullam who built two sections and then married his daughter to Tobiah’s son (6:18). Names on a covenant are only as good as the hearts behind them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–31 — To Walk in God's Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole people joins the covenant, and it is specific. Everyone old enough to understand, wives and children included, and every convert who had separated himself to the law of God, join their nobles under a curse and an oath to walk in God’s law (vv. 28–29). The terms fall where the pressure was greatest. They will not intermarry with the peoples of the land, whose gods would come with them (v. 30). They will not buy from foreign traders on the Sabbath, and they will keep the seventh year, letting the land rest and releasing debts (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant addresses the three places where the community had actually been failing: its marriages, its Sabbaths and its debts. It is specific because their disobedience had been specific.

verseByVerse.quote: "The rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the temple servants, and all who have separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to the Law of God, their wives, their sons, their daughters, all who have knowledge and understanding, join with their brothers, their nobles, and enter into a curse and an oath to walk in God's Law that was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord and his rules and his statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole people, women and converts included, joins the covenant under oath, reconciled to one another.

All who have knowledge and understanding. Everyone who could understand joins, as at the reading (8:2), wives and daughters included. And belonging is defined by a separation “to the Law of God”, toward something. A foreigner who turned from his gods to the LORD was inside this sentence, as such people had been at the Passover (Ezra 6:21). What marked a person as belonging was whom he worshipped, not who his ancestors were.

Join with their brothers, their nobles. These are the same people who had raised a great outcry against the nobles holding their fields and daughters (5:1–5). The debts had been returned, and the brothers were brothers again: reconciliation came before the covenant.

Enter into a curse and an oath. They swore, and called down on themselves the curses of the law if they broke it. They meant it, and chapter 13 will show how soon it was broken.

verseByVerse.quote: We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land or take their daughters for our sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They promise not to marry their children to the surrounding peoples, because a marriage brings its gods into the home.

We will not give our daughters. This is Deuteronomy 7:3, and the law gave its reason in the next verse: “they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods” (Deuteronomy 7:4). The concern is the worship of the home, not the blood of the partner, which is why the convert is included in verse 28. Nehemiah will find the promise broken when he comes back from Persia, with children who could not speak the language of Judah (13:23–24).

How does this apply now? The New Testament answers both halves plainly. To the unmarried: marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). To the believer already married to an unbeliever: “he should not divorce her”, and “she should not divorce him”, “for the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:12–14). This verse is about marriages not yet made. It gives no one a warrant to leave a marriage that already exists.

verseByVerse.quote: And if the peoples of the land bring in goods or any grain on the Sabbath day to sell, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day. And we will forgo the crops of the seventh year and the exaction of every debt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They promise to keep the Sabbath against foreign traders, and the seventh year with its release of debts.

We will not buy from them on the Sabbath. The Sabbath law forbade Israel to work; it did not stop foreign traders from setting up stalls. The covenant closes the gap: if we cannot sell, we will not buy either. Nehemiah will find this gap wide open (13:15–16).

We will forgo the crops of the seventh year. Every seventh year the land was to lie fallow, “that the poor of your people may eat” (Exodus 23:11), and debts between Israelites were to be released (Deuteronomy 15:2). This makes the debt reform of chapter 5 a standing promise. The fathers who had sold their daughters for debt (5:5) now have the nobles’ sealed word that debts will not grind a family down for ever.

Our buying, selling and lending. The Sabbath and the seventh year were God’s people saying with their calendars and their account books that they trusted him to provide. Is there anything in the way we buy, sell and lend that says we belong to a God who gives rest and forgives debts?

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath bind Christians today? The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 31:13), and the New Testament calls Sabbaths “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), so no day binds the conscience (Romans 14:5); Christians gladly keep the Lord’s Day for worship and rest as a gift. Faithful believers differ here and can differ as brothers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–39 — We Will Not Neglect the House of Our God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant ends with God’s house, and its last words sum it up: “We will not neglect the house of our God” (v. 39). They pledge a yearly third of a shekel for the bread, offerings and feasts of the temple, including the sin offerings that made atonement for Israel (vv. 32–33). They cast lots for who will bring wood so the altar fire never goes out (v. 34). They will bring the firstfruits of field and tree, redeem their firstborn, and bring the first of their dough to the priests (vv. 35–37). The tithes go to the Levites, who tithe in turn, and everything is stored in the temple chambers (vv. 37–39).
verseByVerse.theology: The support of worship is not left to feeling; it is written into a yearly order.

verseByVerse.quote: "We also take on ourselves the obligation to give yearly a third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God: for the showbread, the regular grain offering, the regular burnt offering, the Sabbaths, the new moons, the appointed feasts, the holy things, and the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They pledge a yearly tax to keep the temple’s worship going, sin offerings included.

A third part of a shekel. The law had set a half shekel for each man, rich and poor alike, “to make atonement for your lives” (Exodus 30:15). The community, poor and in debt, pledges a third, every year.

The Son paid it anyway. By Jesus’ day the tax was a half shekel again, and Jesus asked whether kings tax their own sons: “Then the sons are free.” The Son owed nothing to his Father’s house, and paid it anyway, with a coin from a fish’s mouth: “give it to them for me and for yourself” (Matthew 17:26–27). One coin, for the Son and for the disciple together.

The sin offerings to make atonement. Year after year the tax paid for “the sin offerings to make atonement for Israel”. The offerings never stopped because the sins never stopped. “But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down” (Hebrews 10:12). The yearly payments for atonement could end, because Christ had paid for sin in full.
verseByVerse.note: Why a third rather than a half is not explained; perhaps the shekel in use was heavier, perhaps poverty made the full sum impossible (Exod 30:13).

verseByVerse.quote: We, the priests, the Levites, and the people, have likewise cast lots for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, according to our fathers' houses, at times appointed, year by year, to burn on the altar of the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They draw lots to bring firewood, so that the altar fire never goes out.

The wood offering. No law in the five books of Moses sets up a rota for firewood. What is written is that the fire on the altar “shall not go out” (Leviticus 6:12), and if it must never go out, somebody must bring the wood. This is obedience taking a command seriously enough to work out its practical cost.

Among Nehemiah’s last words. It is one of the last things Nehemiah mentions in his whole book: “and I provided for the wood offering at appointed times, and for the firstfruits” (13:31). Faithfulness in God’s house is often a matter of firewood.

verseByVerse.quote: We obligate ourselves to bring the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of the LORD; also to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God, the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, as it is written in the Law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks; and to bring the first of our dough, and our contributions, the fruit of every tree, the wine and the oil, to the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God; and to bring to the Levites the tithes from our ground, for it is the Levites who collect the tithes in all our towns where we labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of everything goes to God, and the tithes go to the Levites, who serve in his house.

The firstfruits of our ground. Then the firsts: firstfruits, firstborn, the first of the dough, each a law of Moses (Exodus 23:19; 13:13; Numbers 15:20). The first of everything went to God, before the family ate or sold any of it. The firstborn sons were redeemed with a price, a reminder that every family owed its eldest to the God who spared them on the night of the Passover.

The tithes from our ground. The tithes go to the Levites, who had no land of their own and lived on what God’s people gave. If the tithes stopped, the Levites went back to the fields and the temple service stopped with them. That is exactly what Nehemiah will find: “the Levites and the singers, who did the work, had fled each to his field” (13:10).

Does the tithe bind Christians today? Israel’s tithes supported the Levites and the worship of a nation under God’s law, and they belonged to that order. The New Testament never commands a tithe to the church. It calls for giving that is regular, proportionate to income, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–5; 9:6–7), and it calls churches to support those who teach them (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14). Many believers find a tenth a good place to start; it is not a ceiling, and it is not a debt.

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest, the son of Aaron, shall be with the Levites when the Levites receive the tithes. And the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes to the house of our God, to the chambers of the storehouse. For the people of Israel and the sons of Levi shall bring the contribution of grain, wine, and oil to the chambers, where the vessels of the sanctuary are, as well as the priests who minister, and the gatekeepers and the singers. We will not neglect the house of our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the Levites tithe, and the covenant closes with the promise that sums it up: they will not forsake God’s house.

The tithe of the tithes. A priest is present at every collection, so that the counting is witnessed, and the Levites give a tenth of what they receive (Numbers 18:26). Nobody is exempt from giving, not even those who live on the gifts.

To the chambers. Notice how often the chambers are mentioned (vv. 37–39): the temple storerooms for the Levites’ grain, wine and oil. In chapter 13 Nehemiah finds that Eliashib the priest has emptied one and moved Tobiah the Ammonite into it, furniture and all (13:4–5).

We will not neglect the house of our God. “Neglect” is the Hebrew word translated “forsake” in the great prayer, which had confessed, “you … did not forsake them” (9:19). God had not forsaken them through centuries of rebellion; they answer that they will not forsake his house. Years later Nehemiah will ask, “Why is the house of God forsaken?” (13:11).

Why a signed covenant is not enough. Their later failure is no reason to despise their promise, which was right and good, but it shows why a covenant signed by us, however sincerely, is not enough. In the new covenant God makes the promises and himself sees that his people keep their side: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), and he gives his Spirit to cause his people to walk in his ways (Ezekiel 36:27). Where we break what we have signed, Christ kept his Father’s will perfectly in our place, and the house of God is safe in the hands of the Son, of whom it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17).

10.theology:
After hearing the law and confessing their history, the people bind themselves in writing to specific obedience in the very places they had failed: marriage, Sabbath, debt, and the support of God's house. It is right that God's people make such commitments, and chapter 13 shows why such commitments cannot save them.

The sin offerings the tax paid for ended only when Christ offered one sacrifice for all time, and in the new covenant God also gives his people the heart to obey.
10.examples: The governor signed first, and the Levites who had taught the law signed beside the priestly house from which John the Baptist's father would come. The debt reform of chapter 5 was written into the covenant, and even the firewood was planned, because the fire on the altar must never go out.

keyVerse.quote: We will not neglect the house of our God.
keyVerse.note: The covenant’s last words gather up all its promises about tax, wood, firstfruits and tithes into one resolve. “Neglect” is the word the great prayer used when it confessed that God “did not forsake” his people (9:19): they answer his faithfulness with theirs. Within a few years Nehemiah will have to ask, “Why is the house of God forsaken?” (13:11), and the promise will wait for the Son who was consumed by zeal for his Father’s house.

10.reflection:
Nehemiah’s name stands first on the covenant, and the Levites who taught the law signed it too (vv. 1, 9). Why does it matter that leaders bind themselves first to what they ask of others? Where is God asking you to go first?

The promises are strikingly practical: marriage, Sabbath trading, debts, firewood, tithes (vv. 30–39). If our church wrote down how grace should change ordinary life this year, what specific things might it include?

The people promised, “We will not neglect the house of our God” (v. 39), yet within a few years they did. What does that teach us about making promises to God, and why do we need the new covenant, with God’s law written on the heart?

Jesus paid the temple tax he did not owe, “for me and for yourself” (Matthew 17:27). How does his generosity to us shape the way we give to God’s work, regularly, gladly and not as a debt?

11.title: Who Will Live in the Holy City?

11.overview:
Where we are. The story picks up the problem left at 7:4: the wall was finished, but “The city was wide and large, but the people within it were few”. The people have heard the law, confessed and sealed their covenant (chapters 8–10). Now the city is filled, before its wall is dedicated in chapter 12.

The message. A city of God needs people willing to live in it. A wall round an empty city defends nothing, so the leaders move in, one family in ten is chosen by lot, and the people bless those who offer themselves freely. The lists that follow are not filler: every name is someone who took up a place in God’s city, and every village is a piece of the promised land lived in again.

Why it was said. Jerusalem was exposed, short of houses and far from most families’ fields, and few wanted to live there (see the introduction). For the first readers these names were records of who belonged where, and a reminder that the restoration God promised had been carried out in real towns by real families.

How the chapter makes its case. The leaders settle in Jerusalem, the rest cast lots to send a tenth, and volunteers are blessed (vv. 1–2). Then the residents are named: the families of Judah and Benjamin with their fighting men (vv. 3–9), the priests (vv. 10–14), the Levites, among them the leader of the praise (vv. 15–18), the gatekeepers (v. 19), and the temple servants and officials, including the king’s provision for the singers (vv. 20–24). Last come the villages: Judah from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom (vv. 25–30), Benjamin from Geba to Lod and Ono (vv. 31–36).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. Jerusalem is “the holy city” (v. 1), a name Scripture finally gives to the new Jerusalem coming down from God (Revelation 21:2). The willing volunteers fit the psalm about the Messiah’s people: “Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power” (Psalm 110:3). Perez and Zerah, both named here, stand at the head of the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). And a people living in their land as if encamped were waiting, with Abraham, for “the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10).

For us. God’s work needs people who will take the harder post, and Christ’s people are volunteers, not conscripts. Bless those who go. But the nine in ten who stayed on their farms were also where God had put them. Whether called to move or to stay, live as citizens of the city that is to come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem is filled by leaders who go first, by a fair lot, and by volunteers whom the people bless. The city had walls and gates but few inhabitants (7:4). So the leaders of the people take up residence there, and everyone else casts lots: one in ten will move to Jerusalem, the holy city, while nine in ten stay in the towns (v. 1). It was a costly move to an exposed, half-built city far from the family land. Some did not wait to be chosen: they offered themselves willingly, and the people blessed them for it (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: They gave God a tenth of their harvest in chapter 10; here they give him a tenth of themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the leaders of the people lived in Jerusalem. And the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in Jerusalem the holy city, while nine out of ten remained in the other towns. And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem is filled by its leaders, by lot, and by volunteers whom the people bless.

One out of ten to live in Jerusalem. The problem was stated in 7:4: a wall round an empty city defends nothing. So the leaders move in, and the rest cast lots to send one family in ten.

Not an easy lot. Jerusalem was the most exposed place in the province, short of houses and far from the fields that fed a family. To move meant leaving the family land for a half-built city on a hill.

Jerusalem the holy city. Isaiah had called her that (Isaiah 52:1), and the name followed her into the Gospels (Matthew 4:5). But its last use is the one this chapter reaches for: “I saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God … Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:2–3). There, nobody has to be chosen by lot to live in it.

All the men who willingly offered. Some did not wait for the lot. They volunteered, and the people blessed them for it. It is what the psalm says of the Messiah’s people: “Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power” (Psalm 110:3). The willingness is itself his gift, and it is still the mark of Christ’s people: not conscripts but volunteers. In the place he has put you, is there a harder post that needs someone to offer, and have you been waiting to be chosen for it?

Should Christians cast lots? In Israel the lot was a recognised way of leaving a fair choice to God (Proverbs 16:33), and the apostles used it once, before Pentecost, to fill Judas’s place (Acts 1:26). After the Spirit was given, the church is never again seen casting lots; it decides by Scripture, prayer and counsel (Acts 15:28). A lot may still settle a fair choice between equal options, but it is not a way of hearing God speak.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–24 — The Chiefs Who Lived in Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list of Jerusalem’s residents shows a city being re-formed around God’s house. First come the families of Judah, sons of Perez, and of Benjamin, with their overseers: nearly fourteen hundred fighting men (vv. 3–9). Then the priests in three groups under Seraiah, of the line of Zadok, “ruler of the house of God” (vv. 10–14). The Levites include those over the outside work of the temple and Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph, who led the thanksgiving (vv. 15–18). The gatekeepers keep watch (v. 19), the temple servants live on Ophel, the singers have a provision from the king, and Pethahiah represents the people at the king’s side (vv. 20–24).
verseByVerse.theology: A city of soldiers, priests, singers and gatekeepers: valiant men and the leader of the praise on the same list. The holy city needed both.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the chiefs of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the towns of Judah everyone lived on his property in their towns: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the descendants of Solomon's servants. And in Jerusalem lived certain of the sons of Judah and of the sons of Benjamin. Of the sons of Judah: Athaiah the son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, of the sons of Perez; and Maaseiah the son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite. All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were 468 valiant men. And these are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah, and his brothers, men of valor, 928. Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer; and Judah the son of Hassenuah was second over the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Families of Judah and Benjamin, nearly fourteen hundred fighting men, hold the city.

Of the sons of Perez. The chiefs are listed with their ancestry. First Judah: 468 valiant men of the sons of Perez (v. 6).

Perez and Zerah. Perez was one of the twin sons of Judah by Tamar, and from Perez came Boaz, David and the kings (Ruth 4:18–22). In verse 24 the other twin appears: Pethahiah, “of the sons of Zerah”. Matthew names them both at the start of the genealogy of Jesus: “Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar” (Matthew 1:3). Both branches of that unlikely family were living in Jerusalem.

Then Benjamin. Benjamin adds 928, with Joel as overseer and Judah son of Hassenuah “second over the city”: together 1,396 fighting men.

Uncertain wording. “Second over the city” may mean that Judah was deputy to Joel, or that he was in charge of the Second Quarter, a district of Jerusalem known by that name (2 Kings 22:14). Either fits.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin, Seraiah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, ruler of the house of God, and their brothers who did the work of the house, 822; and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and his brothers, heads of fathers' houses, 242; and Amashsai, the son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer, and their brothers, mighty men of valor, 128; their overseer was Zabdiel the son of Haggedolim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests serve under a ruler of the house of God whose line ran back to Solomon’s high priest.

Ruler of the house of God. The priests, in three groups, 1,192 in all, serve under “Seraiah … ruler of the house of God” (v. 11). His line runs back through Hilkiah, probably the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah’s day (the list skips generations), to Zadok, Solomon’s high priest. The house of Zadok had come through the exile unbroken.

Mighty men of valor. Some of the priests are “mighty men of valor”: in a city under threat, the same men were both holy and brave.

Uncertain wording. Haggedolim (v. 14) means “the great ones”: a family name, as the ESV takes it, or a way of saying Zabdiel came from a leading family.

verseByVerse.quote: And of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni; and Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chiefs of the Levites, who were over the outside work of the house of God; and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, who was the leader of the praise, who gave thanks, and Bakbukiah, the second among his brothers; and Abda the son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun. All the Levites in the holy city were 284. The gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates, were 172.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levites lead the praise, and gatekeepers keep watch at the doors.

The leader of the praise. The Levites include men “over the outside work of the house of God”, the repairs and supplies, and Mattaniah, of the sons of Asaph, “the leader of the praise”. Asaph was David’s chief musician, and twelve psalms bear his name (Psalms 50; 73–83). Five centuries on, his descendant is leading the thanksgiving in the rebuilt temple.

The gatekeepers. The gates Nehemiah had hung (7:1) now had keepers. Praise inside and watchmen at the doors: a church still needs both.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of Israel, and of the priests and the Levites, were in all the towns of Judah, every one in his inheritance. But the temple servants lived on Ophel; and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants. The overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, of the sons of Asaph, the singers, over the work of the house of God. For there was a command from the king concerning them, and a fixed provision for the singers, as every day required. And Pethahiah the son of Meshezabel, of the sons of Zerah the son of Judah, was at the king's side in all matters concerning the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of Israel lived on their family land, and the temple servants, singers and officials each had their place.

Every one in his inheritance. “His inheritance” is the family land allotted in Joshua’s day, returned to after the exile (see inheritance). The nine in ten who stayed were not failing to answer a call; they were living on the land God had promised them.

A command from the king. The temple servants lived on Ophel, where they had built their stretch of wall (3:26). The king who provided for the singers is probably the Persian king, who had already exempted them from tax (Ezra 7:24). If so, an emperor who worshipped other gods was paying the daily wages of the choir that sang Asaph’s psalms to the LORD.

Pethahiah the son of Meshezabel. Pethahiah, at the king’s side in all matters concerning the people, held a post not unlike Nehemiah’s own at Susa. God always had one of his people close to the king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–36 — From Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The villages complete the picture: the people are back in the land, town by town. Judah lives from Kiriath-arba, the old Hebron, down to Beersheba and up to the edge of the Valley of Hinnom (vv. 25–30), a land full of memories of Abraham, David and the last stand against Babylon. Benjamin lives from Geba through Michmash, Bethel, Anathoth, Ramah and Nob to Lod and Ono near the coast (vv. 31–35). Some Levites of Judah are assigned to Benjamin, so that the law is taught throughout the land (v. 36). Yet they “encamped”: back home, and still pilgrims.
verseByVerse.theology: Every name on the list is a town God had given their fathers, and nearly every one has a story.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the villages, with their fields, some of the people of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba and its villages, and in Dibon and its villages, and in Jekabzeel and its villages, and in Jeshua and in Moladah and Beth-pelet, in Hazar-shual, in Beersheba and its villages, in Ziklag, in Meconah and its villages, in En-rimmon, in Zorah, in Jarmuth, Zanoah, Adullam, and their villages, Lachish and its fields, and Azekah and its villages. So they encamped from Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah lives again in towns full of its history, yet still like a people encamped.

From Beersheba to the Valley of Hinnom. Kiriath-arba is the old name of Hebron (Joshua 14:15), where Abraham bought a grave and David was first crowned. Then Beersheba, where Abraham dug his wells; Ziklag, given to David; Zorah, where Samson was born; Adullam, David’s cave; Lachish and Azekah, the last fortresses to hold out against Babylon (Jeremiah 34:7). Every town is a chapter of their history, lived in again.

So they encamped. The old measure of the land was “from Dan to Beersheba”, from the far north to the far south; now it runs from Beersheba to the edge of Jerusalem, a fraction of what they had once held. And they “encamped”, the word used of Israel in the wilderness: back in the land, and still living like pilgrims in it.

The Valley of Hinnom. This is the valley of Topheth, where Judah’s kings had burned their children in the fire (Jeremiah 7:31). Its name in the Greek of the Gospels is Gehenna, the word Jesus used for hell. The people lived up to the edge of the place of their worst sin, in a land given back to them, still looking for more than it could give. We are in the same position: “here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come” (Hebrews 13:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Benjamin also lived from Geba onward, at Michmash, Aija, Bethel and its villages, Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah, Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim, Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat, Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen. And certain divisions of the Levites in Judah were assigned to Benjamin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin too is resettled, and every part of the land has Levites to teach it.

Michmash, Bethel, Anathoth, Ramah, Nob. Michmash, where Jonathan climbed the cliff; Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder; Anathoth, Jeremiah’s town; Ramah, Samuel’s home. And Nob, “the city of the priests”, which Saul put to the sword (1 Samuel 22:19). The town of a massacre is a town of families again.

Lod, and Ono. The list runs on to Lod and Ono, the plain where Sanballat had tried to lure Nehemiah (6:2). And Levites of Judah were assigned to Benjamin, so that no part of the land was left without teachers of the law.

Strangers in the land. The patriarchs had lived in this land as strangers too: “he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God”, and “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:10, 16). Those who moved and those who stayed were all waiting for that city. Christ has built it, and in it no lot is needed: every one of his people lives there.

11.theology:
A tenth of the people is given to the holy city, some by lot and some by free offering, and those who stayed on their inheritance were no less God's people.

Yet all of them, in the city and the villages, were still only encamped, like travellers, in a land far smaller than before, waiting for the holy city coming down from heaven where God dwells with his people (Rev 21:2-3).
11.examples:
The volunteers who moved to the most exposed place in the province were blessed by everyone else. In the city, both of Tamar's twins had descendants, and a descendant of Asaph led the praise while a Persian king paid the singers.

Outside it, Nob, where Saul killed the priests, was lived in again.

keyVerse.quote: And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s lists rest on this one sentence. Jerusalem was rebuilt, but it would live only if people were willing to make their homes in it, at real cost. Their free offering of themselves pictures the people of the Messiah, who “will offer themselves freely on the day of your power” (Psalm 110:3), and the people’s blessing shows how God’s people should honour those who take the harder post.

11.reflection:
A wall round an empty city defends nothing (7:4). What might be the equivalent in a church: buildings, programmes or structures without people willing to give themselves to them?

Some were chosen by lot; others “willingly offered” and were blessed for it (vv. 1–2). Is there a harder post in your church or community that needs someone to volunteer? How can we honour those who take such posts?

The nine in ten who stayed on their land were also where God had put them (v. 20). How do we hold together the call to sacrifice and the goodness of faithful ordinary life where God has placed us?

The people “encamped” in their own land (v. 30), and Hebrews says “here we have no lasting city” (Hebrews 13:14). How does looking forward to the new Jerusalem change the way we live in our own towns now?

12.title: Joy Heard Far Away
