And Ezra the scribe went before them.<sup>37</sup>At the Fountain Gate they went up straight before them by the stairs of the city of David, at the ascent of the wall, above the house of David, to the Water Gate on the east.<sup>38</sup>The other choir of those who gave thanks went to the north, and I followed them with half of the people, on the wall, above the Tower of the Ovens, to the Broad Wall,<sup>39</sup>and above the Gate of Ephraim, and by the Gate of Yeshanah, and by the Fish Gate and the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, to the Sheep Gate; and they came to a halt at the Gate of the Guard.<sup>40</sup>So both choirs of those who gave thanks stood in the house of God, and I and half of the officials with me;<sup>41</sup>and the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets;<sup>42</sup>and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang with Jezrahiah as their leader.<sup>43</sup>And they offered great sacrifices that day and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy; the women and children also rejoiced. And the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away.<sup>44</sup>On that day men were appointed over the storerooms, the contributions, the firstfruits, and the tithes, to gather into them the portions required by the Law for the priests and for the Levites according to the fields of the towns, for Judah rejoiced over the priests and the Levites who ministered.<sup>45</sup>And they performed the service of their God and the service of purification, as did the singers and the gatekeepers, according to the command of David and his son Solomon.<sup>46</sup>For long ago in the days of David and Asaph there were directors of the singers, and there were songs of praise and thanksgiving to God.<sup>47</sup>And all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah gave the daily portions for the singers and the gatekeepers; and they set apart that which was for the Levites; and the Levites set apart that which was for the sons of Aaron.
12.overview:
Where we are. The wall is built (chapter 6), the people have renewed the covenant (chapters 8–10) and the city has been filled (chapter 11). Now comes the day the whole book has been building towards, the dedication of the wall, before the sad return of chapter 13.

The message. When God restores his people, the right end of all their work is worship and joy, and the joy is his gift: “God had made them rejoice with great joy” (v. 43). The wall built with swords at the builders’ sides is walked by singing choirs, and everything leads to the house of God. The joy rests on generations of quiet faithfulness, and it shows itself at once in care for those who serve.

Why it was said. The first readers were a small community still poor and surrounded by enemies, whose return had often seemed “the day of small things” (Zechariah 4:10; see the introduction). They needed to know that the rebuilding was God’s doing, that its purpose was his praise, and that their families’ long service at his house mattered.

How the chapter makes its case. First the roll of the priests and Levites, from those who came home with Zerubbabel through six generations of high priests to the days of Nehemiah and Ezra (vv. 1–26): the celebration stands on generations of service. Then the dedication: Levites and singers are gathered and everything purified (vv. 27–30); two great choirs walk the top of the wall in opposite directions, Ezra leading one and Nehemiah following the other (vv. 31–39); both meet in the house of God, where sacrifices are offered and “the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away” (vv. 40–43). That same day storekeepers are appointed, because Judah rejoiced over those who ministered (vv. 44–47).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The priesthood whose roll is kept here produced Eliashib, whose family married into Sanballat’s (13:28), and it needed a better Priest, “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). The joy heard far away was a foretaste of “good news of great joy that will be for all the people” (Luke 2:10), and when the King rode toward this city, his disciples’ praise was such that, he said, if they were silent “the very stones would cry out” (Luke 19:40).

For us. Let worship be the goal of your work, and receive joy as God’s gift rather than a reward for finishing. Thank God for the unnoticed faithfulness of those who went before you, and let your gladness in Christ show in care for those who serve you in his name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — In the Days of Nehemiah the Governor and of Ezra
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The dedication of the wall stands on a century of faithful service, and this roll of priests and Levites shows it. It begins with the twenty-two heads of priestly houses and the Levites who came home with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, including the singers who answered one another in thanksgiving (vv. 1–9). It traces the high priests from Jeshua to Jaddua, six generations (vv. 10–11), then names the head of each priestly house in the next generation, among them Zechariah of the house of Iddo (vv. 12–21). It ends with the Levites who praised “watch by watch” as David had commanded, and the gatekeepers, in the days of Nehemiah and Ezra (vv. 22–26).
verseByVerse.theology: Before the celebration comes the roll-call of the men who led the worship for three generations: the joy of verse 43 had a history behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the priests and the Levites who came up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra, Amariah, Malluch, Hattush, Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth, Iddo, Ginnethoi, Abijah, Mijamin, Maadiah, Bilgah, Shemaiah, Joiarib, Jedaiah, Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah. These were the chiefs of the priests and of their brothers in the days of Jeshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dedication begins with the priestly families of the first return: the celebration stands on generations of faithfulness.

Who came up with Zerubbabel. Twenty-two heads of priestly houses from the first return under Zerubbabel, ninety years before. (The Ezra here is not the scribe, who came much later.) Among them are Abijah (v. 4), the house of John the Baptist’s father (Luke 1:5), and Joiarib and Jedaiah (v. 6), whose names head David’s list of the divisions of the priests (1 Chronicles 24:7).

Why put a list here, just before the dedication? Because the wall was dedicated by the heirs of families who had kept the worship going through exile and return, a faithfulness nobody had noticed at the time.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Levites: Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who with his brothers was in charge of the songs of thanksgiving. And Bakbukiah and Unni and their brothers stood opposite them in the service.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levite singers answered one another in thanksgiving.

Stood opposite them in the service. Two groups of singers facing each other, one answering the other. That is how many psalms were meant to be sung: a line and its reply, “for he is good” and “his steadfast love endures forever”. Mattaniah’s family kept that thanksgiving going for a century.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jeshua was the father of Joiakim, Joiakim the father of Eliashib, Eliashib the father of Joiada, Joiada the father of Jonathan, and Jonathan the father of Jaddua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six generations of high priests are listed, among them a family that would betray the covenant.

Six generations of high priests. From the Jeshua who came home with Zerubbabel (Joshua the high priest) to Jaddua, three generations after Eliashib, the high priest of Nehemiah’s day. The list has been kept up to date by later hands; verse 22 mentions a Darius who reigned after Artaxerxes (see the introduction).

Eliashib and Joiada. The third name is the Eliashib who built the Sheep Gate (3:1), and a son of the fourth, Joiada, became the son-in-law of Sanballat (13:28): the high priest’s own family married into the enemy’s. The priesthood of Aaron needed a better Priest than any it could produce: one “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And in the days of Joiakim were priests, heads of fathers' houses: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah; of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan; of Malluchi, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph; of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai; of Iddo, Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam; of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin, of Moadiah, Piltai; of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jehonathan; of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi; of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber; of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; of Jedaiah, Nethanel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A generation later each priestly house still had its head, one of them the prophet Zechariah.

In the days of Joiakim. For each of the old houses, the man who led it a generation later: “of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah; of Ezra, Meshullam”, and so on down the list.

Of Iddo, Zechariah. One line is easy to pass over (v. 16). The prophet Zechariah was “the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo” (Zechariah 1:1), and Ezra calls him simply “Zechariah the son of Iddo” (Ezra 5:1). This is almost certainly the same man: the prophet who urged the people to finish the temple was the head of a priestly house. He had written, “Behold, your king is coming to you” (Zechariah 9:9), words the Gospels would quote of Christ riding into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5), and here he sits quietly in a list of priests, between a Helkai and a Meshullam.

Of Abijah, Zichri. The priestly house of John the Baptist’s father (v. 17; Luke 1:5) was still serving.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua, the Levites were recorded as heads of fathers' houses; so too were the priests in the reign of Darius the Persian. As for the sons of Levi, their heads of fathers' houses were written in the Book of the Chronicles until the days of Johanan the son of Eliashib. And the chiefs of the Levites: Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua the son of Kadmiel, with their brothers who stood opposite them, to praise and to give thanks, according to the commandment of David the man of God, watch by watch. Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers standing guard at the storehouses of the gates. These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and of Ezra, the priest and scribe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites praised in shifts, as David had ordered five centuries before.

David the man of God. “The man of God” was Moses’ title, and here it is David’s (as at 2 Chronicles 8:14), because David ordered the worship of the house as Moses had ordered the tabernacle. His pattern of praise, choir answering choir “watch by watch”, was still being kept.

The Book of the Chronicles. This (v. 23) is probably the temple’s own register of priestly and Levitical families, not the biblical books of Chronicles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–43 — The Joy of Jerusalem Was Heard Far Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The work of the wall ends in worship, and the joy is God’s gift. The Levites and singers are fetched from their villages, and priests, people, gates and wall are purified (vv. 27–30). Nehemiah brings the leaders up onto the wall and sets two great thanksgiving choirs walking along the top of it in opposite directions: one south with Ezra the scribe in front (vv. 31–37), the other north with Nehemiah following (vv. 38–39). They meet in the house of God (vv. 40–42), and with great sacrifices the whole people, women and children too, rejoice, for “God had made them rejoice with great joy”, and the sound carries far away (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: The day of dedication is worship from first to last: purification, music, sacrifice and joy.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites in all their places, to bring them to Jerusalem to celebrate the dedication with gladness, with thanksgivings and with singing, with cymbals, harps, and lyres. And the sons of the singers gathered together from the district surrounding Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites; also from Beth-gilgal and from the region of Geba and Azmaveth, for the singers had built for themselves villages around Jerusalem. And the priests and the Levites purified themselves, and they purified the people and the gates and the wall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levites and singers are gathered, and everyone and everything is made clean for God.

At the dedication of the wall. The wall was finished in Elul (6:15); its dedication is not dated. They sent into every village for the Levites, because the dedication was to be an act of worship, and worship was their work.

The singers had built for themselves villages. At Netophah, Beth-gilgal, Geba and Azmaveth: a ring of singers’ families close enough to come in for their turn.

They purified the people and the gates and the wall. What is given to God is made clean first, beginning with those who give it, and the wall built by families with swords at their sides was set apart as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I brought the leaders of Judah up onto the wall and appointed two great choirs that gave thanks. One went to the south on the wall to the Dung Gate. And after them went Hoshaiah and half of the leaders of Judah, and Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah, and certain of the priests' sons with trumpets: Zechariah the son of Jonathan, son of Shemaiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micaiah, son of Zaccur, son of Asaph; and his relatives, Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God. And Ezra the scribe went before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two great choirs climb onto the mocked wall, and the first sets off with Ezra at its head.

Up onto the wall. Tobiah had said a fox would knock the wall down (4:3). Now hundreds of people, with trumpets, harps and cymbals, walk along the top of it, singing: the wall held a choir.

And Ezra the scribe went before them. The southern choir goes toward the Dung Gate with half the leaders of Judah, priests with trumpets, and Zechariah son of Jonathan, a descendant of Asaph, with his relatives playing “the musical instruments of David the man of God”. Ezra, who had read the law from early morning until midday (8:3), leads the procession on the wall: the word goes first.

With trumpets. Moses had given the trumpets to the priests (Numbers 10:8), to be blown “on the day of your gladness” over the offerings as “a reminder of you before your God” (Numbers 10:10). In Hebrew “reminder” comes from the same word as Nehemiah’s constant prayer, “remember”. The trumpets on the wall asked God to remember his people on the day of their gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: At the Fountain Gate they went up straight before them by the stairs of the city of David, at the ascent of the wall, above the house of David, to the Water Gate on the east. The other choir of those who gave thanks went to the north, and I followed them with half of the people, on the wall, above the Tower of the Ovens, to the Broad Wall, and above the Gate of Ephraim, and by the Gate of Yeshanah, and by the Fish Gate and the Tower of Hananel and the Tower of the Hundred, to the Sheep Gate; and they came to a halt at the Gate of the Guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second choir walks back over the stretch whose building opened chapter 3: the route of the work becomes the route of a hymn.

The route against chapter 3. Chapter 3 began at the Sheep Gate and ran past the Tower of Hananel, the Fish Gate, the Broad Wall and the Tower of the Ovens (3:1–11), and the northern choir walks the same stretch in reverse. The stones that Eliashib, the men of Jericho, the goldsmiths and Shallum’s daughters had laid are walked over by a choir giving thanks. And the Tower of Hananel, named in Jeremiah’s promise that the city would be rebuilt for the LORD (Jeremiah 31:38), hears the singing.

I followed them. Nehemiah does not lead this choir; the governor who had driven the whole work walks behind the singers.

Uncertain wording. The Gate of Yeshanah (v. 39; 3:6) may mean “the Old Gate”, as some versions translate it, or be named for the town of Jeshanah to the north. The site of the Gate of the Guard is also unknown, though the route as a whole is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: So both choirs of those who gave thanks stood in the house of God, and I and half of the officials with me; and the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets; and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang with Jezrahiah as their leader.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two processions meet in the house of God.

Both choirs stood in the house of God. Two processions set out in opposite directions round the city and meet at the house of God. Every stretch of the wall has been walked and sung over, and everything converges on the place where God had put his name. The wall was never the point.

verseByVerse.quote: And they offered great sacrifices that day and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy; the women and children also rejoiced. And the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole people rejoices with a joy God gave, heard far away.

God had made them rejoice. Count them: “rejoiced”, “made them rejoice”, “joy”, “rejoiced”, “joy”, five times in one verse. And the source is named: “God had made them rejoice”. The joy was not the natural relief of a project finished; it was given. They had been told that the joy of the LORD was their strength (8:10), and here is that joy, poured out.

The women and children also rejoiced. The wives who had raised the outcry about debt (5:1), the children who had been sold for it (5:5), were singing in the city that had been ruins.

Heard far away. These words were written once before. When the temple foundation was laid ninety years earlier, the old men wept while the young shouted for joy, and no one could tell the joyful shout from the weeping, “and the sound was heard far away” (Ezra 3:13). That day joy and grief were mixed; this day, only the joy is heard.

The very stones would cry out. It was still not the last word; the next chapter is a sad one. But it was a sound of what was coming: “Behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people” (Luke 2:10). When the King came down the Mount of Olives toward this city, “the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice”; told to silence them, he said, “if these were silent, the very stones would cry out” (Luke 19:37, 40). Sanballat had asked whether they could revive the stones (4:2). The King said the stones themselves would sing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–47 — For Judah Rejoiced over the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joy turns at once into faithful provision. That same day men are put in charge of the storerooms where the contributions, firstfruits and tithes for the priests and Levites are gathered, because Judah rejoiced over those who ministered (v. 44). Priests, singers and gatekeepers serve as David and Solomon had ordered, in a tradition of praise going back to David and Asaph (vv. 45–46). All Israel gives the daily portions for the singers and gatekeepers, the Levites receive their share and set apart a share for the priests (v. 47). These were the best years; the next chapter will show how fragile they were.
verseByVerse.theology: The joy was turned into provision the same day, which is the right order.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day men were appointed over the storerooms, the contributions, the firstfruits, and the tithes, to gather into them the portions required by the Law for the priests and for the Levites according to the fields of the towns, for Judah rejoiced over the priests and the Levites who ministered. And they performed the service of their God and the service of purification, as did the singers and the gatekeepers, according to the command of David and his son Solomon. For long ago in the days of David and Asaph there were directors of the singers, and there were songs of praise and thanksgiving to God. And all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah gave the daily portions for the singers and the gatekeepers; and they set apart that which was for the Levites; and the Levites set apart that which was for the sons of Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joy turns at once into provision for those who serve.

Appointed over the storerooms. On the same day as the singing, Nehemiah appoints storekeepers. That is not a fall from joy into bookkeeping but joy doing what joy does: people glad of those who serve them want to see them fed. The covenant promises of 10:35–39 were being put into practice.

Joy that is not guarded. Verse 47 sums up the best years, and the next chapter shows how quickly the giving could fail: when Nehemiah came back from Susa, the portions had stopped and the Levites had gone home to their fields (13:10). Joy that is not guarded does not last. But the sound of verse 43 had been real, and God, who made them rejoice, has promised a city where the joy is never interrupted and the singers never go hungry: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore” (Revelation 7:16).

12.theology:
The book that began with a man weeping over a burned city (1:4) reaches a city whose joy is heard far away, and the joy is God's gift. The wall was built round a people, and the people were gathered round God; the two choirs end in his house.

This joy points ahead to the King Zechariah promised, whose coming made the disciples rejoice, and to a last city whose joy will not be interrupted (Rev 7:16-17).
12.examples:
The prophet Zechariah appears as one quiet line in a list of priests. On the day of dedication the northern choir walked the stretch of wall listed in chapter 3, in the opposite direction, Ezra went in front while Nehemiah walked behind, and the women and children sang.

That same day they appointed storekeepers, so that the joy would feed those who served.

keyVerse.quote: And they offered great sacrifices that day and rejoiced, for God had made them rejoice with great joy; the women and children also rejoiced. And the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the book. Five times in one verse the Hebrew speaks of joy, and its source is named: God made them rejoice. The sorrow mixed into the shout at the temple’s foundation (Ezra 3:13) is gone, and the sound carries far beyond the walls, a foretaste of the “good news of great joy” that would one day be announced for all the people (Luke 2:10).

12.reflection:
The dedication opens with a long list of priestly families who had served for ninety years (vv. 1–26). Whose quiet, unnoticed faithfulness stands behind the joys of your own Christian life or church? How might you thank God for them?

The work of the wall ended in worship, with the choirs meeting in the house of God (vv. 40–42). How can we keep worship, rather than the project itself, as the goal of the things we build for God?

“God had made them rejoice with great joy” (v. 43). What is the difference between joy given by God and the relief of finishing a task? How does the gospel give joy that does not depend on our achievements?

Their joy turned at once into provision for those who served (v. 44), yet within a few years the giving had stopped (13:10). What helps joy in Christ last, and show itself in practical care for those who minister among us?

13.title: Remember Me, O My God
13.text: <sup>1</sup>On that day they read from the Book of Moses in the hearing of the people. And in it was found written that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God,<sup>2</sup>for they did not meet the people of Israel with bread and water, but hired Balaam against them to curse them—yet our God turned the curse into a blessing.<sup>3</sup>As soon as the people heard the law, they separated from Israel all those of foreign descent.<sup>4</sup>Now before this, Eliashib the priest, who was appointed over the chambers of the house of our God, and who was related to Tobiah,<sup>5</sup>prepared for Tobiah a large chamber where they had previously put the grain offering, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of grain, wine, and oil, which were given by commandment to the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the contributions for the priests.<sup>6</sup>While this was taking place, I was not in Jerusalem, for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon I went to the king. And after some time I asked leave of the king<sup>7</sup>and came to Jerusalem, and I then discovered the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, preparing for him a chamber in the courts of the house of God.<sup>8</sup>And I was very angry, and I threw all the household furniture of Tobiah out of the chamber.<sup>9</sup>Then I gave orders, and they cleansed the chambers, and I brought back there the vessels of the house of God, with the grain offering and the frankincense.<sup>10</sup>I also found out that the portions of the Levites had not been given to them, so that the Levites and the singers, who did the work, had fled each to his field.<sup>11</sup>So I confronted the officials and said, "Why is the house of God forsaken?" And I gathered them together and set them in their stations.<sup>12</sup>Then all Judah brought the tithe of the grain, wine, and oil into the storehouses.<sup>13</sup>And I appointed as treasurers over the storehouses Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites, and as their assistant Hanan the son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers.<sup>14</sup>Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and do not wipe out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God and for his service.<sup>15</sup>In those days I saw in Judah people treading winepresses on the Sabbath, and bringing in heaps of grain and loading them on donkeys, and also wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of loads, which they brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. And I warned them on the day when they sold food.<sup>16</sup>Tyrians also, who lived in the city, brought in fish and all kinds of goods and sold them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah, in Jerusalem itself!<sup>17</sup>Then I confronted the nobles of Judah and said to them, "What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day?<sup>18</sup>Did not your fathers act in this way, and did not our God bring all this disaster on us and on this city? Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath."<sup>19</sup>As soon as it began to grow dark at the gates of Jerusalem before the Sabbath, I commanded that the doors should be shut and gave orders that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. And I stationed some of my servants at the gates, that no load might be brought in on the Sabbath day.<sup>20</sup>Then the merchants and sellers of all kinds of wares lodged outside Jerusalem once or twice.<sup>21</sup>But I warned them and said to them, "Why do you lodge outside the wall? If you do so again, I will lay hands on you." From that time on they did not come on the Sabbath.<sup>22</sup>Then I commanded the Levites that they should purify themselves and come and guard the gates, to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember this also in my favor, O my God, and spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love.<sup>23</sup>In those days also I saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.<sup>24</sup>And half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod, and they could not speak the language of Judah, but only the language of each people.<sup>25</sup>And I confronted them and cursed them and beat some of them and pulled out their hair. And I made them take an oath in the name of God, saying, "You shall not give your daughters to their sons, or take their daughters for your sons or for yourselves.<sup>26</sup>Did not Solomon king of Israel sin on account of such women? Among the many nations there was no king like him, and he was beloved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Nevertheless, foreign women made even him to sin.<sup>27</sup>Shall we then listen to you and do all this great evil and act treacherously against our God by marrying foreign women?"<sup>28</sup>And one of the sons of Jehoiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was the son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite. Therefore I chased him from me.<sup>29</sup>Remember them, O my God, because they have desecrated the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and the Levites.<sup>30</sup>Thus I cleansed them from everything foreign, and I established the duties of the priests and Levites, each in his work;<sup>31</sup>and I provided for the wood offering at appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.
13.overview:
Where we are. This is the latest history the Old Testament tells. Chapter 12 ended in joy and gladly given tithes (12:43–47). Then the story jumps some years: Nehemiah returns from the Persian court to find the covenant of chapter 10 broken clause by clause.

The message. Reform, however real, cannot change a heart. God’s people drifted back as soon as their governor was out of sight, and the best of leaders could only clear a room, shut a gate and extract an oath. So the chapter calls God’s people to guard his house, his day and their homes, and throws them, with Nehemiah, on the steadfast love of a God who remembers his servants for good.

Why it was said. The first readers knew how quickly their promises about marriage, the Sabbath and God’s house had been broken (see the introduction); Malachi seems to have preached against the same sins. The chapter told them that God’s law still stood, and that their hope lay not in their governor but in God’s mercy.

How the chapter makes its case. The law shutting out Ammon and Moab is read and obeyed (vv. 1–3), yet Tobiah the Ammonite is lodged in a temple storeroom, and Nehemiah throws his furniture out (vv. 4–9). The unpaid Levites have gone back to their fields; Nehemiah asks, “Why is the house of God forsaken?” and restores them (vv. 10–14). Jerusalem has become a Sabbath market, and he shuts the gates (vv. 15–22). Men have married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, the high priest’s grandson has married Sanballat’s daughter, and Nehemiah confronts them with the fall of Solomon (vv. 23–31). Four short prayers beginning “Remember” punctuate the story (vv. 14, 22, 29, 31).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes. Nearly every clause of the covenant was broken within a few years, and only God’s promised new covenant answers that: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). By pattern too: Nehemiah cleansed one temple room for a season, and Christ, consumed by zeal for his Father’s house, gave his own body as the true temple (John 2:17–21); the failing priesthood needed “such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). And the book’s last prayer, “Remember me, O my God, for good”, was answered outside this city’s walls, when Jesus told a dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

For us. Ask where your first promises to God have quietly slipped, in worship, in giving, in whom you let shape your home, and act on it. But do not rest your hope on your reforms. Pray Nehemiah’s prayer through Christ, “spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love”, and you will be remembered for good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — In the Courts of the House of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s law was read and obeyed, yet the man in charge of God’s house had already let God’s enemy into it. On the day the law was read, the people heard that Ammon and Moab, who had refused Israel bread and water and hired Balaam to curse them, were barred from the assembly, and they separated those of foreign descent (vv. 1–3). But while Nehemiah was away at the Persian court, Eliashib the priest had emptied a storeroom of the Levites’ tithes and given it to Tobiah the Ammonite, his relative (vv. 4–6). Nehemiah returned, threw Tobiah’s furniture out in anger, had the rooms cleansed and brought the holy things back (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The enemy the wall had kept out while Nehemiah was there was let in by the priest’s own family.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day they read from the Book of Moses in the hearing of the people. And in it was found written that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God, for they did not meet the people of Israel with bread and water, but hired Balaam against them to curse them—yet our God turned the curse into a blessing. As soon as the people heard the law, they separated from Israel all those of foreign descent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the law was read, the people learned that Ammon and Moab were barred from Israel’s assembly for trying to curse them, and they obeyed at once. Yet the reason given ends in grace: God turned the curse into a blessing.

On that day they read from the Book of Moses. The phrase ties this reading to the days of the dedication (12:44), before the story jumps forward (v. 6). The law is still being read, as at the Water Gate, and still obeyed. The passage is Deuteronomy 23:3–5: Ammon and Moab had refused a thirsty people bread and water in the wilderness and hired Balaam to curse them, but God turned the curse into a blessing “because the LORD your God loved you” (Deuteronomy 23:5).

They separated from Israel all those of foreign descent. The text does not say how. Read beside the law just quoted, it most likely meant excluding them from the assembly, the gathering of Israel for worship and decision, not driving them out of the land.

Not about race. Two things show it. The first is Ruth, a Moabite and David’s great-grandmother (Ruth 4:17), who said, “your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16), and who had come, Boaz said, to take refuge under the wings of the LORD (Ruth 2:12). The law closed the door to Moab the nation, never to a Moabitess who came to the LORD. The second is the last line: “our God turned the curse into a blessing”.

The curse turned into a blessing. That is what God does. “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us… so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:13–14). The cross has opened the door to every Ammonite and Moabite who comes, and in him the dividing wall between peoples is broken down (Ephesians 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now before this, Eliashib the priest, who was appointed over the chambers of the house of our God, and who was related to Tobiah, prepared for Tobiah a large chamber where they had previously put the grain offering, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of grain, wine, and oil, which were given by commandment to the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the contributions for the priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Nehemiah was away, the priest in charge of the temple storerooms emptied a storeroom of the offerings for God’s servants and gave it to Tobiah, Israel’s old enemy and his own relative.

Now before this. The law excluding Ammonites has just been read, and an Ammonite is already living in the temple. Tobiah, who had mocked the wall (4:3), plotted against it (4:7–8), hired a prophet to frighten Nehemiah (6:12) and written him threatening letters (6:19), had been given a room in the house of God by the man in charge of those rooms. Eliashib was probably the high priest of that name (3:1; 13:28), though some think he was another priest.

Where the tithes had been. It was the very storeroom meant for the tithes the covenant had promised (10:37–39). The Levites’ food had been moved out to make room for the enemy’s furniture. Family loyalty had done what open hostility never could: compromise rarely comes over the wall by force, but is let in by someone we love.

Uncertain wording. “Related to” is literally “near to”, which can mean a relative or simply a close associate. Tobiah’s marriage ties in Jerusalem (6:18) make a family link likely, but the exact relationship is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: While this was taking place, I was not in Jerusalem, for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon I went to the king. And after some time I asked leave of the king and came to Jerusalem, and I then discovered the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, preparing for him a chamber in the courts of the house of God. And I was very angry, and I threw all the household furniture of Tobiah out of the chamber. Then I gave orders, and they cleansed the chambers, and I brought back there the vessels of the house of God, with the grain offering and the frankincense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Returning from the Persian court, Nehemiah found God’s enemy lodged in God’s house, and in anger threw his belongings out, had the rooms cleansed and put the holy things back.

I was not in Jerusalem. Twelve years after he arrived (5:14), Nehemiah had gone back to the king, as he had promised (2:6). How long he was away we are not told, but it was long enough for this. Artaxerxes is called “king of Babylon” because Persian kings took over the titles of the empires they had conquered (compare Ezra 6:22, “king of Assyria”).

I threw all the household furniture of Tobiah out. Picture the governor of Judah carrying an Ammonite’s household goods out of a temple storeroom, then having the chambers cleansed and the vessels and offerings brought back in. His anger was zeal for God’s honour, not wounded pride.

He cleared one room for a season. Some four and a half centuries later another man found the temple courts full of traders and drove them out, and his disciples “remembered that it was written, ‘Zeal for your house will consume me’” (John 2:15–17). Christ’s zeal for his Father’s house cost him his life, and the temple, he said, was his own body, which he would raise in three days (John 2:19–21).

The myth of steady progress. Modern people tend to assume that, with enough education, technology and good policy, each generation will be wiser and kinder than the last. The twentieth century, whose worst horrors were organised by some of the best-educated nations on earth, should have cured us of that faith. Nehemiah’s last chapter is a cold shower for it. The wall is up, the law read, the covenant sealed, and within a few years an enemy is living in the temple, the Levites are back in the fields and the Sabbath market is open. Reform was real, and it did not stick, because the deepest problem was never the walls but the human heart. That is not a counsel of despair: Nehemiah went on reforming, and so should we. But the Bible’s hope is a Builder who will not have to come back and do it all again, because he writes his law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).
verseByVerse.note: Nehemiah returned to the king in about 433 BC (the thirty-second year) and later came back to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — Why Is the House of God Forsaken?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s people stop providing for his house, his work stops too, and Nehemiah will not let it stay that way. The tithes had stopped coming, so the Levites and singers had gone home to farm (v. 10). Nehemiah confronts the officials with one question, “Why is the house of God forsaken?”, echoing the people’s own vow not to neglect it, and puts the workers back in their stations (v. 11). The tithes come in again, and he appoints trustworthy men to distribute them (vv. 12–13). Then he asks God not to wipe out the service his people had so quickly undone (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The people's promise to care for God's house had lasted only while someone was watching.

verseByVerse.quote: I also found out that the portions of the Levites had not been given to them, so that the Levites and the singers, who did the work, had fled each to his field. So I confronted the officials and said, "Why is the house of God forsaken?" And I gathered them together and set them in their stations. Then all Judah brought the tithe of the grain, wine, and oil into the storehouses. And I appointed as treasurers over the storehouses Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah of the Levites, and as their assistant Hanan the son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tithes had stopped, so the Levites and singers had gone home to farm; Nehemiah rebuked the officials, brought the workers back and put the storehouses in trustworthy hands.

The portions of the Levites had not been given. The men who led the worship had gone back to their farms to feed their families; the singers whose joy was heard far away (12:43) were out in the fields. Malachi named the same neglect: “Will man rob God? Yet you are robbing me” (Malachi 3:8).

Why is the house of God forsaken? Forsaken is the Hebrew verb behind their oath, “We will not neglect the house of our God” (10:39), and behind their prayer, which confessed that God “did not forsake them” (9:17, 19). God had not forsaken his people through centuries of rebellion; they forsook his house as soon as their governor was out of sight. The same verb was later cried from a cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1; Mark 15:34): the Son was forsaken so that God would never forsake those who trust him.

For they were considered reliable. Nehemiah does not only rebuke: he sets the Levites back in their stations, and the tithes come in. His treasurers were “considered reliable”, in Hebrew “faithful”, the word used of Abraham’s heart (9:8). Money for God’s work is to be handled by people who can be trusted: “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2).

For us. God’s house today is his people (Ephesians 2:21–22), and it is forsaken in the same quiet ways: drifting from the gathering (Hebrews 10:25), and leaving those who serve it unprovided for (Galatians 6:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and do not wipe out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God and for his service.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah asks God to remember his service and not wipe it from his record, though the people had so quickly undone it.

Do not wipe out my good deeds. Wipe out recalls his prayer in chapter 4: “let not their sin be blotted out from your sight” (4:5). There he asked God not to blot out his enemies’ sins; here, not to blot out his own good deeds. He is not claiming to have earned heaven (see v. 22), but asking that his service would not be lost from God’s record.

The gospel’s answer. Every believer who has watched years of work unravel knows this prayer, and the gospel answers it beyond Nehemiah’s hope: God blots out, not our good deeds, but our sins. “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins” (Isaiah 43:25). The record of debt against us is cancelled, “nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14), and of the one who belongs to Christ he says, “I will never blot his name out of the book of life” (Revelation 3:5).

The longing to be remembered. Almost everyone wants to be remembered: a name on a building, a body of work, children who speak well of us. Where belief in a life beyond this one has faded, legacy has to carry the weight heaven once carried, and it is not strong enough. Reputations are revised, buildings renamed, and within a few generations nearly all of us will be names nobody can place: “There is no remembrance of former things” (Ecclesiastes 1:11; see the note on Ecclesiastes 1:2–3). The hunger is not foolish; we were made for something that lasts. The mistake is to look for it in the memory of people as forgetful and mortal as we are. Nehemiah took his work to the one Memory that does not fail. And God does more than keep a record of what his people did: he keeps them, by name, in the Lamb’s book of life, and the One who remembers them is the One who was forsaken so that they would never be forgotten.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — To Keep the Sabbath Day Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day God gave for rest and worship had become market day in Jerusalem, and Nehemiah treats it as the sin that once burned the city. He finds wine pressed, grain loaded and fish sold on the Sabbath, in Jerusalem itself, against the covenant just signed (vv. 15–16). He reminds the nobles that their fathers did this and the city was destroyed (vv. 17–18). He shuts the gates before the Sabbath, posts guards, and threatens the traders camped outside the wall until they stop coming (vv. 19–21). Then he sets purified Levites at the gates, and asks to be remembered and spared by God’s great steadfast love (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The governor who asks to be remembered asks, in the same breath, to be spared.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days I saw in Judah people treading winepresses on the Sabbath, and bringing in heaps of grain and loading them on donkeys, and also wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of loads, which they brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. And I warned them on the day when they sold food. Tyrians also, who lived in the city, brought in fish and all kinds of goods and sold them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah, in Jerusalem itself! Then I confronted the nobles of Judah and said to them, "What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day? Did not your fathers act in this way, and did not our God bring all this disaster on us and on this city? Now you are bringing more wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah found Judah working and Jerusalem trading on the Sabbath, against the covenant just signed, and warned the nobles that this was the very sin that had brought the city to ruin.

In Jerusalem itself! Grapes were trodden in the winepresses, donkeys loaded, and merchants from Tyre sold fish to the people of Judah. The exclamation is Nehemiah’s own. The covenant had said, “we will not buy from them on the Sabbath” (10:31). The fish stalls were open.

Did not your fathers act in this way? Jeremiah had stood at these gates and said, “do not bear a burden on the Sabbath day or bring it in by the gates of Jerusalem”, and warned, “I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 17:21, 27). They carried their loads all the same, and the gates were burned: the news that broke Nehemiah’s heart in Susa (1:3). Little more than a decade after the new gates were hung, loaded donkeys were walking through them on the Sabbath. Nehemiah enforced the day as governor of a people under the law of Moses, where the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant and breaking it a crime (Exodus 31:13–14).

The rest the day pictured. The New Testament calls Sabbaths “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). The rest is found in him: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28); “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9).

A Christian on Sunday. A Christian who must work or shop on a Sunday is not breaking God’s law. But Nehemiah’s grief still teaches: a people who let trade swallow every day of the week soon have no time left for God, and a Lord’s Day guarded for worship and rest is a gift from the One who has given us rest, not a burden.

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath bind Christians today? Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession of Faith and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment, and keep it with a seriousness every Christian can admire; Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and the Lord’s Day, the day of his resurrection, is a gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy and wisdom, not a binding law with rules about work; no one may bind another’s conscience about days (Romans 14:5). Faithful Christians can differ here as brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as it began to grow dark at the gates of Jerusalem before the Sabbath, I commanded that the doors should be shut and gave orders that they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. And I stationed some of my servants at the gates, that no load might be brought in on the Sabbath day. Then the merchants and sellers of all kinds of wares lodged outside Jerusalem once or twice. But I warned them and said to them, "Why do you lodge outside the wall? If you do so again, I will lay hands on you." From that time on they did not come on the Sabbath. Then I commanded the Levites that they should purify themselves and come and guard the gates, to keep the Sabbath day holy. Remember this also in my favor, O my God, and spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah shut the gates for the Sabbath, drove off the traders and set Levites to guard the day, then asked God to remember him and to spare him by the greatness of his steadfast love.

I commanded that the doors should be shut. The doors he had hung (7:1) to keep out Sanballat are now shut to keep the Sabbath: the wall has become a servant of holiness. When the merchants camped outside it, he threatened them, and they stopped coming. Then he replaced his own servants at the gates with purified Levites, so that guarding the day was itself an act of worship.

The key to the remember-me prayers. In the sentence in which he asks God to remember his service, he asks to be spared, and grounds it in God’s hesed, his steadfast love. The man who kept the Sabbath knew he still needed mercy. So do we: none of us has kept God’s law perfectly, but Christ obeyed perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). A Christian can pray both halves of Nehemiah’s sentence: Lord, remember what I have done for you; and Lord, spare me, not because of it, but because of your love.

What steadfast love means. Hesed is not a passing feeling but love that has bound itself by a promise and keeps faith when the other side has not. Nehemiah had come back to find the covenant his people sealed with their own names broken clause after clause (10:30–39). If God’s love were only a reward for faithfulness, there would be nothing left to plead. But “the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end” (Lamentations 3:22). And that love has a face: on the night his friends would all desert him, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). So when you have let God down again, do not bargain with him; pray Nehemiah’s words, and then show the same love to someone who has not kept faith with you. See also Steadfast Love in the Theological Dictionary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Remember Me, O My God, for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Marriages that drew Judah away from God threatened its children, its faith and even its priesthood, and Nehemiah confronts them. Men had married women of Ashdod, Ammon and Moab, and half their children could not speak the language of Judah (vv. 23–24). Nehemiah rebukes them fiercely, makes them swear an oath for the future, and reminds them that such marriages led even Solomon into sin (vv. 25–27). A grandson of the high priest had married Sanballat’s daughter, so Nehemiah drives him away and asks God to remember those who defiled the priesthood (vv. 28–29). He sets the priests and Levites in order, provides for the altar, and closes his book with a prayer: “Remember me, O my God, for good” (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends with a prayer, not a triumph. The man who rebuilt the wall could not rebuild a heart, and he knew it, so his last words ask God to remember him, the prayer Jesus answered for a dying thief (Luke 23:43; see on v. 31).

verseByVerse.quote: In those days also I saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. And half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod, and they could not speak the language of Judah, but only the language of each people. And I confronted them and cursed them and beat some of them and pulled out their hair. And I made them take an oath in the name of God, saying, "You shall not give your daughters to their sons, or take their daughters for your sons or for yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men of Judah had married women of peoples who served other gods, and their children could no longer speak the language in which God’s law was read; Nehemiah confronted them fiercely and made them swear not to arrange such marriages again.

They could not speak the language of Judah. At the Water Gate the law was read “so that the people understood the reading” (8:8); these children could not have understood a word of it, nor followed the psalms or the prayers. It is a warning to every Christian home: children learn to speak of, and to love, what they hear loved at home.

I confronted them and cursed them. The record is honest about Nehemiah’s methods. Ezra, faced with the same sin, pulled out his own hair (Ezra 9:3); Nehemiah pulled out theirs. Unlike Ezra (Ezra 10), he does not break up these marriages: the oath, repeating the people’s own promise (10:30), concerns marriages still to come.

What it does not mean. Nehemiah’s blows were the act of a governor under Israel’s law, not a pattern for church leaders: Christ’s servant “must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone… correcting his opponents with gentleness” (2 Timothy 2:24–25). No husband, parent or pastor may use this verse to excuse striking anyone.

Is this about race? No. The danger was that the children could not hear the law, and that foreign wives drew men to their gods (v. 26); Ruth the Moabite was welcomed by faith. The Christian rule is marriage “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39), and for a Christian already married to an unbeliever Paul’s word stands: “he should not divorce her” (1 Corinthians 7:12).

Uncertain wording. “The language of Judah” is Hebrew (as in 2 Kings 18:26). What “the language of Ashdod” was is not known: the old Philistine tongue had probably died out long before, so it may have been a local dialect of Aramaic or of the coastal Canaanite languages. Either way, these children could not understand the language of God’s law and worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Did not Solomon king of Israel sin on account of such women? Among the many nations there was no king like him, and he was beloved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Nevertheless, foreign women made even him to sin. Shall we then listen to you and do all this great evil and act treacherously against our God by marrying foreign women?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Solomon, the wisest and most blessed king Israel ever had, was led into idolatry by foreign wives, no one in Jerusalem could think himself safe.

Did not Solomon king of Israel sin? Nehemiah argues from the best example Israel had. “Beloved by his God”: at his birth God had named Solomon Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD (2 Samuel 12:25). Yet his wives turned his heart, and he built high places “for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites, on the mountain east of Jerusalem” (1 Kings 11:7): Moab and Ammon, the very peoples of verse 23. No one is too wise or too mature to be drawn away by those closest to him, and whom we marry shapes whom we worship.

Act treacherously against our God. Act treacherously is the Hebrew word translated unfaithful in Nehemiah’s first prayer: “If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you” (1:8). The sin that had once ended in exile was being committed again inside the rebuilt wall.

Something greater than Solomon. Jesus said, “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Solomon’s brides drew his heart away from God; Christ’s heart never turned, and he gave himself up for his bride to make her holy (Ephesians 5:25–27).

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the sons of Jehoiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was the son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite. Therefore I chased him from me. Remember them, O my God, because they have desecrated the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the high priest’s family had married into Sanballat’s, so Nehemiah drove the offender away and asked God to remember those who had defiled the priesthood.

The son-in-law of Sanballat. Sanballat, who had jeered at the Jews and plotted against their governor, had married his daughter into the high priest’s own family. The law required the high priest to marry “a virgin of his own people” (Leviticus 21:14), and this was a grandson who might one day hold that office. The enemy who could not get over the wall had married into the priesthood. (The Jewish historian Josephus tells of a priest who married Sanballat’s daughter and served the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim, though he dates it a century later; many think it is a garbled memory of this event.)

Remember them, O my God. This prayer is “remember them”, not “remember me”: Nehemiah hands the guilty to God’s justice. Malachi, who seems to have preached at about this time, said the same to the priests: “You have corrupted the covenant of Levi” (Malachi 2:8).

A Priest who cannot fail. The priesthood of Aaron was failing from the top. It needed “such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26), whose covenant could not be corrupted, and whose bride, the church, would be made clean by his own blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus I cleansed them from everything foreign, and I established the duties of the priests and Levites, each in his work; and I provided for the wood offering at appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nehemiah’s account ends not with the wall but with firewood and firstfruits, quiet provision for God’s worship, and a last prayer to be remembered for good.

The wood offering and the firstfruits. Having set the priests and Levites back in their duties, he sums up a life’s work with firewood and firstfruits: the wood offering arranged by lot (10:34), so that the fire on the altar would never go out, and the first of the harvest brought to God. Not the wall, not the fifty-two days, not the king’s favour. He had learned what matters.

Remember me, O my God, for good. Good is the word that ran through chapter 2, where the good hand of God was on him and the people strengthened their hands for the good work (2:8, 18). The reforms he had made once he had to make again, so he left the final verdict on his work with God.

Jesus, remember me. Four and a half centuries later, outside the walls of this same city, a dying thief prayed almost the same prayer: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” He was answered at once: “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). The King on that cross remembers everyone who asks, and brings them where the wall never needs rebuilding and nothing unclean gets in. “I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12). So they are remembered for good, and their sins are forgotten.

13.theology:
Every promise of chapter 10 (marriages, Sabbath, tithes, the house of God) is found broken. The law was good and the covenant sincere, but the heart was unchanged. Nehemiah could reform a city, but not write the law on a heart. That needs the new covenant (Jer 31:33), in which God puts his Spirit within his people and causes them to walk in his ways (Ezek 36:27), and says, I will remember their sins no more (Heb 8:12).

His three prayers to be remembered (vv. 14, 22, 31) rest on God’s steadfast love, not on Nehemiah’s own record (v. 22), and their answer is the crucified King who remembered a dying thief.
13.examples:
The chapter lists promise after promise let slip. The law against Ammonites was read while an Ammonite was living in the temple, in a storeroom emptied of the Levites' food to make room for his furniture. The singers whose joy had been heard far away were back in their fields, fish was sold on the Sabbath in Jerusalem itself, and Sanballat's daughter had married into the high priest's family.

Against all that, Nehemiah's last recorded acts were humble ones, providing firewood and firstfruits, and his last words were a prayer: Remember me, O my God, for good.

keyVerse.quote: Remember this also in my favor, O my God, and spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love.
keyVerse.note: In the chapter where nearly every promise of the covenant is found broken, Nehemiah asks God to remember his service and, in the same breath, to spare him by the greatness of his love. This shows what all his “remember me” prayers rest on: not his record but God’s steadfast love. It is the prayer of every believer who has served God and still needs mercy, and in Christ it is always answered.

13.reflection:
Within a few years of signing the covenant (10:30–39), the people had let slip their promises about God’s house, the Sabbath and marriage. Why do good resolutions so often fade once the pressure is off? Where have your own first promises to God quietly slipped?

Tobiah got into the temple through a family connection, not an attack (vv. 4–5), and Solomon was drawn away by those he loved (v. 26). Why are the relationships closest to us often the greatest danger to our faithfulness? How can we love people well without letting them pull us away from Christ?

Nehemiah asked, “Why is the house of God forsaken?” (v. 11) when the Levites were unpaid and the singers back in their fields. What might it look like today for a church, or a Christian, to forsake the house of God? What would putting it right involve?

Nehemiah asked God to remember his service, yet in the same breath to “spare me according to the greatness of your steadfast love” (v. 22). How does the gospel let us pray both halves of that prayer? How does the thief’s prayer, “Jesus, remember me” (Luke 23:42), complete it?
